Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.

For a code with a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $C$ be its finite
crossing set, $D$ its darts, $\alpha$ its fixed-point-free edge-pairing
involution, $\sigma$ its clockwise crossing rotation, and
$\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ its face permutation. A **spherical realization**
means a polygonal embedding on the oriented sphere whose vertex rotations and
edge pairings are exactly $\sigma$ and $\alpha$; its faces are the cycles of
$\phi$. If every crossing has four darts with the prescribed opposite
over/under pairs, arrows, and sign-consistent cyclic order, then such a
realization exists if and only if $V-E+F=2$, where $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and
$F$ is the number of cycles of $\phi$. Choosing one face as the outer face
and deleting a point in it gives the corresponding plane realization. The
crossingless one-component code is the single circle and is handled
separately.

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or
oriented planar-diagram code in the conventions of this page. The crossing
count $c$ is a nonnegative integer. When $c>0$, the code includes the finite
crossing labels, edge-end incidences, strand arrows, over/under data, crossing
signs, and a distinguished outer face. When $c=0$, the only admissible input
for this procedure is the one-component crossingless code specified in the
code definition.

**Output:** Either `Invalid(reason, witness)`, where `reason` is the first
failed check below and `witness` identifies the offending field, label, or
crossing, or `Valid(diagram, components, faces, outerFace)`. Here `diagram` is
a finite gluing record consisting of one crossing disk per vertex, one
rectangular edge band for each pair of darts under $\alpha$, and one cap disk
per cycle of the face permutation. Each band is attached at its recorded dart ports, and each
crossing disk records its clockwise order, strand orientations, over/under
pair, and sign. `components` lists the oriented link cycles, `faces` lists the
face-permutation cycles, and `outerFace` is the selected cycle. The gluing
record represents a polygonal spherical diagram; deleting a point in its
selected face gives the plane model. The procedure tests realizability of
this code only; it does not compare the represented link with another code.

**Instructions:**

1. Read the tag and crossing count. If the tag is unknown or $c$ is not a
   nonnegative integer, return `invalid-header` with that field.

2. If $c=0$, accept only one empty Gauss component word, the empty signed-DT
   code, or the single `Loop[1]` PD record, each with exactly one orientation
   marker, `ccw` or `cw`. Return
   `invalid-crossingless-code` otherwise. For an accepted input return the
   standard circle with the marked orientation, one component, its two sphere
   faces, and the `outside` face selector. Do not run crossing-graph tests.

3. For a Gauss code with $c>0$, reject an empty component word. Check that
   every label lies in $\{1,\ldots,c\}$, occurs exactly twice in total, and
   occurs once with each over/under sign. Check that its separate crossing-sign
   vector has length $c$ and entries in $\{+1,-1\}$. Return
   `invalid-crossing-label` for the first out-of-range label,
   `invalid-crossing-visit-count` with the label and its over/under counts for
   any visit failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position. Turn successive visits on each component word into directed edge
   labels, including each cyclic last-to-first edge, numbering these segments
   in the listed component order and then in traversal order, and form the
   crossing records from the over/under visits and the stored crossing signs.

4. For a signed DT code, check that its pairing list and sign vector each have
   length $c$, each pairing value has absolute value in
   $\{2,4,\ldots,2c\}$, every such absolute value occurs once, and every sign
   is $+1$ or $-1$. Return `invalid-dt-pairing` with the first bad index for a
   pairing failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position for a sign failure. The odd visit $2j-1$ is crossing $j$; if
   $d_j>0$ it is the over-visit and if $d_j<0$ it is the under-visit. At the
   even visit paired with $2j-1$, use crossing label $j$ and the opposite
   over/under sign. Decode visits in order $1,\ldots,2c$ into the corresponding
   signed Gauss word and continue with step 3.

5. For a PD code, check that there are exactly $c$ crossing records and four
   dart occurrences at each record. Return `invalid-crossing-record` with the
   first bad record otherwise. Use the edge labels and arrows in the records
   to form the paired-dart involution, crossing rotations, over/under pairs,
   and crossing signs.

6. In every nonempty encoding, check that each edge label has exactly two
   occurrences, one incoming and one outgoing; each crossing has exactly four
   incident darts; the opposite pairs are exactly one over-strand and one
   under-strand; each strand has one incoming and one outgoing end; and the
   cyclic order matches the stored crossing sign. Return, in that order,
   `invalid-edge-incidence`, `invalid-crossing-valence`,
   `invalid-over-under-pair`, `invalid-strand-orientation`, or
   `invalid-crossing-sign-order`, with the first offending label or crossing.

7. Starting at each as-yet unvisited outgoing dart, cross its edge by $\alpha$
   to the incoming dart at the other endpoint and continue through the
   opposite dart of that same strand. Stop only when the starting outgoing
   dart is reached. If an end is missing, a dart repeats before that return, or
   any dart remains uncovered after all cycles are traced, return
   `invalid-component-closure` with the first such dart. Then test the crossing
   graph for connectedness; if it is disconnected, return
   `disconnected-crossing-graph`.

8. Compute $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ on all darts by finite table lookup and
   list its cycles. Put $V=c$, $E=|D|/2$, and $F=$ the number of cycles. If
   $V-E+F\ne2$, return `non-spherical-face-count` with $(V,E,F)$. If the
   supplied outer-face identifier is not one of these cycles, return
   `invalid-outer-face` with that identifier.

9. For a passing code, choose the lexicographically first spanning tree in the
   finite edge ordering. Root it at the least crossing label and attach its
   tree bands in increasing distance from that root, using the recorded cyclic
   gaps. Then attach the remaining edge bands in increasing edge-label order.
   Use the distinguished face for the plane projection, replace each crossing
   disk by its prescribed transverse crossing, attach one cap disk along each
   face cycle, and lift the over-strand above the under-strand. Return this
   finite gluing record, the directed components, the face cycles, and the
   outer-face identifier.

For every finite input in the three code formats, the validation and
reconstruction procedure terminates. It returns an invalid-code reason
exactly when the first failed syntax, incidence, orientation, component,
connectedness, face-count, or outer-face condition in its stated order occurs;
otherwise it returns the crossing-disk/edge-band model of the represented
oriented diagram, its oriented components, its face cycles, and its selected
outer face.

derivations.claim: If $n>0$, there are $4n$ darts and $2n$ paired edges. The connected crossing graph has $V=n$, $E=2n$, and hence $F=2-V+E=n+2$ faces by [F2]. The sum of face-boundary port occurrences, counted with multiplicity, is $2E=4n$. Choose disjoint small disks around the graph vertices and disjoint narrow rectangular bands along its edges, attached in the prescribed cyclic order. Their union $N(G)$ is a connected planar subsurface of the sphere; each boundary component is one face cycle, and the closure of each complementary component is a disk. The total number of vertex-disk ports, band sides and boundary occurrences is bounded by a universal constant times $n$.

Triangulate each vertex disk and edge band by fixed templates. Subdivide every side occurrence on each complementary face boundary circle by a fixed number of new vertices and cone the resulting simple polygon to one interior vertex. Each face of boundary length $d$ contributes at most $c_0d$ triangles for a fixed $c_0$, and $\sum d=O(n)$ by step 1.1. Since the face boundary circles of $N(G)$ are embedded circles with port occurrences kept distinct, these are regular disk triangulations; matching subdivisions along shared ports and one fixed barycentric subdivision give a genuine finite simplicial triangulation of the projection sphere with $O(n)$ triangles.

Take the product of this triangulated sphere with an interval. Each triangular prism is split into three tetrahedra by the fixed staircase subdivision; cap the two ends by fixed triangulated balls to obtain a triangulated $S^3$ with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. In each crossing disk, place the over- and under-strand arcs at distinct interval heights and connect each pair of opposite ports; along each edge band connect its end ports by a linear arc whose height interpolates between the endpoint heights. In a crossing block the two arcs are disjoint because their heights differ; interiors of distinct edge blocks are disjoint, and every edge arc joins only its designated crossing ports. A fixed subdivision of each crossing and edge block makes these finitely many local arc templates subcomplexes. Their number per block is bounded independently of $n$, so the resulting polygonal knot $P$ lies in the 1-skeleton and has exactly the given projection and over/under data by [F4].

Around each vertex and edge of the 1-subcomplex $P$, take the fixed ball and tube blocks from the definition of a good exterior triangulation. Choose a normal 2-frame at one point, extend it across the finitely many edge and vertex blocks, and adjust the final frame along the last edge by a path of rotations in $SO(2)$ to agree with the initial frame. Thus their union is the product $S^1\times D^2$, a solid torus with triangulated boundary. The number of blocks and tetrahedra per block is constant, so removing its interior leaves a compact triangulated exterior with $O(n)$ tetrahedra. At an interior point of a chosen knot edge, the fixed local tube template has a meridian circle using a fixed number of boundary edges; mark that path.

If $n=0$, use the standard genus-one product decomposition of $S^3$ into two solid tori and the fixed product triangulation of the exterior solid torus as a triangle times a three-edge circle. Splitting its three triangular prisms into three tetrahedra each and marking the three-edge fibre meridian gives a fixed-size model. Increasing $C$ to dominate this model and all fixed local template constants in steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 yields both stated $C(n+1)$ bounds. All code-dependent choices use the finite label and port order, so the construction is explicit.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied product tubular embedding $\Phi:S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}\to S^3$. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside this tube and a smooth rounding $K'$ of $P$ such that $K'$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$ by an isotopy supported in the tube. If $K$ is supplied with a finite regular projection diagram $D$, the polygonal approximation and rounding can be chosen to have the same crossing code as $D$. A homeomorphism supported in the larger tube carries $P$ to $K'$, preserves the boundary torus of the radius-$\epsilon$ tube, and sends each marked fibre meridian to itself up to orientation. Conversely, every polygonal knot $P$ with a finite product regular neighborhood can be rounded in pairwise disjoint vertex balls to a smooth knot $P^\sharp$; a homeomorphism supported in those balls carries its compact exterior and marked meridian to those of $P^\sharp$. If a regular projection diagram is supplied, the rounding balls can be chosen away from crossing charts, so the crossing code is unchanged. These clauses compare smooth knot type through smooth knots and polygonal exterior models through homeomorphisms; they do not treat a nonsmooth polygonal curve as a smooth isotopy slice.

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or oriented planar-diagram code in the code conventions of the planar-code definition, and a mode, either **Haken** or **JT**.

**Output:** The first validation error with its witness; **not-a-knot** for a valid code with more than one component; **disk-certificate** with a normal-coordinate vector and its finite witness data; or **no-candidate** after the selected search is exhausted.

**Procedure:**

1. Run the planar-code validation procedure. Return its first invalid result if validation fails. If the validated code represents more than one component, return **not-a-knot**.
2. Let $n$ be its crossing count. Construct the good triangulated exterior $E$ with $t\le C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and the marked original meridian path.
3. In Haken mode, enumerate all vectors $v\in\mathbb Z^{7t}$ with $0\le v_i\le t2^{7t+2}$ in lexicographic order. Retain a vector only if it satisfies all matching equations and quadrilateral restrictions and is fundamental. Fundamentalness supplies connectedness. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first vector passing these tests; return **no-candidate** after the finite box is exhausted.
4. In JT mode, let $A$ be the integer matching matrix and put $m=7t$. Enumerate all subsets $Z\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in lexicographic order. For each $Z$, append the equations $v_i=0$ for $i\in Z$ to $Av=0$. If the combined matrix has rank $m-1$ and its one-dimensional kernel contains a nonzero nonnegative vector, compute the unique relatively prime nonnegative integer generator $v$ of that ray. Require that its positive-coordinate support be exactly the complement of $Z$; this visits each ray once, at its exact zero-coordinate support. Discard vectors that violate the quadrilateral restriction. A primitive generator on an extreme ray is fundamental, so its surface is connected. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first passing vector; return **no-candidate** after all subsets have been processed.

The candidate tests use the boundary arcs and Euler-characteristic data computed from the compressed normal coordinates. No correctness or complexity assertion is part of this algorithm definition.

derivations.claim: The code and each encoded field are finite, so the planar-code validation procedure terminates. Its prescribed return is passed through unchanged; a valid multi-component code returns **not-a-knot** immediately. For a valid one-component code, the good exterior triangulation is a finite combinatorial output by [F1].

In Haken mode the integer bound $B=t2^{7t+2}$ is finite and nonnegative, so the lexicographic box contains exactly $(B+1)^{7t}$ vectors. Each matching, quadrilateral, and disk test scans finite coordinates and faces. Fundamentalness is decided by checking every coordinatewise split $v=x+(v-x)$; there are at most $\prod_i(v_i+1)$ such splits, each tested by finitely many integer comparisons. Therefore every loop and the complete Haken search terminate.

In JT mode there are exactly $2^{7t}$ subsets $Z$. For each, computing the rank and, when the nullity is one, an integer kernel generator by exact finite matrix operations terminates. Checking admissibility, deduplicating, and testing the boundary data are finite scans. Thus the complete JT search terminates.

The algorithm's ordered validation branch returns its first invalid result; its component branch returns **not-a-knot** exactly for a valid multi-component input. In either one-component mode, all candidates are drawn from the stated finite enumeration and a return of **no-candidate** occurs only after that enumeration ends. Steps 1.1–1.3 prove the stated termination and output form.

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or oriented planar-diagram code in the code conventions of the planar-code definition, and a mode, either **Haken** or **JT**.

**Output:** The first validation error with its witness; **not-a-knot** for a valid code with more than one component; **disk-certificate** with a normal-coordinate vector and its finite witness data; or **no-candidate** after the selected search is exhausted.

**Procedure:**

1. Run the planar-code validation procedure. Return its first invalid result if validation fails. If the validated code represents more than one component, return **not-a-knot**.
2. Let $n$ be its crossing count. Construct the good triangulated exterior $E$ with $t\le C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and the marked original meridian path.
3. In Haken mode, enumerate all vectors $v\in\mathbb Z^{7t}$ with $0\le v_i\le t2^{7t+2}$ in lexicographic order. Retain a vector only if it satisfies all matching equations and quadrilateral restrictions and is fundamental. Fundamentalness supplies connectedness. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first vector passing these tests; return **no-candidate** after the finite box is exhausted.
4. In JT mode, let $A$ be the integer matching matrix and put $m=7t$. Enumerate all subsets $Z\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ in lexicographic order. For each $Z$, append the equations $v_i=0$ for $i\in Z$ to $Av=0$. If the combined matrix has rank $m-1$ and its one-dimensional kernel contains a nonzero nonnegative vector, compute the unique relatively prime nonnegative integer generator $v$ of that ray. Require that its positive-coordinate support be exactly the complement of $Z$; this visits each ray once, at its exact zero-coordinate support. Discard vectors that violate the quadrilateral restriction. A primitive generator on an extreme ray is fundamental, so its surface is connected. Compute nonempty-boundary, Euler-characteristic, and mod-two meridian-intersection data from the compressed coordinates, without expanding the surface. Return **disk-certificate** at the first passing vector; return **no-candidate** after all subsets have been processed.

The candidate tests use the boundary arcs and Euler-characteristic data computed from the compressed normal coordinates. No correctness or complexity assertion is part of this algorithm definition.
Every nonempty fundamental normal surface in a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold is connected.

Let $E$ be a triangulated compact exterior of a smooth knot with peripheral torus $T$ and a marked simple fibre meridian $\mu$ in the boundary triangulation. For an admissible normal-coordinate vector $v$ and its associated normal surface $S$, the following tests hold exactly when $S$ is a connected properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in $T$: (i) $S$ is connected; (ii) $\partial S\ne\varnothing$; (iii) $\chi(S)=1$; and (iv) $\partial S$ has odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$. If $v$ is fundamental, connectedness follows from fundamentalness.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the returned vector satisfies the candidate tests in [F2], including normal matching and quadrilateral admissibility.
By [F2], the returned fundamental normal surface is connected. The remaining tests in [F1], together with [F3], identify it as a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary.

Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

Let $M$ be a compact triangulated piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with nonempty boundary and with no embedded projective plane. If $M$ contains a properly embedded disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then $M$ contains such a disk that is a fundamental normal surface.

Let $E$ be a triangulated compact exterior of a smooth knot with peripheral torus $T$ and a marked simple fibre meridian $\mu$ in the boundary triangulation. For an admissible normal-coordinate vector $v$ and its associated normal surface $S$, the following tests hold exactly when $S$ is a connected properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in $T$: (i) $S$ is connected; (ii) $\partial S\ne\varnothing$; (iii) $\chi(S)=1$; and (iv) $\partial S$ has odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$. No closed nonorientable piecewise-linear surface embeds in the standard oriented piecewise-linear three-sphere $S^3$.

derivations.claim: If the Haken search accepts, [F1] says the vector is admissible and passes the candidate tests. By [F4], its normal surface is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary.

Conversely, suppose $E$ contains such a disk. Any embedded projective plane in $E$ would also be a closed nonorientable PL surface in $S^3$, contradicting [F5]. The exterior has nonempty boundary by its construction. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold, and [F3] gives a fundamental normal disk $S$ with essential boundary. Let $v(S)$ be its normal-coordinate vector. By [F2], each coordinate is at most $t2^{7t+2}$, so the Haken box enumerates $v(S)$. Its boundary is nonempty, it is connected by fundamentalness, its Euler characteristic is one, and its boundary has odd meridian intersection by [F4]. Therefore the algorithm accepts no later than when it reaches $v(S)$.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove that acceptance is equivalent to existence of an essential disk. If the finite search exhausts without acceptance, step 1.2 shows no such disk can exist.

derivations.claim: If the JT search accepts, its vector is an admissible normal vector passing the candidate tests by [F1]. The vector is primitive on an extreme ray, hence fundamental: a sum of two nonzero cone vectors on an extreme ray would have each summand on that ray, and the primitive integer generator cannot split into two positive integer multiples. By [F4], the associated surface is a properly embedded disk with essential boundary.

If $E$ contains an essential disk, [F3] supplies such a disk whose vector lies on a primitive extreme ray. By [F2], each coordinate is at most $2^{7t-1}$ and therefore has at most $7t$ bits. Let $Z$ be exactly the set of zero coordinates of this vector. The support loop in [F1] examines this subset, the combined matrix has nullity one, and its kernel generator is the stated vector. The vector is admissible and its normal disk passes the remaining tests by [F4], so the JT search accepts.

There are $2^{7t}$ coordinate supports, so [F1] examines at most that many candidates and stores no list of prior rays because each ray is found at its unique exact zero support. Each candidate has $7t$ coordinates of $O(t)$ bits by [F2]. The matching and active-coordinate matrix has $O(t)$ rows and columns with entries in $\{0,1,-1\}$. Implement its rank, independent-row and cofactor-kernel calculations by [F5]. That supplier stores one prime-field residue matrix with $O(\log(t+2))$-bit entries, streams its primes and determinant residues, stops reconstruction as soon as the modulus exceeds twice the integer determinant bound, and reuses the matrix space for successive cofactors. Thus these exact calculations take polynomial bit time and $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ workspace without retaining a matrix of large exact elimination fractions. The candidate, support counter and finite boundary linear-form tests fit within the same bound.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove acceptance exactly when an essential disk exists. Step 2.1 proves the stated candidate, bit-length and space bounds.

citations.quote: For every finite input code and either selected mode, the Haken–Jaco–Tollefson procedure terminates. It returns the prescribed first validation error for an invalid code, returns **not-a-knot** for a valid multi-component code, and for a valid one-component knot code returns either a finite normal-coordinate disk-candidate certificate or **no-candidate** after exhaustive search.

For a valid one-component knot code, the Haken finite-box search accepts if and only if the triangulated exterior contains a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. On acceptance it returns a normal-coordinate vector for such a disk; after exhaustive rejection, no such disk exists.

For a valid one-component knot code, the JT primitive extreme-ray search accepts if and only if the triangulated exterior contains a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. It examines at most $2^{7t}$ support subsets for a $t$-tetrahedron exterior, each candidate coordinate has $O(t)$ bits, and its sequential Turing space is $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ bits.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied product tubular neighborhood, and let $E_K$ be its compact exterior with peripheral torus $T_K$, fibre meridian $\mu$, and the unique degree-one generator $[\lambda]$ of the kernel of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ supplied by the product-tube Mayer–Vietoris calculation. Then $K$ is ambient isotopic in the smooth category to the standard unknot if and only if $E_K$ contains a properly embedded piecewise-linear disk $D$ whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $T_K$. Every such disk has $[\partial D]=[\lambda]$ or $-[\lambda]$ and has odd mod-two intersection with the original marked meridian $\mu$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite regular projection diagram $D$ having $n$ crossings and a supplied product tube. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside that tube with the same crossing code as $D$ and a smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ of $P$ such that $K^\sharp$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$. The compact exterior of this same $P$ has a good triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a marked path for the original meridian with at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges, for one universal constant $C$. The peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism transfers this model to $K^\sharp$.

Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let $A$ be an integer matrix with at most $n$ rows and at most $n$ columns, all entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Deterministic algorithms compute its rational rank and an independent set of original rows in time polynomial in $n$ and sequential Turing workspace $O(n^2\log(n+2))$ bits. The determinant of any specified square submatrix is computable within the same bounds. If $A$ has $b\ge1$ columns and rational rank $b-1$, a primitive integer generator of its one-dimensional rational kernel is computable within those bounds, with either choice of its overall sign. The zero-row and zero-column matrices and the $0\times0$ determinant convention are included.

derivations.claim: The given countable-choice hypothesis [A1] supplies the choice assumption in [F5]. That item constructs a finite good exterior triangulation with $t\le C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a marked original meridian; the zero-crossing case uses its fixed product model. By [F1], validation and either search mode terminate.

For Haken mode, the box has $(t2^{7t+2}+1)^{7t}=2^{O(t^2)}$ vectors. Testing fundamentalness checks at most the same number of coordinatewise decompositions per vector, so the squared count remains $2^{O(t^2)}$; all tests on each compressed vector take polynomial time. Store only the current vector, one decomposition vector, counters and the matching matrix, using $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ bits.

For JT mode, the support enumeration has at most $2^{7t}$ subsets. Use the streamed modular rank/kernel implementation [F7], whose prime bound and stopping rule give polynomial bit time and $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ workspace for each support. The candidate tests use polynomial time in $t$ and the $O(t)$-bit coordinates from [F6], giving total $2^{O(t)}$ time. The implementation reuses one residue matrix and a bounded CRT accumulator, while the candidate and support counter fit within $O(t^2\log(t+2))$ bits; no list of prior rays is stored because each ray is enumerated at its exact zero support.

In Haken mode, [F2] identifies acceptance exactly with existence of an essential disk in that exterior; by [F4], this is equivalent to the smooth knot being the unknot. In JT mode, the same conclusion follows from [F3] and [F4]. Thus each terminating branch returns the correct decision using the proved Haken and JT existence suppliers.
Substituting $t\le C(n+1)$ in steps 1.2–1.3 yields the stated time and space bounds; the fixed $n=0$ branch is constant size.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a finite regular projection diagram $D$ having $n$ crossings and a supplied product tube. There is a polygonal knot $P$ inside that tube with the same crossing code as $D$ and a smooth rounding $K^\sharp$ of $P$ such that $K^\sharp$ is smoothly ambient isotopic to $K$. The compact exterior of this same $P$ has a good triangulation with at most $C(n+1)$ tetrahedra and a marked path for the original meridian with at most $C(n+1)$ boundary edges, for one universal constant $C$. The peripheral-preserving exterior homeomorphism transfers this model to $K^\sharp$.

Let $T$ be a good triangulation of a knot exterior with $t$ tetrahedra and a marked meridian path in its triangulated boundary torus. A certificate consists of a nonnegative integer vector $v$ with $7t$ binary-encoded coordinates, a set of active matching and zero-coordinate constraints, a nonzero $(7t-1)$-minor witnessing their rank, and the marked boundary data. A deterministic verifier can check the certificate in time polynomial in the certificate bit length. Acceptance verifies that $v$ is a primitive admissible extreme-ray vector of the Haken cone and that its associated normal surface is a properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary. The verifier uses arithmetic on the compressed coordinates and does not expand the normal surface into its potentially exponentially many normal disks.

Let $M$ be a compact triangulated piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with nonempty boundary. If $M$ contains a properly embedded disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then $M$ contains such a disk whose primitive normal-coordinate vector lies on an extreme ray of the Haken cone.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a supplied product tubular neighborhood, and let $E_K$ be its compact exterior with peripheral torus $T_K$, fibre meridian $\mu$, and the unique degree-one generator $[\lambda]$ of the kernel of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ supplied by the product-tube Mayer–Vietoris calculation. Then $K$ is ambient isotopic in the smooth category to the standard unknot if and only if $E_K$ contains a properly embedded piecewise-linear disk $D$ whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $T_K$. Every such disk has $[\partial D]=[\lambda]$ or $-[\lambda]$ and has odd mod-two intersection with the original marked meridian $\mu$.

Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

derivations.claim: The given countable-choice hypothesis [A1] is the choice assumption used by [F1]'s exterior model. Reconstruct $T_D$ and the marked path using its fixed code order and local templates. The verifier does not accept a triangulation supplied by the certificate, so the certificate cannot substitute an unrelated manifold.

If the verifier accepts, [F2] gives an essential disk in the exterior of the represented smooth knot. By [F4], the knot is the unknot. The relative rounding and disk-boundary isotopy in [F4] apply to exactly this compatible exterior model.

Conversely, suppose the knot is the unknot. By [F4], its exterior contains an essential disk. By [F3], there is such a disk represented by a primitive vertex vector $v$. By [F5], each coordinate is at most $2^{7t-1}$ and therefore has $O(t)$ bits; the full vector has $O(t^2)$ bits. The active matching and zero-coordinate rows at this extreme ray have rank $7t-1$, so choose $7t-1$ independent rows and a nonzero square minor. Such a minor exists by the rank definition and has polynomial encoded length. The resulting certificate is accepted by the polynomial verifier [F2]. The primitive vertex-disk theorem [F3] supplies completeness, and the disk criterion [F4] supplies both conversion directions.

Since $t=O(n+1)$ by [F1], the vector, row indices and determinant witness all have polynomial bit length in $n$. The verifier reconstructs $T_D$ in polynomial time and checks matching equations, gcd, rank, boundary, Euler characteristic and meridian parity through compressed arithmetic as in [F2]; it never lists the exponentially many normal disks.

For the prism over $b_0b_1$, write $a_i^0=(a_i,b_0)$ and $a_i^1=(a_i,b_1)$. Use the staircase tetrahedra
$$T_1=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_2^0,a_2^1],\qquad T_2=[a_0^0,a_1^0,a_1^1,a_2^1],\qquad T_3=[a_0^0,a_0^1,a_1^1,a_2^1].$$
Their common faces are triangulated by the same ordered diagonals, so the three tetrahedra form the triangular-prism block; repeating this order on the three-cycle of $S^1$ gives the product triangulation in [F2].

The level disk at the midpoint of the product edge separates the bottom vertices $a_i^0$ from the top vertices $a_i^1$. In $T_1$ it cuts off the single top vertex $a_2^1$, giving one triangle; in $T_2$ it separates the pair $\{a_0^0,a_1^0\}$ from $\{a_1^1,a_2^1\}$, giving one quadrilateral; in $T_3$ it cuts off the single bottom vertex $a_0^0$, giving one triangle. It misses all tetrahedra in the other two prism blocks. Its intersections on shared faces agree because they are the same level section of the product, so the matching equations hold. Only one quadrilateral coordinate is nonzero, so [F1] gives an admissible normal disk vector.

The geometric surface is exactly $D^2\times\{s_*\}$, hence is a connected disk. Its boundary is $\partial D^2\times\{s_*\}$, which is nonempty and has $\chi=1$. The marked meridian $\{a_0\}\times S^1$ passes through exactly one point of this boundary at $(a_0,s_*)$, in the interior of the chosen fiber edge; the intersection is transverse and has parity $1$.
Thus the explicit vector satisfies the matching, quadrilateral, connectedness, boundary, Euler-characteristic and mod-two meridian checks claimed in the statement.

citations.quote: Let $E$ be a triangulated compact exterior of a smooth knot with peripheral torus $T$ and a marked simple fibre meridian $\mu$ in the boundary triangulation. For an admissible normal-coordinate vector $v$ and its associated normal surface $S$, the following tests hold exactly when $S$ is a connected properly embedded disk with non-null-homotopic boundary in $T$: (i) $S$ is connected; (ii) $\partial S\ne\varnothing$; (iii) $\chi(S)=1$; and (iv) $\partial S$ has odd mod-two intersection with $\mu$. If $v$ is fundamental, connectedness follows from fundamentalness.

derivations.claim: The link $Lk_E(v)$ of a boundary vertex in a triangulated $3$-manifold is a closed disk: its local link is a $2$-ball. In each tetrahedron containing $v$ the link meets that tetrahedron in the small triangle parallel to the opposite face; it misses tetrahedra not containing $v$. Across each shared face these triangles have matching normal arcs, so [F1] makes the link a normal surface. Its boundary is $Lk_T(v)$, a simple closed curve in the small boundary-star disk of $v$, hence contractible in $T$. The local half-ball star shows the disk is boundary-parallel.

The link disk is connected, has nonempty boundary, and has Euler characteristic one. Its boundary is null-homotopic, so its projection to the product-circle factor has degree zero. After a transverse PL perturbation, the parity of intersections with a fibre meridian equals the parity of preimages of a regular point under that projection; a lift with zero net degree crosses the level an even number of times. Hence the intersection parity is zero.

The disk therefore passes the first three tests in [F2] but fails the odd-intersection test, so the filter rejects this candidate. This conclusion concerns this boundary-parallel disk only; it does not rule out any other normal essential disk in $E$ and therefore does not classify the knot.

citations.quote:
Let $K$ be finite and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ a whole-star smooth immersion in the
sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong piecewise $C^1$
$\delta$-approximation $g:K'\to\mathbb R^q$, on any finite subdivision $K'$,
is a whole-star immersion. If $f$ is also an embedding, $\delta$ may be chosen
so that $g$ is an embedding. The subdivision need not have a mesh or shape
bound.

Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in
the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh
tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every
positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine
interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise
$C^1$ to $f$.

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the
approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood
of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled
subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and
every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original
simplices is preserved.

There is also a local extension statement: given a finite subcomplex
$A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any
subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a
subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged
outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the
requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the
subdivision of $A$. If $p$ is an affine target map and $p(g)=p(f)$ on $A$, then $p(G)=p(f)$
everywhere; equivalently, the linear part of $p$ annihilates each correction. This last extension does not assert a shape bound on its
coned simplices.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: First restrict the nonsmooth locus to the complement of a protected open neighborhood of the given compact smooth set and a smaller boundary collar. Subdivide along the boundaries of finitely many smaller coordinate neighborhoods as necessary. Compactness and finiteness give positive separation between disjoint closed simplices away from their common stars, and between a sufficiently small replacement neighborhood and the closed complement of the prescribed neighborhood. Thus it suffices to smooth the finitely many unprotected vertices and edge portions inside these neighborhoods. All other points are already in smooth face interiors.

At an unprotected vertex use an ambient smooth chart centered at its image and affine coordinates on its finitely many incident triangles centered at the vertex. Write their common map as $f(x)=A(x)+R(x)$, where $A$ is the piecewise linear differential fan. On a sufficiently small star, $|R(x)|=o(|x|)$ and $\|DR(x)\|=o(1)$, uniformly over those triangles. Let $\eta$ be a radial cutoff equal to one on a smaller star and zero outside a slightly larger star of radius $\epsilon$, with derivative bounded by $C/\epsilon$. Replacing $f$ by $f-\eta R$ changes its derivative by $o(1)$, because $|R|\,|D\eta|=o(\epsilon)/\epsilon=o(1)$. Apply [F1] to keep it an embedding. This makes the surface exactly its linear cone near the vertex, with the original map retained outside the larger star. The vertices have disjoint neighborhoods, so these finite replacements do not interfere. The link of the resulting cone on a small round sphere is a simple closed piecewise smooth curve: the surface vertex link is a circle and the differential fan is injective.

Smooth an open edge portion away from the vertex centers. Its two incident smooth half-surfaces have distinct tangent half-planes meeting along their common edge. In a small tubular coordinate box their union is a graph $z=h(s,u)$ over a plane, with the edge at $u=0$ and $h$ smooth for each sign of $u$. For unit transverse rays $v_+$ and $v_-$ pointing out from the edge into the two half-surfaces, whole-star injectivity gives $v_+\ne v_-$. The linear functional $\ell(w)=\langle v_+-v_-,w\rangle$ has $\ell(v_+)>0$ and $\ell(v_-)<0$. Projection onto the plane consisting of the edge direction and this signed transverse coordinate therefore gives the required graph, and remains regular on a smaller box by continuity. Replace $h$ near $u=0$ by convolution in $(s,u)$, using a cutoff supported in that box and equal to one near a smaller edge core. The new graph is smooth at its core, remains an embedded graph, and agrees with the old surface outside the box. Where the cutoff changes the old graph is already smooth, so the interpolation is smooth there. Use arbitrarily small value errors and the finite separation margins to prevent collisions with the rest of the surface. Covering each remaining compact edge portion by finitely many such boxes and retaining earlier smooth cores completes the open-edge smoothing.

In the linear conical neighborhoods of step 2.1 choose the edge rounding radially: round the finitely many corners of the link curve on the unit sphere in disjoint spherical graph charts, and take rays over this rounded link. A radial cutoff joins this choice to the open-edge graph choices farther out. On the overlap the chosen graph projection is still injective, so graph interpolation joins them without intersections. After this operation the only unsmoothed point in each vertex neighborhood is its center, and on an annulus about that center the surface is $r\gamma(s)$, where $\gamma:S^1\to S^2$ is a smooth embedded circle. These operations are fixed near the protected set.

By [F2], $\gamma$ bounds a smoothly parametrized disk region $e:D^2\to S^2$. The circles $s\mapsto e(\rho s)$, with $\rho$ decreasing from $1$ to a small positive number, give a smooth isotopy of embedded circles. In a small chart about $e(0)$, choose a fixed small $r>0$ and use the expression $E(trs)/t$, continued at $t=0$ by $r\,dE_0(s)$; these circles remain inside that chart and are smooth and embedded for sufficiently small $r$: its derivative is uniformly close to the injective linear map, and projection onto its image plane gives injectivity by integration on segments. Deform the final linear ellipse to a round circle by its positive Gram square root, and carry it back through a spherical chart. This gives an isotopy $\gamma_t$ of smooth embedded spherical circles from $\gamma$ to a small latitude circle. Flatten its time parameter near both endpoints. No extension to a diffeomorphism of $S^2$ or of a three-ball is used.

In a smaller conical annulus replace $r\gamma(s)$ by $r\gamma_{\tau(r)}(s)$, where $\tau$ goes from zero on its outer collar to one on its inner collar. This is an embedded smooth annulus: different radial levels lie on disjoint round spheres, and at each fixed level the curve is embedded; its radial derivative has nonzero radial component, while its circle derivative is tangent to that sphere. Near the inner collar it is a circular cone. Close that cone by a surface of revolution lying inside the inner sphere: in coordinates around its axis, replace the conical graph $z=a\varrho$ near $\varrho=0$ by $z=a\psi(\varrho)$, where $\psi$ is smooth and even near zero, agrees with $\varrho$ near the outer radius and is positive at zero. Choose its modification supported in a much smaller radius so its graph lies strictly inside the inner sphere; a smooth convex rounding of the graph of $|\varrho|$ has these properties. This gives a smooth disk cap, unchanged on the annular seam. The cap replaces a conical disk by a disk with the same boundary, hence preserves the surface's homeomorphism type relative to everything outside the vertex neighborhood.

Apply step 6.1 in each of the disjoint vertex neighborhoods. The result is smooth on the face interiors, the edge cores, the connecting annuli and the caps, with identical maps on open seam collars. It is embedded by the graph, radial-level and separation arguments, and is unchanged on the protected smooth neighborhood. Replacing finitely many disks and edge strips by disks and strips with the same attaching collars gives a homeomorphism from the original surface to the result fixed there. All changes fit inside the prescribed neighborhood by step 1.1.

Finally, a surface PL in the specified compatible triangulation becomes a subcomplex after a common finite subdivision. Each restricted ambient simplex map is smooth and its differential fan is injective on the ambient star, hence on the surface's substar. Thus it has exactly the piecewise smooth whole-star data used in steps 1.1–4.1. The argument requires only this supplied compatibility and the stated countable choice, proving all clauses.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

derivations.claim: After a small smooth perturbation, keep $e$ proper and transverse to $\partial M$ and make it transverse to the finite strata of $h(T)$, avoiding the vertices. Here the elementary finite parameter argument suffices: in each of finitely many ambient chart cores add small coordinate translations multiplied by a bump equal to one on the core. Evaluation on that core is a submersion in the translation parameters, so the regular values of the projection of the corresponding inverse-image stratum give transverse perturbations by [F2]. At boundary points use the tangential chart translations on $\partial M$ and their product extensions in its collar. Choose the finitely many perturbations successively small enough to retain already obtained transversality and the disk's embedding and proper collar. Compact transverse intersections with the edge strata are finite; intersections with face interiors are compact regular arcs and circles after adding those edge endpoints, hence a finite embedded graph. There are no intersections with vertex strata.

Cut the disk along the finite inverse-image graph. Regard repeated slit sides as separate boundary copies before regluing. The pieces are compact smooth surfaces with corners: face-intersection arcs have nonzero differential; at an edge intersection their incident tangent directions are distinct, since the disk plane is transverse to that edge, so the two bounding equations in each sector give a corner chart by the inverse theorem. Supply each common boundary arc with one smooth regular parametrization, subdivided identically on its two copies. These are admissible boundary data in [F2], because the two corner rays are independent. Apply its finite relative whole-star construction to the pieces and reglue their identical boundary subdivisions. This gives a finite piecewise smooth whole-star triangulation of the disk with each simplex mapping into one ambient simplex. The inverse of $h$ on that simplex is smooth up to its indicated faces by the full-rank extension and inverse theorem. Consequently $g=h^{-1}e$ on this finite source complex is piecewise smooth. Its differential fan is injective: the ambient differential fan of $h$ is a homeomorphism onto the tangent half-space or space, and the disk differential is injective, so taking its inverse on the subdivided tangent sectors is injective. Thus $g$ is a whole-star embedding into a Euclidean realization of $|T|$.

Apply the shape-controlled secants of [F1] to $g$. Every refined simplex maps by affine interpolation of its vertex values into the same convex ambient simplex as its original carrier. Adjacent source simplices have identical interpolants on their common face. Thus these secants define a PL map into $|T|$, and sufficiently small strong error makes it an embedding by [F1]. They send boundary into the boundary subcomplex, since all the vertices of a boundary source simplex lie in its one boundary ambient face and the interpolant preserves that face.

Properness is retained as well. In a smooth disk collar the inward boundary defining coordinate of $M$ has strictly positive inward derivative, uniformly after a finite shrink, by the given transversality. Cellulate that collar as strips with its boundary as the only zero-coordinate face. In each ambient half-space simplex the corresponding affine boundary coordinate is nonnegative and positive on the vertices off that boundary face. Its affine interpolant is therefore zero precisely on the source boundary face. The derivative lower bound ensures these are precisely the collar sectors, even after a finer shape-controlled subdivision. Away from the collar the compact disk has a positive distance from $\partial M$, and a sufficiently small value error retains that separation. Hence the PL disk meets $\partial M$ exactly in its own boundary.

Along the original boundary, the secant curve lies in an arbitrarily small annular neighborhood and is transverse to its interval fibres: its tangential derivative is close to the nonzero derivative of the original parametrized curve in each of the finitely many sectors. Projection to the original circle is therefore a degree-one local homeomorphism, hence a homeomorphism. The new boundary is a graph in that annulus; interpolating its graph coordinate with zero gives an isotopy to the original boundary. Thus its nullhomotopy class, including its essentiality, is unchanged. The image under $h$ of the secant disk is the required properly embedded PL disk in the supplied compatible structure.

citations.quote: Let $T=S^1\times S^1$ be the standard oriented product torus. If $C\subset T$ is an embedded piecewise-linear simple closed curve that is not null-homotopic, then its class $[C]\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is nonzero and primitive, meaning that it is not $k x$ for any $x\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ and integer $|k|>1$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

derivations.claim: Reverse the parametrization of $C$ if necessary so its class is $(1,q)$. Round its finitely many corners in disjoint torus coordinate disks, using a coordinate in which the two incident arcs are graphs and replacing the graph corner by a smooth arc fixed near its endpoints. Each change is an isotopy of simple curves supported in that disk: interpolate graph values, which preserves the graph projection. Thus $C$ has an isotopy through finite piecewise smooth embedded curves to a smooth curve $C_0$ in the same class. Write $L_q(s)=(s,\exp(2\pi iqs))$. This is a simple smooth curve in that class.

Put $C_0$ transverse to $L_q$ by an arbitrarily small finite graph perturbation. The shear $(s,z)\mapsto(s,z\exp(-2\pi iqs))$ is a torus diffeomorphism carrying $L_q$ to a product section, so cutting the torus along $L_q$ gives an explicit annulus. The cut pieces of $C_0$ are finitely many properly embedded arcs. A returning arc, whose endpoints are on the same boundary circle, cuts off a disk with a subarc of that boundary. One elementary way to verify this familiar annulus fact is to cut the annulus to a rectangle along a spanning arc, lift the returning arc to its strip of translated rectangles, and choose an outermost lifted arc: its union with the interval between its endpoints on the same strip boundary bounds a polygonal disk. If a translate or another arc enters this disk, choose an innermost such arc instead. Finiteness of the intersections gives a disk with embedded interior in the annulus. Equivalently the finite disk-and-band reductions in [F2] give the same disk. Choose an innermost returning arc among the cut pieces; its disk interior misses the other cut pieces. Sliding it across that disk and a little beyond is an isotopy supported in the disk's collar and removes two intersections of $C_0$ with $L_q$. For smooth curves use smooth graph slides, stationary near the endpoints of the time interval.

Repeat the preceding removal while a returning arc remains. There are strictly fewer intersection points at each removal. If intersections remain when no returning arc is left, all cut arcs span the annulus. Traversing the connected oriented curve then meets $L_q$ always with the same crossing sign: after a spanning arc one arrives at the opposite copy of the cut circle, and gluing crosses it in the same direction as at the preceding crossing. Hence its algebraic intersection with $L_q$ is nonzero. This contradicts [F1], because both classes are $(1,q)$ and their determinant is zero. Thus the finite sequence ends with a smooth curve disjoint from $L_q$. The two curves bound an annulus: cutting along $L_q$ places the other essential circle in the interior of an annulus; cutting along it gives two annuli, as is seen by the same finite surface normal form [F2], or by lifting to a strip and taking the region between adjacent lifts. Sliding through that annulus supplies an isotopy to $L_q$. Concatenate with step 1.1 to obtain a finite piecewise smooth isotopy of simple curves from $C$ to $L_q$, smooth after the initial corner rounding.

Put the isotopy of step 3.1 into a radial collar of the tube. More precisely choose a strictly decreasing smooth radius $r(t)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ and map $(s,t)$ to $(u_t(s),r(t)z_t(s))$, where $(u_t(s),z_t(s))$ parametrizes the curve isotopy on the boundary torus. Distinct $t$ give distinct radii, so this is an embedded annulus irrespective of overlaps between different curve images on the torus. On each smooth piece its circle derivative is nonzero and tangent to the radius torus, whereas its time derivative has nonzero radial component, so it is regular. Make the isotopy constant near its final time; its inner collar is then the product collar of the radius-$1/2$ copy of $L_q$.

Continue inward by $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r\exp(2\pi iqs))$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. This is an embedded smooth annulus including its core boundary $r=0$: the first coordinate separates distinct $s$, and the $r$ derivative is a nonzero normal vector even at zero. Its outer collar agrees with the preceding annulus after the chosen radial reparametrization. The joined annulus meets the boundary torus only in $C$ and has the smooth core as its other boundary. Its interior lies on the tube side of that torus, while a proper exterior disk lies on the exterior side, so their union is an embedded disk, with a smooth product collar at the core. This proves the statement.

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

derivations.claim: Put $D$ in finite PL general position: it misses vertices, meets edges transversely in finitely many points, and meets faces in finitely many arcs and circles. This is obtained by finite subdivision and small generic vertex displacements, choosing each displacement outside finitely many forbidden affine planes and lines. Preserve its proper boundary in the boundary faces. Every component $P$ of its intersection with a tetrahedron is a compact planar surface, because it is a subsurface of a disk. Components have nonempty boundary; an entire closed component in a tetrahedron would be a closed component of $D$. Put $w(D)=|D\cap T^{(1)}|$ and $\lambda(D)=\sum_P(1-\chi(P))$. A connected planar piece with $b\ge1$ boundary curves has $1-\chi(P)=b-1\ge0$, as is seen by cutting it along $b-1$ disjoint connecting arcs to a disk and counting the cuts. Thus $(w,\lambda)$ is a pair of nonnegative integers.

We first record the permitted disk replacement inside a tetrahedron. Whenever a new cap is disjoint from the other pieces, a disk piece may be replaced, fixing its boundary and a smaller attaching collar, by that cap just inside its chosen boundary disk region. This preserves the topology of the entire surface: two disk parametrizations with the same boundary identification are homeomorphic relative to that boundary, extending the circle map radially. It is enough to choose the new cap disjoint from the other pieces. If all the pieces in question are disks, choose a point away from their boundary curves and take the disk side not containing that point for each curve. These disks are nested or disjoint by [F1]. Put the caps at successively deeper levels for successively larger nested regions, rounding their finite collar corners PL. This realizes all those disk pieces by disjoint caps. The same construction works in a boundary disk region containing only boundary curves of disk pieces, with other pieces kept outside its collar. The chosen depth intervals can be arbitrarily small. Boundary curves, edge intersections and the planar Euler deficits are unchanged. No assertion that the old disk is isotopic to the cap in the tetrahedron is needed.

If $\lambda>0$, select in some tetrahedron a boundary circle $c$ of a non-disk piece $P$ that is innermost among such boundary circles, using either fixed planar diagram of the boundary sphere. All boundary circles in its inner disk region are boundaries of disk pieces. Move those disk pieces to nested boundary-parallel caps as in step 2.1, at shallower collar depths. A copy of the inner boundary disk placed deeper than those caps, with boundary on a curve just inside the collar of $c$ in $P$, is then an embedded compressing disk disjoint from all other pieces. Its boundary is essential in $P$, since $P$ is planar with at least two boundary circles. Compress along it. Locally this splits off a disk and replaces $P$ by a planar piece with one fewer boundary circle, so $\lambda$ decreases by one, while $w$ is unchanged. Globally compression of a disk along an interior simple circle gives a disk with the original boundary and a sphere. Keep the disk and discard the sphere; discarding pieces cannot increase $w$ or $\lambda$. The boundary of the retained disk is still essential.

Repeat step 3.1 until $\lambda=0$ unless a preceding sphere discard has already decreased $w$; in that event restart with the smaller weight. At $\lambda=0$ every tetrahedral intersection piece is a disk. We may rearrange these disk pieces as boundary-parallel caps by step 2.1, without changing $w$ or $\lambda$. This rearrangement is only preparation for the next simplifying move, so it introduces no infinite sequence of equal-complexity moves.

Suppose some disk boundary meets a tetrahedral edge $e$ more than once. The finite disjoint boundary circles on the tetrahedral sphere then admit an edge-return interval $\beta\subset e$ with endpoints on the same boundary circle and interior disjoint from all the boundary circles. To verify this, the complementary regions of finitely many disjoint circles on a sphere have a tree as their incidence graph: each added circle separates one region into two, by [F1]. The edge $e$ traces a walk in that tree. Crossing one circle more than once repeats a tree edge; any such walk has an immediate backtrack. The two consecutive crossings of that backtrack are the required endpoints of $\beta$. Choose the cap side of its disk piece containing $\beta$ and use the compatible nested cap arrangement of step 2.1. The strip between $\beta$ and its parallel arc $\alpha$ on this cap is a disk $E$ with $E\cap D=\alpha$, $\partial E=\alpha\cup\beta$, and interior disjoint from all pieces: inner caps miss $\beta$ and outer caps lie deeper. This is an actual embedded edge-compressing disk.

If $e$ is an interior edge of $M$, slide the strip of $D$ adjacent to $\alpha$ across $E$ and beyond $\beta$ into the other sectors of the edge star. In the local product of an edge interval and a normal disk this is the elementary removal of a bigon; it removes precisely the two intersections at the ends of $\beta$ and creates no new edge intersections. It is an isotopy supported in that edge star and preserves the global boundary. Hence $w$ decreases. The new disk may have a larger local Euler deficit, which does not matter because the first complexity coordinate has decreased.

If $e\subset\partial M$, the same disk $E$ gives a boundary compression. Cutting the global disk along the proper arc $\alpha$ and adding the two parallel copies of $E$ gives two proper disks. At least one has essential boundary. Indeed, after choosing a base point and whiskers in $\partial M$, the old boundary loop is the product of the two new boundary loops, with one conjugated by the connecting arc $\beta$. If both new loops were nullhomotopic, so would be the old one. Keep an essential-boundary disk. The total edge intersection number of the two new disks is smaller than the old one by two, so the retained disk has strictly smaller $w$. Again any increase of $\lambda$ is permitted.

Each compression macro-move of step 3.1 either decreases $w$ or leaves it fixed and decreases $\lambda$; each edge macro-move decreases $w$. The intervening cap preparations are finite. Lexicographic descent in $\mathbb N^2$ therefore terminates with an essential-boundary proper disk all of whose tetrahedral pieces are disks and all of whose boundary circles meet each tetrahedral edge at most once. A circle of intersection with an interior face would now be the entire boundary of a disk piece on either side, making a sphere component of the global disk. A circle on a boundary face would be the boundary of a disk lying entirely in one tetrahedron and would be nullhomotopic in that face. Both are impossible. Each face intersection is therefore an arc, and an arc returning to the same edge would violate the just established edge condition.

Each tetrahedral boundary circle meets an edge, since otherwise it would lie in one face and would have been excluded in step 7.1. It separates the four vertices into two subsets. An edge with endpoints on opposite sides must be crossed, and one with endpoints on the same side must be crossed an even number of times, hence not at all. The crossing set is consequently either the three edges separating one vertex from the other three, or the four edges separating two vertices from the other two. The boundary is thus a triangle or quadrilateral normal curve. Replace the finitely many disk pieces by standard parallel normal disks with those same boundary matchings; disjoint boundary curves permit only one quadrilateral type in a tetrahedron. Their finite gluing has exactly the same abstract surface topology and boundary essentiality as the retained disk. It is the required normal disk. This proof used only finite planar disk constructions and preserves essentiality at every retained-disk step.
