derivations.claim: For each disk, the two cut paths partition its cyclic list of edge symbols. To form a new word, follow its chosen $f$-to-$g$ path and then the reverse of the chosen $f$-to-$g$ path of the other disk. Once the paths paired in one output have been chosen, the two remaining paths must be paired in the second. Thus there are exactly two pairings. We now check the compatible type cases. The edge sets displayed below also inherit their orders from [F1], so their concatenations determine the indicated cyclic words.

If the two types are equal, their two path edge sets are the same nonempty complementary sets $U,V$. Pairing $U$ with $V$ in each output recovers the original word twice. Pairing $U$ with $U$ and $V$ with $V$ repeats every edge in the corresponding nonempty set, so [F2] excludes that pairing. This covers equal triangles and equal quadrilaterals, for every pair of common faces, including the two-edge paths between opposite faces of a quadrilateral boundary.

For distinct triangles, relabel so they are $T_A,T_B$. Their common faces are exactly $ABC,ABD$. The paths of $T_A$ have edge sets $\{AB\}$ and $\{AC,AD\}$; those of $T_B$ have $\{AB\}$ and $\{BC,BD\}$. Pair the singleton in one disk with the two-edge path of the other. The resulting words are $T_B$ and $T_A$. The other pairing repeats $AB$ in one output, so is excluded by [F2].

For a triangle and quadrilateral, relabel them $T_A,Q_{AB\mid CD}$. If the common faces are $ABC,ABD$, their common edge $AB$ is avoided by the quadrilateral. The triangle paths have edge sets $\{AB\}$ and $\{AC,AD\}$; the quadrilateral paths have $\{AC,AD\}$ and $\{BC,BD\}$. Pair $\{AB\}$ with the quadrilateral's $\{AC,AD\}$, giving $T_A$. The remaining two paths concatenate in the order $(AC,AD,BD,BC)$, giving the same quadrilateral. The other pairing joins the two copies of $\{AC,AD\}$ in one output, repeating both edges, and is excluded.

The other common-face pairs are $ABC,ACD$ and $ABD,ACD$, whose common edges $AC,AD$ are crossed by the quadrilateral. Interchanging $C,D$ identifies these two cases, so consider $ABC,ACD$. The triangle paths have $\{AC\}$ and $\{AB,AD\}$; the quadrilateral paths have $\{AC\}$ and $\{AD,BD,BC\}$. Pair the singleton $\{AC\}$ from the triangle with the three-edge path of the quadrilateral, giving the quadrilateral word up to reversal. Pair the two-edge triangle path with the other singleton, giving $T_A$. The other pairing repeats $AC$, so is excluded. Vertex relabeling covers any other triangle–quadrilateral pair.

The allowed pairs consist of equal types, distinct triangles, and a triangle with a quadrilateral; distinct quadrilateral types were excluded in the hypothesis. Steps 2.1–2.4 cover them all and prove both existence and uniqueness of the type-preserving pairing, with the stated repeated-edge obstruction for its alternative. All lists and relabelings are finite and refer to the original seven types.

derivations.claim: Move the finitely many edge-intersection points of $Y$ slightly along their edges, preserving their order on each edge, to avoid those of $X$. The normal side matchings for $Y$ are retained. For each triangular face, replace every arc of each family by its straight chord between the corresponding endpoints. Each family remains embedded by [F2]. Choose the point displacements generically so no two chords overlap or are tangent where they meet: equality of their supporting lines is one nontrivial determinant equation in finitely many edge parameters, and can be avoided by successively choosing parameters outside finitely many forbidden values, with arbitrarily small displacements and the prescribed orders. Since each family is disjoint, a point lies on at most one chord from each, so there are no triple points.

The new boundary curves of the disk pieces on every tetrahedral sphere retain their individual normal boundary types and side matchings. Each family separately is a finite disjoint family of those curves. Realize it by the nested disjoint caps [F1], leaving its boundary exactly the chosen straight face chords. Do this for both colors. It gives two embedded proper normal surfaces with the original coordinate vectors. Their abstract disk-side gluing data are unchanged, so their abstract surfaces are homeomorphic to the originals: map each old disk to its new disk with the prescribed boundary correspondence, extending its boundary parametrization over a disk by coning a finite polygonal subdivision. For boundary components, moving endpoints along their edges and replacing a face arc by its chord gives a homotopy within the convex boundary faces, and these homotopies concatenate around each boundary circle.

Keep the first family of boundary-parallel caps fixed. Put the interiors of the second family into finite PL transverse position relative to it, while keeping all boundaries fixed. Subdivide finitely and displace second-family interior vertices by successively sufficiently small generic amounts. The excluded affine coincidences form finitely many proper planes, lines and determinant-zero conditions; avoiding them makes the sheet intersections one-dimensional with no tangencies. Smallness preserves each family's embedding and avoids all tetrahedral edges. Near boundary crossings, use fixed half-plane product charts extending the already transverse chord intersections. Consequently the intersection in each tetrahedron is a finite disjoint union of proper arcs and circles, with every endpoint a crossing of one straight chord from each family in a face.

No proper intersection arc has both endpoints in the same face. Its two branches lie in a fixed disk of each family, since pieces of the same family are disjoint. Each of those normal disks meets a given face in at most one arc. Two endpoints in that face would therefore be two intersections of the same two straight chords, contradicting [F2]. Thus all proper intersection arcs join distinct faces. Moreover, a fixed pair of normal pieces has at most one crossing in each of their common faces by [F2]. A triangle meets only three faces, so at most two endpoints, hence at most one arc, can occur for a pair containing a triangle. Two quadrilaterals have at most four endpoints, hence at most two arcs. These counts remain valid after circle removal, which changes no face arc or proper intersection arc.

Suppose an intersection circle remains in some tetrahedron. Choose a circle $c$ innermost on one disk $P$ of the first family, and let $E\subset P$ be the disk it bounds. Its interior misses the entire second family. There is no circle there by innermost choice. Nor can a proper intersection arc lie inside $E$: its endpoints would be on $\partial P$, outside $E$, while it cannot cross the disjoint intersection circle $c$. Thus $E$ is an actual disk with interior disjoint from the second family. It lies in the interior of the tetrahedron.

The circle $c$ lies on a disk $Q$ of the second family and bounds an interior subdisk $Q_0\subset Q$. Remove $Q_0$ and replace it by a nearby parallel copy of $E$, joining it to $Q\setminus\operatorname{int}Q_0$ in a small transverse collar of $c$. Choose the copy on the side of $P$ occupied by that outside collar of $Q$. The needed product coordinates are explicit for this $E$: the first-family disk $P$ is still the fixed boundary-parallel cap from step 2.1. Its graph in the boundary collar has the product coordinates supplied in [F1]; restrict them to the compact interior subdisk $E$ and take sufficiently small levels on its two sides. Thus no regular-neighborhood theorem for an arbitrary PL disk is needed. Compactness away from the attaching collar permits its interior to miss the entire second family. It also misses every first-family disk, since $E$ lies in one of their mutually disjoint disks and the push is to one side of that disk. Therefore the replacement is embedded, preserves the second family's embedding and leaves its tetrahedral boundary unchanged. It removes $c$ and every intersection circle inside $Q_0$, creates no new intersections, and changes no proper intersection arc. For the last assertion, a proper arc cannot enter $Q_0$ without crossing its boundary circle $c$, which is already a distinct intersection component. The disk $Q$ remains a disk with exactly its previous boundary type.

Reapply step 5.1 to a remaining circle, if any, and step 6.1 to remove it. The finite number of intersection circles strictly decreases, while no new one is created. This ends with no tetrahedral intersection circles. Edge points and straight face chords have not changed, so step 4.1 still excludes same-face arc endpoints. Every replacement changed only an interior subdisk of one piece, preserving the abstract surface and its boundary. Gluing across the faces now gives the asserted finite global double-curve system, since the local intersection arcs match at the fixed transverse face crossings and have endpoints only on boundary faces. The boundary homotopies from step 2.1 preserve null-homotopy or its failure. All operations were finite in the original triangulation.

derivations.claim: Label the vertices $A,B,C$ and choose a smaller homothetic central triangle with corresponding vertices $a,b,c$. The spokes $Aa,Bb,Cc$ divide the region outside it into three convex quadrilaterals, one along each original edge. Regard each quadrilateral as a rectangular strip from its outer original edge to the corresponding central edge, using [F2]. All original arc endpoints lie in the relative interiors of the outer strip edges.

In the central triangle put disjoint normal chords with the combined numbers of all three types. They may be chosen in small disjoint corner neighborhoods of $a,b,c$. For each type, designate one of its two original endpoint edges, using a fixed ordering of the three edges. Order that type's combined $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ chords by the order of their corresponding original endpoints away from the common vertex on the designated edge. Assign their colors and individual labels in that order. By [F1], this order respects the order within each original family on both endpoint edges. The central chords therefore impose compatible same-color orders on their two central strip gates. On a central gate the two incident types occupy their separate canonical corner blocks.

In every strip join each original endpoint to the gate endpoint of its labeled central chord by the straight wire in the rectangular parametrization. For either color separately, its wire order at the outer edge equals its wire order at the gate: order within a type agrees by step 2.1, and the two types have the same separate corner blocks by [F1]. Thus wires of the same color do not cross by [F2]. A wire from the other color crosses it at most once. Distinct crossings cannot coincide, since that would make two same-color wires meet. All intersections are consequently transverse double points. Join the wires to their central chords. Each resulting arc has exactly one central chord and one wire in each of two distinct strips, so is embedded and has its original type.

Two original arcs of different types share only one strip, so intersect at most once. Two original arcs of the same type share two strips, but on that type's designated strip their combined endpoint and gate orders coincide, by step 2.1. They cannot intersect there, so can intersect only once in their other strip. This proves the first assertion, including the original pairwise bound.

At a wire crossing, choose the uncrossing that reconnects each incoming wire from the outer side to the other outgoing wire toward the gate. In a small rectangle this is the reconnection by two horizontal-monotone strands. The other uncrossing joins the two outer-side branches to one another and the two gate-side branches to one another. After any subset of the chosen reconnections, every parametrizing strand within a strip is still strictly monotone in its horizontal coordinate: following it from an outer endpoint always goes toward a gate, and conversely. It cannot form a circle or self-intersect, and no component can have both ends on the same side of that strip. All strips still have the same gate endpoints, and the central chords have not changed. Hence each full parametrizing component has exactly one central chord and wires in its two distinct strips. It is an embedded normal arc. No remaining crossing can be a self-crossing of such a component: it lies inside one strip, where that component has exactly one monotone wire. The central chords count its type, so all type counts are unchanged.

To check the local characterization, the two crossing arcs share the strip's original edge $e$. The chosen uncrossing pairs each outer branch, whose endpoint is on $e$, with one gate branch. The other endpoint of that gate branch lies on a different original edge, determined by its unchanged central chord. This recovers the original unordered pair of types. The alternative joins the two outer branches and therefore has both endpoints on $e$, an edge-return arc. Thus exactly one uncrossing preserves the two normal types. Since the preceding argument worked for any subset of crossings, all assertions follow without altering the original face or its edge endpoints.

citations.quote: Let $T$ be a finite tetrahedral triangulation of a compact piecewise-linear $3$-manifold with $t\ge1$ tetrahedra. A nonzero nonnegative integer vector in $\mathbb Z^{7t}$ is the normal-coordinate vector of a normal surface exactly when it satisfies every face-matching equation and at most one quadrilateral type is nonzero in each tetrahedron. Every primitive integer generator of an extreme ray of the Haken cone has each coordinate at most $2^{7t-1}$. Every fundamental normal-surface vector has each coordinate at most $t\,2^{7t+2}$.

Let $f$ be an affine triangle and let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ be two finite families of normal arcs in $f$, each family embedded and pairwise disjoint, with disjoint endpoint sets on $\partial f$. There are PL representatives of the same individual arc types, fixing those endpoints, with these properties:

1. Every intersection is a transverse double point between the two families. Each original pair of arcs intersects at most once.
2. At every double point there is a chosen regular reconnection. For every subset of the double points, perform just those reconnections and otherwise retain the original transverse crossings. The resulting parametrizing components are embedded normal arcs, never circles, and their total counts of the three normal arc types are unchanged. Every remaining double point lies on two distinct parametrizing arcs.
3. The chosen reconnection at a crossing is the unique one of the two uncrossings that preserves the unordered pair of the two normal arc types there. Its alternative creates an edge-return arc in that local two-arc endpoint pairing. The same characterization holds at each remaining crossing after any partial reconnection.

Here parametrizing components follow the strands through unswitched crossings without joining them. The construction uses a small central triangle and three quadrilateral strips inside this original face. It changes no triangulation and uses only finite choices.

Let $P,Q$ be two normal disk types in one tetrahedron, subject to quadrilateral compatibility. Thus if both are quadrilaterals they have the same type. Choose two distinct faces $f,g$ met by both types, and cut each normal boundary word at one point of its arc in $f$ and one point of its arc in $g$. Each boundary is divided into two paths from $f$ to $g$.

There are two pairings that join one path from $P$ to one from $Q$ at both ends, producing two new closed boundary words. Exactly one pairing gives the original two normal disk boundary types, as an unordered pair, up to cyclic rotation and reversal of the words. The other pairing has a word crossing some tetrahedral edge at least twice and therefore cannot give those two normal types.

The conclusion concerns the finite boundary words and type counts in the original tetrahedron. It does not assert that arbitrary surface intersections already have the geometric regular-position or partial-switching properties.

derivations.claim: Realize $x,y$ by [F1]. Choose disjoint intersection-point sets on every triangulation edge, moving points of one family slightly while preserving their orders. Put the two normal arc systems on each face into the position [F2], retaining those endpoints and their individual types. Apply [F4] separately inside each tetrahedron. We obtain normal surfaces $X,Y$ with their original vectors and with only proper transverse tetrahedral intersection arcs. Each such arc joins distinct faces, since two endpoints in one face would be two crossings of the same pair of face arcs, excluded by [F2]. Globally these arcs form finitely many double circles and proper double arcs, missing the edges.

Let $F_1,F_2$ be any two embedded normal realizations of the same vector. On each global edge their numbers of points agree: the local edge count is a sum of the prescribed disk coordinates, and face matching identifies this count around the edge star. Match the points in their linear order, after fixing an orientation of that edge. On a face, arcs cutting off a fixed vertex form the endpoint blocks nearest that vertex on its two sides, with the same nested ordering. Thus the ordered point matching determines the arc matching. It determines the same entire boundary circles on each tetrahedral sphere, and therefore a bijection of the normal disk pieces attached to those circles. Map each disk to its counterpart with these boundary maps; a boundary map of a PL disk extends over it by coning a finite subdivision of its polygonal parametrization. These maps agree on all glued sides and points. Their finite gluing and its inverse give a PL homeomorphism $F_1\to F_2$. Its boundary maps are homotopies in $\partial M$: move the matched edge points monotonically along their edges and join the corresponding arc maps by homotopies inside each convex boundary face. These homotopies agree at their endpoints and concatenate around each boundary circle.

Along a tetrahedral intersection arc choose the local switch prescribed by [F3]. At each endpoint on a face it induces the type-preserving uncrossing of its two face arcs: the two resulting disk boundary words have the same normal disk types, so their face arcs have the original two arc types and no edge return. By uniqueness in [F2], this is exactly that face's chosen monotone-strip reconnection. The adjacent tetrahedron prescribes the same reconnection, because its two face arc types are the same matched types. The local switches therefore continue consistently across faces and around each full double curve. Choose sufficiently small pairwise disjoint neighborhoods of the finitely many curves, missing $T^{(1)}$, and perform these local reconnecting strips there. Their local definitions agree on overlaps by the established endpoint agreement.

We prove that any partial choice preserves normal disk pieces. It is enough first to work in one tetrahedron, allowing any subset of its intersection arcs; its face systems are then partial resolutions of the face braid. Order the chosen local arcs arbitrarily and use induction. Initially all pieces are embedded normal disks. Suppose this holds before processing the next remaining arc $\alpha$. Its two branches lie in distinct current disk pieces. Otherwise an endpoint of $\alpha$ on a face would be a transverse self-intersection of that disk's unique arc in the face. But every current face parametrizing arc is embedded by [F2]. This is impossible.

Cut the two distinct disks along $\alpha$. Each becomes two disks, since the arc is proper. Reconnecting them crosswise by either switch gives two abstract disks, each obtained by gluing one cut disk from each original disk along their cut boundary interval. Their current types are still compatible: the induction has preserved the original multiset of types. Apply [F3] to them. Its unique type-preserving choice agrees at both face endpoints with [F2], hence with the fixed switch in step 2.1. The two new disk boundary words consequently have their previous triangle or quadrilateral types, each with a single arc on every face it meets.

These new disk pieces are embedded. Local strip reconnection creates no new double points and removes just $\alpha$; all remaining double arcs are among the previous ones, still joining faces. If both branches of one belonged to the same new disk, its face endpoint would self-intersect that disk's unique face arc, again forbidden by [F2]. Thus no new disk has a self-intersection. There are no other singularities, since the original diagram was transverse and every switching neighborhood replaces two crossing sheets by two disjoint strips. This completes the induction for all partial local choices and proves that the local normal disk-type multiset is unchanged.

For a subset of whole global double curves, the partial face reconnections match from both incident tetrahedra by step 2.1. Thus their normal disk diagrams glue into a proper immersed surface, with only the unswitched curves and no branch points. Every tetrahedral multiset is unchanged by step 5.1, so its total vector is $x+y$. Disjoint switching neighborhoods commute because each map changes only its own neighborhood. When all curves are switched, no double curves remain and the surface $F$ is embedded and normal. All neighborhoods miss the edges, hence $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

If $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk, apply step 1.2 to $F,D$. It makes $F$ a connected disk, and its boundary homotopic to that of $D$, hence essential. If both $x,y$ are nonzero then their realizations are nonempty. The preceding construction is then an actual regular sum diagram for the decomposition of $D$ with every property asserted. It has used only finite original-tetrahedron disk words, face braids, cap replacements and ordered gluings; no transfer from a different normal-coordinate system was made.

derivations.claim: Write $\Gamma$ for the finite set of double curves. For each subset $A\subseteq\Gamma$, perform just its chosen switches and take the normalization of the resulting diagram. The empty subset gives at least two components because it is parametrized by the nonempty disjoint union $X\sqcup Y$. The full subset gives the connected surface $F$. Choose a subset $A$ of maximal cardinality among those giving disconnected normalization. The finite list of subsets makes this a finite choice. Then $A\ne\Gamma$, and every strict superset of $A$ gives connected normalization.

The normalization after switching $A$ has exactly two components. Otherwise choose any remaining double curve. By [F2], its switch affects at most two components; at least one component remains unaffected and at least one affected component remains nonempty. The normalization after that additional switch would still be disconnected, contrary to maximality in step 1.1. It already had at least two components by the choice of $A$, so it has exactly two. Denote them by $G,H$.

No remaining double curve has both branches in the same one of $G,H$. If it did, its switch would leave the other component unchanged and nonempty, and the affected component would also remain nonempty by [F2]. This would again contradict step 1.1. Thus every remaining crossing is between $G$ and $H$. There are no self-intersections of either component, because any such self-intersection would lie on a remaining double curve. There are no other singularities by the diagram hypothesis. Consequently each component is an embedded normal surface: its tetrahedral disk pieces are normal by [F1], their sides match as in the partial diagram, and their interiors have no self-intersections. They are connected by their definition as normalization components.

Let $B$ be any nonempty subset of the remaining curves. Switching it gives the normalization for $A\cup B$, which is connected by step 1.1. For the separation consequence, suppose a remaining circle or arc separates both $G$ and $H$. Cutting along its preimages gives exactly two pieces of each connected surface. The crosswise switch pairs the two cut copies from $G$ with the two cut copies from $H$, producing exactly two nonempty parametrizing components. This applies to annular cutting collars of separating circles and to rectangular cutting collars of separating proper arcs. Other unswitched double curves are merely intersections of the images and do not join normalization components. Thus that one switch would have disconnected normalization, contrary to the first assertion of this step.

The partial diagram and its full resolution have the same total number of normal disks of every type by [F1]. The two normalization components therefore satisfy $v(G)+v(H)=v(F)$. All switches miss the triangulation edges, giving $w(G)+w(H)=w(F)$ as well. Each nonempty normal surface contains a normal triangle or quadrilateral and hence meets an edge, so both summand weights are strictly positive. Their sum is $w(F)$, making both strictly smaller than $w(F)$. All operations took place in the supplied neighborhoods in the original $T$, proving every assertion.

If $K$ is a finite simplicial complex and $f_n(K)$ denotes the number of
$n$-simplices of $K$, the **simplicial Euler characteristic** of $K$ is
$$\chi(K):=\sum_{n \geq 0} (-1)^n f_n(K).$$
The sum is finite because a finite simplicial complex has only finitely many
simplices.

Let $S=|K|$ be a connected compact surface with nonempty boundary, where $K$ is a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex, each edge lies in one or two triangles, and each vertex link is a circle or interval. If its simplicial Euler characteristic is $\chi(K)=1$, then $S$ is homeomorphic to a closed disk.

Let $S := [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be the unit square, which carries one topology by
claim 1 of [[thm-product-of-subspaces-and-closures]]
([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-interval]]). Define two relations on $S$, in each case leaving every point
not on the two vertical edges alone:

$$\text{cylinder:}\quad (0,y) \sim_{\mathrm{c}} (1,y); \qquad\qquad \text{Mobius band:}\quad (0,y) \sim_{\mathrm{m}} (1, 1-y) \qquad (y \in [0,1]).$$

Precisely, $\sim_{\mathrm{c}}$ has as classes the pairs $\{(0,y),(1,y)\}$ and the
singletons $\{(s,t)\}$ with $0 < s < 1$; $\sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ has as classes the
pairs $\{(0,y),(1,1-y)\}$ and the same singletons. Write
$M_{\mathrm{c}} := S/\!\sim_{\mathrm{c}}$ (the **cylinder**) and
$M_{\mathrm{m}} := S/\!\sim_{\mathrm{m}}$ (the **Mobius band**), each with the
quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]]) and canonical projection
$P_{\mathrm{c}}$, $P_{\mathrm{m}}$. Then:

1. **Both projections are closed quotient maps**: the saturation of a closed
   subset of $S$ is closed, so $P_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $P_{\mathrm{m}}$ carry closed
   sets to closed sets ([[lem-open-or-closed-surjection-is-quotient]]).
2. **The cylinder is $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}) \times [0,1]$.** With
   $T = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and its open quotient map $q$
   ([[ex-circle-as-r-mod-z]]), the map $Q_1 := q \times \mathrm{id}_{[0,1]}$ is an
   open quotient map $\mathbb{R} \times [0,1] \to T \times [0,1]$ and induces a
   homeomorphism $M_{\mathrm{c}} \cong T \times [0,1]$
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

**Nothing here claims that the cylinder and the Mobius band are different
spaces.** Distinguishing them needs an invariant, and the standard ones are not
available at this point in the reading order
([[rem-constructions-this-page-stops-short-of]]). Both are recorded as
constructions, and only the cylinder is identified with a space built earlier.

The digon whose two sides are paired in the same boundary direction — the
one-polygon word $a\,a$ — realizes the real projective plane
$\mathbb{RP}^2$, taken here as the antipodal quotient $S^2/(x\sim -x)$,
equivalently as the closed upper hemisphere with antipodal boundary points
identified. It is nonorientable and has $V=1$, $E=1$, $F=1$, so
$\chi(\mathbb{RP}^2)=1-1+1=1$
([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]]). This direct finite
quotient uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that $P$ has boundary. Apply the finite dual-tree collapse [F2], choosing a lexicographically first spanning tree, to obtain a connected graph $G$. Take small polygonal vertex disks and narrow rectangular edge bands inside $P$ to form a regular neighborhood $N(G)$. One can choose them after a finite subdivision by taking sufficiently small rational distances in the finitely many triangle charts. Reversing a free triangle-edge collapse enlarges this neighborhood by a boundary finger across that triangle. To see that its homeomorphism type is unchanged, use a triangle chart in which the removed edge is the base: the two retained sides make the tip of the finger, and moving its polygonal boundary from a small parallel arc to the base expands a disk along one boundary interval. Triangulate the region between these two arcs and map corresponding triangles linearly. This gives a PL homeomorphism between the two neighborhoods, fixed off that triangle and its small vertex sectors. Reverse the finitely many collapses in order and finally expand the boundary collar. Thus $P$ is PL homeomorphic to $N(G)$. This construction uses a finite list of local maps, rather than a general regular-neighborhood uniqueness theorem.

A spanning tree of the connected graph $G$ has $V(G)-1$ edges. Write $h=E(G)-V(G)+1\ge0$ for the number of remaining edges. The collapses and [F1] give $\chi(P)=V(G)-E(G)=1-h\le1$. If equality holds, $h=0$, so $G$ is a tree and its neighborhood is a disk by [F2].

If $\chi(P)=0$, the graph $G$ has exactly one edge outside a spanning tree. Delete its leaf edges successively. A leaf vertex disk and its band merely form a finger on the neighboring disk; removing that finger changes no neighborhood homeomorphism type by the same finite polygonal expansion as in step 1.1. The graph remaining is one cycle: alternatively, the unique extra edge and the unique tree path joining its endpoints form that cycle, and every other tree edge belongs to a tree attached to it. Thus $N(G)$ is the union of the vertex disks and bands around a single cycle.

Now suppose $P$ is closed. Remove the interior of a small polygonal disk $B$ inside one triangle and triangulate the remaining surface $P_0$. It is connected: any path crossing the disk can have each crossing segment replaced by a path along its boundary, and a finite polygonal path has only finitely many such segments after a small general-position displacement. It has exactly one boundary circle. By [F1], $\chi(P_0)=\chi(P)-1$, and step 2.1 gives $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P_0$ is a disk by step 2.1. Capping a disk by a disk gives a sphere. Any PL boundary identification can be reduced to the identity by extending the boundary map over a disk: cone a finite subdivision of its circle to the center, and map the resulting triangles linearly. Thus this identification is PL.

Cut this cycle across one band. Its neighborhood becomes one rectangular strip: glue the remaining vertex disks and bands consecutively, each along one boundary interval, and use the polygonal disk expansions of step 1.1 to straighten the strip. At its two ends the transverse intervals are identified by a PL interval homeomorphism. If this map is increasing, change the transverse coordinate at one end and interpolate that change along the strip to make the gluing the identity. Explicitly, prescribe the required increasing map on one short side of the rectangle and the identity on its other three sides. This is a PL homeomorphism of its boundary. Subdivide at its finitely many breakpoints, cone both boundary subdivisions to interior points and map corresponding triangles linearly. This extends the boundary map to a PL homeomorphism of the rectangle. If the gluing is decreasing, first compose with $y\mapsto1-y$ and apply the same construction. The two resulting quotients are exactly the two models in [F3]. In the first, the two long sides of the strip give two boundary circles; in the second they join to one. Hence $P$ is respectively an annulus or a Mobius band.

If $\chi(P)=1$, then $P_0$ has Euler characteristic zero and exactly one boundary circle. Steps 3.1–4.1 make it a Mobius band, since the annulus has two boundary circles. Capping a Mobius band gives the antipodal-boundary disk of [F3]: in that disk model, a small collar of the identified outer circle is the twisted interval band, while the remaining inner disk is the cap. Conversely those two pieces recover the model. Changing the cap's boundary identification does not change the resulting PL surface, by the coning extension from step 3.2. Therefore $P$ is a projective plane. Every construction above used only finite trees, finite collapses and finite polygonal maps. The final embedded-surface consequence follows by composing these homeomorphisms with the given embedding.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

1. Every intersection is a transverse double point between the two families. Each original pair of arcs intersects at most once.
2. At every double point there is a chosen regular reconnection. For every subset of the double points, perform just those reconnections and otherwise retain the original transverse crossings. The resulting parametrizing components are embedded normal arcs, never circles, and their total counts of the three normal arc types are unchanged. Every remaining double point lies on two distinct parametrizing arcs.
3. The chosen reconnection at a crossing is the unique one of the two uncrossings that preserves the unordered pair of the two normal arc types there. Its alternative creates an edge-return arc in that local two-arc endpoint pairing. The same characterization holds at each remaining crossing after any partial reconnection.

Here parametrizing components follow the strands through unswitched crossings without joining them. The construction uses a small central triangle and three quadrilateral strips inside this original face. It changes no triangulation and uses only finite choices.

Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. If $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then it contains a normal disk with that property. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is required. The construction is allowed to replace disk pieces and to change the isotopy class of the original disk; it asserts existence of a normal replacement.

derivations.claim: All switching neighborhoods miss $T^{(1)}$. Hence every original edge-intersection point belongs to exactly one parametrizing component, and the sum of their edge weights is $W$. In particular $w(P)\le W$. If $w(P)<W$, apply [F2] to obtain an essential normal disk of weight at most $w(P)$, which proves the result. It remains to consider $w(P)=W$. In this case every original edge-intersection point belongs to $P$, and every other parametrizing component has weight zero.

An irregularly switched global curve crosses some face by [F1]. Choose one of that face's rectangular strips containing an irregular reconnection. Parametrize it so the horizontal coordinate runs from the original edge $e$ to its central gate. Order its finitely many crossing neighborhoods from the outer edge toward the gate. If distinct neighborhoods have the same horizontal coordinate, shrink them and perturb their positions slightly along their monotone wires to order them; this keeps the wires monotone, preserves their crossings and changes none of their endpoint orders. Thus we may speak of the first irregular reconnection in this strip. To its outer side, all selected switches are regular, and any unswitched crossing just follows its original monotone wire.

Before that first irregular reconnection, every incoming parametrizing strand is horizontally monotone and joins its crossing neighborhood to an original endpoint on $e$. The two incoming branches come from distinct such strands and distinct endpoints: all preceding crossings either keep two monotone strands separate in the normalization or regularly reconnect them from outer side to gate side. The irregular reconnection joins precisely these two incoming branches. It consequently creates a parametrizing arc with its two distinct endpoints on $e$, lying entirely on the outer side of this reconnection except for its small turning cap. Later reconnections farther toward the gate cannot change this arc, since their neighborhoods lie beyond its maximal horizontal coordinate. This gives an edge-return parametrizing arc in the completed face diagram.

In the equality case of step 1.1, both endpoints of that return arc belong to $P$. A face parametrizing arc lies in one global parametrizing component, so this entire arc belongs to $P$. Its image is an embedded proper arc in the face, because $P$ is embedded. Its ends are two distinct intersections with the same original edge $e$. Possible intersections with other parametrizing components do not affect this assertion about the arc within $P$.

Normalize $P$ using [F2]. If a preliminary sphere discard or other move removes any edge intersection before all tetrahedral pieces are disks, its weight has already decreased and the final normal essential disk has weight less than $w(P)$. Otherwise no edge intersection has been removed. The cap preparations and tetrahedral compressions fix the face curves. A sphere discard could not have removed the return arc of step 3.1 without removing its two edge endpoints. Thus that arc remains on the retained essential disk when its tetrahedral pieces become disks. On either incident tetrahedron, its boundary circle then meets $e$ at least twice. The explicit bigon construction in [F2] gives a strictly weight-decreasing edge move; if $e$ is a boundary edge its two disk outputs have total weight smaller by two, and at least one has essential boundary. Keeping that disk again decreases weight strictly.

Finish the finite normalization [F2]. No subsequent move increases weight, so its essential normal disk satisfies $w(D')<w(P)=W$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the Statement. The strict decrease comes from a return to an original edge, and has not used an auxiliary normal-coordinate objective or an ambient sphere theorem.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Suppose a **regular normal-sum diagram** is supplied with the following data:

- Two nonempty embedded normal surfaces $X,Y$ in transverse PL position, with no triple points and finitely many disjoint double circles and proper double arcs.
- Pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods of those double curves, disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, with compatible chosen regular switches. In each tetrahedron the local switch reconnects two crossing normal disks to normal disks of the same two types. A partial switch therefore leaves a finite immersed normal-disk diagram, with only the unswitched double curves and without branch points. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
- Performing all the switches gives a connected embedded normal surface $F$.

Then some partial switching gives a diagram whose normalization has exactly two components $G,H$. Here normalization means separating the two branches at every remaining double point; its components are the parametrizing surfaces, regardless of intersections between their images. Both $G$ and $H$ are connected embedded normal surfaces. They have

$$v(G)+v(H)=v(F),\qquad w(G)+w(H)=w(F),\qquad 0<w(G),w(H)<w(F).$$

Their remaining switching system is reduced in the following precise sense: switching any nonempty subset of its curves gives a diagram with connected normalization. In particular no remaining intersection circle or proper intersection arc separates both $G$ and $H$ when each is cut along its corresponding preimage.

All surfaces and vectors remain in the original triangulation $T$. No orientability, irreducibility or choice hypothesis is needed. The existence of a regular normal-sum diagram from an arbitrary coordinate decomposition is an input to this lemma, not a conclusion.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

Let $P$ be a connected compact surface supplied with a finite PL triangulation. The following conclusions require no choice axiom.

1. If $\partial P\ne\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le1$. Equality holds only for a disk. If instead $\chi(P)=0$, then $P$ is an annulus or a Mobius band; these have respectively two and one boundary circles.
2. If $\partial P=\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P$ is a two-sphere; if $\chi(P)=1$, then $P$ is a projective plane.

Consequently, every positive-Euler connected finite PL surface is a disk, sphere or projective plane. These identifications can be made by PL homeomorphisms between finite polygonal models. In a PL three-manifold without an embedded projective plane, a connected embedded positive-Euler surface is therefore a disk or a sphere.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

Start with the normal diagram constructed by the original-triangulation regular-sum construction, retaining its central-triangle and three-strip face braids. Let $W=w(X)+w(Y)$. A preliminary subset of its double curves may already have been switched regularly.

On some of its remaining double curves choose either the regular switch or its opposite, called an **irregular switch**, leaving the others unswitched. Suppose at least one irregular switch is performed. If a parametrizing component $P$ of the resulting diagram has an embedded proper PL disk as its image and its boundary is essential in $\partial M$, then there is an essential normal disk $D'$ in the original triangulation with

$$w(D')<W.$$

Other components may intersect the image of $P$ along unswitched double curves; only $P$ itself is required to be embedded. Parametrizing components separate the branches at unswitched crossings. No irreducibility, orientability, projective-plane or choice hypothesis is imposed.

derivations.claim: Suppose $G=S$ is a sphere and put $Y=H$. Their remaining intersection is nonempty, since otherwise their full resolution would be a disconnected union. It consists only of circles, because $S$ is closed. Each circle separates $S$, and therefore is nonseparating in $Y$ by [F1]. Each is also two-sided in $Y$, using only the coherent switching neighborhoods. Indeed, choose one of its two disk sides on $S$ by [F3]. In a transverse cross-section there are two $S$ rays and two $Y$ rays. The retained regular pairing pairs this chosen $S$ ray with one $Y$ ray. Transport it around the circle. The $S$ ray returns to itself, as the chosen disk side is global on $S$, and the regular pairing returns to itself by [F1]. Consequently the selected $Y$ ray returns to itself. The local rectangular collars on $Y$ thus glue without reversal and give an annular collar of the circle in $Y$. No ambient sphere collar was used.

The full resolution has boundary exactly $\partial Y$ and Euler characteristic $2+\chi(Y)=1$, since interior-circle cutting and regluing preserves Euler characteristic. Hence $Y$ has one essential boundary circle $C$ and $\chi(Y)=-1$. Cut it along one intersection circle $c_0$, using its annular collar from step 1.1. It stays connected and has Euler characteristic $-1$ and three boundary circles, so is a pair of pants by [F2]. Any other intersection circle is inessential or boundary-parallel there by [F3]. It cannot be inessential or parallel to $C$, since then it would separate $Y$ after regluing the copies of $c_0$. Thus every other circle is parallel to one of those two copies. Cutting along the whole family consequently yields a single pair of pants $K$ containing $C$ and otherwise annuli. This follows by ordering the finitely many nested parallel circles at the two ends of the cut pair of pants.

If the intersection family consists of $c_0$ alone, cutting $S$ gives two disks $E_1,E_2$, and cutting $Y$ gives $K$. Either local switch along $c_0$ attaches one of these disks to each of the two cut boundary circles of $K$. Both choices therefore produce one connected disk with boundary $C$. With all double curves resolved its image is embedded. Choose the irregular switch. Its disk is essential, so [F4] produces a normal essential disk of weight less than $w(F)$, contradicting minimality.

If there are at least two intersection circles, the other two boundary circles $a,b$ of $K$ are distinct members of the family. On $S$ take the two disjoint disks $E_a,E_b$ bounded by them whose interiors avoid the other boundary circle; [F3] gives those disks and a remaining nonempty annulus. Resolve just $a,b$, choosing at each the pairing that joins the $K$ side to the corresponding cap side, and leave all other curves unswitched. Then $K\cup E_a\cup E_b$, rounded only in those switching neighborhoods, is one parametrizing disk component $P$ with boundary $C$. Its image is embedded: the cap interiors are disjoint subsets of $S$, the interior of $K$ misses $S$, and each local switch joins adjacent rays of the two transverse sheets by a disjoint strip. Other intersection circles inside a cap meet only portions of $Y$ outside $K$; their unswitched crossings do not join parametrizing components and do not give self-intersections of $P$. Thus no global side of $S$ or displacement of entire caps is needed.

The remaining spherical annulus supplies points outside $P$, so the normalization in step 3.2 is disconnected. If both selected pairings were regular, this would contradict the reduced property [F1]. At least one is irregular. Apply [F4] to its embedded essential disk component $P$. Previous regular switches and these two switches miss the original edges, and the total original weight is $w(S)+w(Y)=w(F)$. The resulting essential normal disk has weight less than $w(F)$, a contradiction. Together with step 3.1 this excludes a spherical $G$, and exchanging names excludes a spherical $H$. Every construction used the original diagram and its existing neighborhoods.

boundaries.reason: Empty intersection would leave the nonempty sphere and other summand disconnected, violating the premise.

Proof, steps 2.1, 3.2: Sphere intersections are closed circles; the original essential boundary is retained by the disk construction.
Proof, steps 1.1, 3.1, 4.1: Finite innermost-circle selection and strict improvement replace any irreducibility assumption.

one-polygon word $a\,a$ — realizes the real projective plane

derivations.claim: Suppose $G=Q$ is a projective plane and put $Y=H$. Their remaining intersection is nonempty, since the full resolution is connected and both summands are nonempty. It consists of circles, since $Q$ is closed. The full resolution has boundary $\partial Y$, namely the one essential boundary circle $C$ of $F$. Cutting out the annular or Mobius neighborhoods [F4] and inserting the switching strips preserves total Euler characteristic: the removed pieces, their boundary circles and the inserted interval-bundle switching pieces have Euler characteristic zero. For the latter, the finite rectangular charts glue around a circle, so their face and side counts cancel just as for an annulus or Mobius band. Hence $1=\chi(F)=\chi(Q)+\chi(Y)$ and $\chi(Y)=0$ by [F3]. By [F2], the connected surface $Y$ with its one boundary circle is a Mobius band.

An intersection circle is two-sided in $Q$ exactly when it is two-sided in $Y$. In a transverse cross-section there are two rays of each surface. A regular uncrossing pairs each $Q$ ray with one $Y$ ray. Following the rays once around the circle preserves this pairing by [F1]. Reversing the two rays of only one surface interchanges the two possible uncrossings, whereas reversing both, or neither, preserves the pairing. Thus the two surfaces' transverse intervals have the same reversal sign. This is the claimed equivalence by [F4].

Every two-sided simple circle separates $Q$. Otherwise cutting out its annular neighborhood would leave a connected boundary surface with Euler characteristic $1$ and two boundary circles. It would be a disk by [F2], a contradiction. Likewise every two-sided circle separates the Mobius band $Y$: a nonseparating annular cut would leave a connected Euler-zero surface with the three boundary circles consisting of $C$ and the two new ones, contrary to [F2]. Hence a two-sided intersection circle would separate both summands by step 2.1, contradicting reducedness [F1]. All remaining circles are one-sided in both surfaces.

A one-sided circle in $Q$ has a Mobius neighborhood with one boundary circle. Its complement is connected: only one component can meet that boundary circle, while any other component would be an open and closed component of the original connected surface. The complement has Euler characteristic $1$ and one boundary circle, so is a disk by [F2]. The neighborhood can be chosen disjoint from all other intersection circles. Any further circle would lie in that complementary disk and would be two-sided there, contradicting step 3.1. Thus there is exactly one intersection circle $c$. The same one-boundary-neighborhood argument makes the complement of its Mobius neighborhood in $Y$ connected. It has Euler characteristic zero and two boundary circles, $C$ and the new circle, so is an annulus by [F2].

Either switch along $c$ replaces the two crossing Mobius strips by one annulus connecting their boundary circles. Here is the finite local calculation. Follow the transverse cross-section once around $c$. Both labeled surface axes reverse by step 3.1. For either smoothing, its two interval pieces in opposite quadrants are therefore exchanged after one turn. After two turns each interval returns, with its endpoints still labeled $Q$ and $Y$ respectively. The two rectangles consequently glue in series into an interval product over the double circle, namely an annulus, with one boundary from $Q$ and one from $Y$. No interval reversal is possible after the two turns because its two endpoint labels are fixed. Attaching the disk remainder from $Q$ and the annulus remainder from $Y$ in step 4.1 gives a connected disk whose boundary is $C$. Since this is the only double curve, either fully resolved image is embedded.

Choose the irregular switch. Step 5.1 gives an embedded proper disk with essential boundary as a parametrizing component. The strict improvement supplier [[lem-irregular-switches-in-original-face-braids-give-strict-essential-disk-improvement]] applies to the retained original braid, after its preliminary regular switches. It gives an essential normal disk of weight strictly below $w(Q)+w(Y)=w(F)$, contradicting minimality. This excludes a projective-plane $G$, and exchanging names excludes a projective-plane $H$. The argument excluded a summand using the actual switching data; it did not exclude projective planes from the ambient manifold.

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.
If $X$ has finitely many cells and $c_n(X)$ is its number of $n$-cells, define $\chi(X)=\sum_n(-1)^nc_n(X)$. The sum is finite by hypothesis.

If a connected plane graph has vertex, edge and face sets $V,E,F$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=2.$$

derivations.claim: Assume $w(P)=0$. Cut each normal disk along its trace arcs. The arcs are finite, disjoint and proper, so [F1] makes each remaining region a polygonal disk. Keep precisely the regions belonging to $P$, with distinct copies on opposite sides of any cut. Their finitely many sides and endpoints give a finite cell structure on the abstract cut completion $P$. The original normal-cell vertices do not occur in these regions, by the assumed zero weight and [F2].

A retained region cannot have two consecutive old side intervals: their meeting point would be an original normal-cell vertex. Nor can two trace sides meet: trace arcs are disjoint and transverse to the old edges, with distinct endpoints there. Thus the boundary of each retained region alternates trace sides and old side intervals. It contains a trace side, since a region with no trace side would be the entire original normal disk and would contain its vertices. If it had only one trace side, the complementary old interval would connect the two endpoints along one old side, so that trace arc would have both endpoints on that side, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore its number $k_j$ of trace sides is at least two, and it has exactly $k_j$ old side intervals.

Put $N=\sum_j k_j$, let $f$ be the number of retained regions, and let $e_i$ and $e_m$ count respectively the glued interior old intervals and the old intervals lying in $\partial F$. Every trace side is a boundary edge of the cut completion, so their number is $N$. An interior old interval has two incident retained region sides; a boundary old interval has one. Consequently $$N=2e_i+e_m.$$ This count concerns abstract sides of $P$, so it remains valid when the same component occurs on both sides of a trace or on both sides of an old cell edge.

Each component of $P\cap\partial F$ contains no original normal-cell vertex, again because $w(P)=0$. Such a component is, by hypothesis, a proper arc, with its two endpoints on the trace family. It therefore lies within one original boundary side. No trace endpoint lies in its interior, since cutting at any such endpoint terminates the corresponding boundary interval in the cut completion. Hence each of the $b$ components is exactly one boundary old edge, and $e_m=b$.

Every vertex of the new cell structure is an intersection of a trace with an old side. It is consequently on the boundary of the cut completion. There are no other vertices, since the original vertices were excluded in step 1.1. The boundary is a finite disjoint union of polygonal circles, so its vertex count equals its edge count. Its edges are the $N$ trace sides and $b$ boundary old intervals, giving $v=N+b$. The full edge count is $e_i+N+b$.

Apply [F3] and substitute the preceding counts: $$\chi(P)=(N+b)-(e_i+N+b)+f=f-e_i=f-\frac{N-b}{2}=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right).$$ Every summand is nonpositive by step 2.1, proving the asserted inequality. If $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $\chi(P)=1$ whereas the inequality gives $\chi(P)\le1/2$, a contradiction. Thus every such disk patch has positive edge weight.

For the exchange-rectangle application, each side of a rectangle lying on a normal disk joins its two face sides. Those face sides lie in distinct tetrahedral faces, so the endpoints lie on distinct sides of that normal disk. Disjoint exchange surfaces give disjoint traces, which can be chosen transverse to the old sides and away from their vertices by finite PL displacement. Thus their cut patches satisfy precisely the trace hypothesis already used. The stated interior and boundary disk patches have respectively zero and one proper original-boundary arcs, so step 6.1 applies without any additional ambient-manifold hypothesis.

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Suppose a **regular normal-sum diagram** is supplied with the following data:

- Two nonempty embedded normal surfaces $X,Y$ in transverse PL position, with no triple points and finitely many disjoint double circles and proper double arcs.
- Pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods of those double curves, disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, with compatible chosen regular switches. In each tetrahedron the local switch reconnects two crossing normal disks to normal disks of the same two types. A partial switch therefore leaves a finite immersed normal-disk diagram, with only the unswitched double curves and without branch points. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
- Performing all the switches gives a connected embedded normal surface $F$.

Then some partial switching gives a diagram whose normalization has exactly two components $G,H$. Here normalization means separating the two branches at every remaining double point; its components are the parametrizing surfaces, regardless of intersections between their images. Both $G$ and $H$ are connected embedded normal surfaces. They have

$$v(G)+v(H)=v(F),\qquad w(G)+w(H)=w(F),\qquad 0<w(G),w(H)<w(F).$$

Their remaining switching system is reduced in the following precise sense: switching any nonempty subset of its curves gives a diagram with connected normalization. In particular no remaining intersection circle or proper intersection arc separates both $G$ and $H$ when each is cut along its corresponding preimage.

All surfaces and vectors remain in the original triangulation $T$. No orientability, irreducibility or choice hypothesis is needed. The existence of a regular normal-sum diagram from an arbitrary coordinate decomposition is an input to this lemma, not a conclusion.

Let $P$ be a connected compact surface supplied with a finite PL triangulation. The following conclusions require no choice axiom.

1. If $\partial P\ne\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le1$. Equality holds only for a disk. If instead $\chi(P)=0$, then $P$ is an annulus or a Mobius band; these have respectively two and one boundary circles.
2. If $\partial P=\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P$ is a two-sphere; if $\chi(P)=1$, then $P$ is a projective plane.

Consequently, every positive-Euler connected finite PL surface is a disk, sphere or projective plane. These identifications can be made by PL homeomorphisms between finite polygonal models. In a PL three-manifold without an embedded projective plane, a connected embedded positive-Euler surface is therefore a disk or a sphere.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

Let $F$ be a least-edge-weight essential normal disk in a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. Put a nontrivial decomposition of $v(F)$ into the original-triangulation regular diagram of the original-triangulation regular-sum construction, and obtain a reduced connected pair $G,H$ by the reduced-connected-pair lemma, retaining the face braids and switch neighborhoods.

Neither $G$ nor $H$ is a two-sphere. No lexicographic tie-break, ambient orientability, projective-plane exclusion, sphere separation, sphere irreducibility or separately supplied bicollar is required. The needed local side choices come from the retained coherent regular switches themselves.

Let $F$ be a least-edge-weight essential normal disk in a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. Suppose a nontrivial decomposition of its normal vector has been put into the original-triangulation regular diagram of the original-triangulation regular-sum construction, and partial regular switches have produced a reduced connected pair $G,H$ as in the reduced-connected-pair lemma. Retain the face braids and switch neighborhoods.

Neither $G$ nor $H$ is a projective plane. The ambient manifold is allowed to contain projective planes; no orientability, irreducibility or choice hypothesis is used.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$, and let $F$ be a normal surface. Its normal disks form polygonal cells with three or four sides. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite disjoint family of PL simple closed curves and properly embedded PL arcs on $F$. Suppose $\Lambda$ misses the normal-cell vertices, is transverse to the cell edges, and meets each normal disk in disjoint properly embedded arcs whose endpoints are on distinct sides of that disk.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. If $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then it contains a normal disk with that property. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is required. The construction is allowed to replace disk pieces and to change the isotopy class of the original disk; it asserts existence of a normal replacement.

Start with the normal diagram constructed by the original-triangulation regular-sum construction, retaining its central-triangle and three-strip face braids. Let $W=w(X)+w(Y)$. A preliminary subset of its double curves may already have been switched regularly.

On some of its remaining double curves choose either the regular switch or its opposite, called an **irregular switch**, leaving the others unswitched. Suppose at least one irregular switch is performed. If a parametrizing component $P$ of the resulting diagram has an embedded proper PL disk as its image and its boundary is essential in $\partial M$, then there is an essential normal disk $D'$ in the original triangulation with

$$w(D')<W.$$

Other components may intersect the image of $P$ along unswitched double curves; only $P$ itself is required to be embedded. Parametrizing components separate the branches at unswitched crossings. No irreducibility, orientability, projective-plane or choice hypothesis is imposed.

derivations.claim: Euler characteristic is additive in this regular sum: cutting along a proper double arc increases the total Euler characteristic by two, and attaching its two switching rectangles decreases it by two. Cutting and switching a circle changes it by zero. These assertions also follow by subdividing the finite strips into rectangles and counting their attaching intervals. Thus $1=\chi(F)=\chi(P)+\chi(H)$. Some summand has positive Euler characteristic; name it $P$. By [F2] and [F3] it is a disk, so $\chi(H)=0$. If $P$ had essential boundary, it would itself be an essential normal disk of strictly smaller weight than $F$, by [F1]. Therefore $\partial P$ is null-homotopic in $\partial M$.

The remaining intersection is nonempty, since otherwise the full resolution would be the disjoint union of the two nonempty summands. It must contain a proper arc. Indeed, if it consisted only of circles, switching those circles would leave the boundary of $P$ as a boundary component of the full resolution. That resolution has the single essential boundary circle of $F$, contrary to step 1.1. In particular $H$ has boundary. By its Euler characteristic and [F2], it is an annulus or a Mobius band.

There are no intersection circles. To see this, a circle in the disk $P$ has a consistently chosen transverse side in $P$ and separates $P$. The regular pairing in a cross-section pairs its two $P$ rays with the two $H$ rays. Following the circle preserves that pairing. If only the $H$ rays reversed, the two possible pairings would be interchanged; hence the $H$ rays do not reverse. The circle is therefore two-sided in $H$. Every two-sided circle separates an annulus or Mobius band: otherwise removal of an annular neighborhood would leave a connected Euler-zero boundary surface with respectively four or three boundary circles, contrary to [F2]. A remaining circle would consequently separate both summands, contradicting [F1].

Write $k\ge1$ for the number of remaining proper arcs. Every such arc separates the disk $P$, by [F2], and therefore does not separate $H$, by [F1]. Cut $H$ along one arc. The result is connected, has boundary, and has Euler characteristic $\chi(H)+1=1$, so is a disk by [F2]. Each of the other $k-1$ arcs remains a proper arc in the cut surface, with distinct endpoints away from the first cut. Repeated disk cutting gives $k$ disks. Applying the same cutting argument directly to $P$ gives $k+1$ disks.

The adjacency graph of the $P$ patches has one vertex per patch and one edge per cut arc. It is connected because regluing the arcs reconstructs the connected disk $P$. Each successive disk cut separates one patch into two, so adds one vertex and one edge without introducing a graph cycle. Thus the graph is a tree with $k+1\ge2$ vertices. A finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves: extend any simple edge path maximally in both directions; either endpoint has no other incident edge, since such an edge would either extend the path or make a cycle. A leaf patch has one cut-arc side. Its remaining boundary is one original-boundary arc, because the patch is a disk and has no other cut sides. Each leaf has positive edge weight by [F1] and [F4].

In fact $k$ cannot equal one. If $\alpha$ were the only arc, cutting $P$ along it would give two disks $E_1,E_2$, and cutting $H$ along it would give one disk $Q$, by step 4.1. Either switch attaches one $E_i$ along each of the two cut sides of $Q$. It therefore gives a disk; as this resolves the only double curve, its image is embedded. Let $p,q$ be the endpoints of $\alpha$ and orient the two complementary arcs of $\partial P$ as paths $u,v$ from $p$ to $q$. The loop $uv^{-1}$ is $\partial P$ up to orientation, so step 1.1 makes $u$ and $v$ homotopic with endpoints fixed in $\partial M$. In either resolution, its boundary is obtained from the boundary of $Q$ by replacing one cut-side copy of $\alpha$ by $u$ and the other by $v$, with the directions of traversal determined by that boundary. The other resolution interchanges these assignments. Replace $u$ by $v$ using their endpoint-fixed homotopy in each occurrence; both resulting loops then traverse the same original-boundary pieces of $Q$ and the same paths on its cut sides, in the same order. The boundaries of the two disk resolutions are consequently freely homotopic, up to reversal of the chosen whole-loop orientation. The regular one is the essential boundary of $F$, so the irregular one is also essential. Apply [F5] to this irregular resolution, contradicting the least weight of $F$. Hence $k\ge2$.

Distinct patches partition the original intersections of $P$ with $T^{(1)}$: the cuts miss those intersections. If $E$ is a smallest-weight leaf, the existence of two leaves gives $2w(E)\le w(P)$. The disk $E$ meets $H$ precisely in its cut-arc side $\alpha$; its other boundary side is in $\partial M$. Boundary compression of $H$ along $E$ is embedded and proper. Explicitly, cut $H$ along $\alpha$ and attach one slightly displaced copy of $E$ to each cut side, joining them in the original transverse switch charts near $\alpha$ and its endpoints. The interior of $E$ misses $H$, so the two copies may be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from the cut surface. A disk has a product transverse neighborhood along this construction: trivialize on a finite triangulation and extend the local interval direction successively from a vertex across the triangles, with no reversal around a loop since every disk loop contracts. On the original-boundary side use the half-space charts of $M$; the two displaced boundary arcs then remain in $\partial M$. Since $H$ cut along $\alpha$ is a disk by step 4.1, attaching the two disks along their cut-side intervals leaves a disk. This is $D_E$.

Choose the displacement sufficiently small to preserve every transverse edge intersection of the copied patches and to create no new ones. This is possible with finitely many intersection charts and disjoint compact complements. All joining strips lie in switch neighborhoods missing $T^{(1)}$ by [F1]. The intersections of $H$ and of the two copies of $E$ are then distinct, so $$w(D_E)=w(H)+2w(E)\le w(H)+w(P)=w(F).$$ If this disk has essential boundary, [F4] gives an essential normal disk of no larger weight. Minimality of $F$ forces both its weight and the weight of that retained normal disk to equal $w(F)$. Thus no strict inequality or subsequent weight loss is possible in the essential case.

Steps 1.1–5.2 give all the asserted restrictions on the reduced pair and its patches; steps 6.1–7.1 give the disk construction and the conditional equality. For two or more arcs the argument has made no assertion that the boundary-compressed disk is essential.

derivations.claim: Fix one tetrahedron and put $\delta=\alpha u+\beta v-(\alpha+\beta)d$ on its seven coordinates. Write its triangle coordinates as $a,b,c,e$ at $A,B,C,D$, and its quadrilateral coordinates as $x,y,z$ at $q_1,q_2,q_3$. The hypothesis $B\delta=0$ and [F1] give the six equations $$\begin{aligned}a+b+y+z&=0,&c+e+y+z&=0,\\a+c+x+z&=0,&b+e+x+z&=0,\\a+e+x+y&=0,&b+c+x+y&=0.\end{aligned}$$ They are listed in opposite-edge pairs.

Subtracting the members of those pairs gives $a+b=c+e$, $a+c=b+e$ and $a+e=b+c$. The first two imply $b=c$ and $a=e$; substituting in the third gives $a=b$. Thus all four triangle differences equal one number $t$. The first equation in each pair now gives $y+z=x+z=x+y=-2t$, so $x=y=z=-t$. Hence the kernel of the six local edge equations is exactly the line generated by $(1,1,1,1,-1,-1,-1)$.

Put $\gamma=-t$. For each of the three quad types, $$\alpha u_{q_i}+\beta v_{q_i}=(\alpha+\beta)d_{q_i}+\gamma.$$ If $\gamma<0$, choose a quad coordinate with $d_{q_i}=0$, which exists by [F2]. Its left side is nonnegative, whereas its right side is negative, a contradiction. If $\gamma>0$, all three left sides are strictly positive. Positivity of $\alpha,\beta$ would then require the union of the positive quad supports of $u$ and $v$ to contain all three types. Each support has size at most one by [F2], so that union has size at most two. This is again a contradiction. Therefore $\gamma=0$.

It follows that $t=0$ and every coordinate of $\delta$ is zero. Apply the same argument independently in each tetrahedron to obtain $\alpha u+\beta v=(\alpha+\beta)d$ on the whole array. No matching equation was used.

For an actual normal surface, its local count on any tetrahedral edge is the number of its intersection points with that global edge: the normal disks in each incident tetrahedron meet exactly those points. Hence an equality of global edge counts gives the six local equalities in every tetrahedron, and step 4.1 proves the surface-vector assertion.

If $u\ne d$, let $j$ be the first coordinate where they differ. The averaging identity gives $\beta(v-d)=-\alpha(u-d)$. Therefore $v$ also agrees with $d$ before $j$, and the differences at $j$ have opposite nonzero signs. One of $u,v$ is consequently lexicographically smaller than $d$, contradicting the assumed minimality. Thus $u=d$, and the same identity then gives $v=d$. Applying this to the set of essential normal disk vectors at the least edge weight proves the final assertion.

For a finite tetrahedral triangulation, let $B$ record the six local edge-intersection counts in every tetrahedron from its seven normal coordinates. $$\alpha Bu+\beta Bv=(\alpha+\beta)Bd,$$

$$\alpha u+\beta v=(\alpha+\beta)d.$$
