derivations.claim: Switch all arcs except $\alpha$. There is at least one switched arc because $k\ge2$. The normalization is connected by [F1], has Euler characteristic one, and has nonempty boundary. For the last assertion, proper-arc switching does not remove all original-boundary intervals: their interiors miss the finite switch endpoints and remain boundary intervals of the normalization. Hence this normalization is a parametrizing disk $Q$ by [F2]. The only image double curve is $\alpha$. Its two preimages are disjoint proper arcs in $Q$. Cutting them gives three disks in a path by [F2]. The original leaf $E$ has not been touched by any of the preliminary switches, so it is one end disk. Name the other end $E'$ and the middle $K$. No cut piece has an interior double point: the only double curve was cut onto their boundaries. Thus their interiors are embedded and mutually disjoint.

In a transverse section of $\alpha$, the ray of $E'$ is adjacent to the ray of $E$. If instead these rays were opposite, they would be the two rays of the same unswitched surface branch. The two rays of $K$ would then be the other opposite pair. Restoring the unswitched identifications would join $E$ to $E'$ and join $K$ to itself, giving two components, contrary to the connected normalization $Q$ in step 1.1. The adjacent-ray uncrossing joining $E$ to $E'$ also joins the two rays of $K$. It cannot be the regular uncrossing: the regular full resolution is the connected disk $F$. It is therefore the irregular uncrossing. Its $E+E'$ component is a disk $W$, since two disks joined along a boundary interval form a disk. Resolving the sole remaining image double arc makes that image embedded and proper.

The boundary of $W$ is null-homotopic in $\partial M$. Otherwise $W$ would be an embedded essential disk component of a resolution with the irregular switch of step 2.1. By [F3] there would be an essential normal disk of smaller weight than $F$, a contradiction. Let $p,q$ be the endpoints of $\alpha$. Orient the complementary original-boundary arcs of $E,E'$ as paths $u,v$ from $p$ to $q$. The boundary of $W$ is $uv^{-1}$ up to reversal. Its null-homotopy therefore says exactly that $u$ and $v$ are homotopic with endpoints fixed in $\partial M$.

Attach two slightly separated copies of $E$ to the two cut sides of $K$, or two copies of $E'$ instead. Both constructions give embedded proper disks $A,A'$. Here all interiors in step 1.1 are disjoint, so the copies can be made in arbitrarily small neighborhoods missing the other pieces. A finite product displacement of a disk is available along these pieces: its local normal intervals are compatible along a disk triangulation after propagating their signs from one chart; every potential sign reversal is a disk loop and contracts. The four-ray sections at $\alpha$ specify the disjoint joining strips. For $A$ they join the two separated $E$ rays to the two $K$ rays without crossing, and for $A'$ use the separated $E'$ rays. Half-space charts at $p,q$ and along the boundary arcs keep the copied boundary in $\partial M$. Attaching one disk along each of two disjoint boundary intervals of the disk $K$ leaves a disk.

Both new disks have essential boundary. The regular disk $F$ is obtained by attaching $E,E'$ to the two cut sides of $K$, so its boundary follows the remaining original-boundary portions of $K$ with those cut sides replaced by $u,v$, in the directions of their traversal. For $A$ those replacements are $u,u$, and for $A'$ they are $v,v$. The endpoint-fixed homotopy of step 3.1 makes all three resulting loops freely homotopic, up to choosing the orientation of the entire loop. Since $\partial F$ is essential, so are $\partial A$ and $\partial A'$. This uses a boundary-path homotopy, not a boundary-parallelity assertion about the three disks.

Every joining strip misses original edges, and the two copies in step 3.2 can preserve all transverse edge counts. Indeed choose disjoint small charts about the finitely many edge crossings and a sufficiently small displacement on their compact complement. Therefore, componentwise, $$N(F)=N(K)+N(E)+N(E'),\quad N(A)=N(K)+2N(E),\quad N(A')=N(K)+2N(E').$$ In particular $N(A)+N(A')=2N(F)$. Apply [F4] to the essential disks from step 4.1 to obtain essential normal disks $U,V$ with $N(U)\le N(A)$ and $N(V)\le N(A')$.

Summing all edge entries gives $$2w(F)\le w(U)+w(V)\le w(A)+w(A')=2w(F),$$ where the first inequality is least-weight minimality. Thus all totals are equal and $w(U)=w(V)=w(F)$. Each componentwise deficit in step 5.1 is nonnegative, and their total is zero, so every deficit is zero. Consequently $N(U)=N(A)$, $N(V)=N(A')$ and $N(U)+N(V)=2N(F)$.

By [F5], $v(U)+v(V)=2v(F)$, and the assumed lexicographic minimality at weight $w(F)$ forces $v(U)=v(V)=v(F)$. Their edge-count vectors therefore both equal $N(F)$. Substitute $N(U)=N(A)$ into the formulas of step 5.1 to get $N(E)=N(E')$ on every original edge. The same formulas now give $w(A)=w(A')=w(F)$, and step 6.1 shows that their normal replacements lost no edge points. Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$, and let $F$ be a normal surface. Its normal disks form polygonal cells with three or four sides. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite disjoint family of PL simple closed curves and properly embedded PL arcs on $F$. Suppose $\Lambda$ misses the normal-cell vertices, is transverse to the cell edges, and meets each normal disk in disjoint properly embedded arcs whose endpoints are on distinct sides of that disk.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

derivations.claim: In the disk case $\chi(R)=1$ and $b=2$; in the annulus or Mobius case $\chi(R)=0$ and $b=0$. In both cases the Euler formula [F1] says that a sum of nonpositive terms is zero. Thus every $k_j=2$. Each normal-cell region is a quadrilateral with two opposite trace sides and two opposite old sides. The old sides of one quadrilateral lie on distinct sides of its original normal disk: either trace side joins these two old sides, and the distinct-side trace hypothesis excludes their lying on the same normal-disk side. A normal disk has at most one side in any tetrahedral face, so these two faces are distinct.

Make a finite graph with one vertex for each quadrilateral and an edge for each glued pair of old intervals, retaining loops and repeated edges if present. It is connected. Indeed, the quadrilaterals reconstruct the connected surface patch by precisely these old-side gluings. They cannot connect only at a vertex: every vertex is a trace endpoint on an old interval, and its half-disk surface chart joins its incident regions across that interval. Each graph vertex has degree two minus its number of unglued old sides, counting a loop twice. In the disk case there are exactly two unglued old sides by [F1], so the connected graph is a path, possibly one vertex with both ends unglued. To check this without a graph classification, start at one unglued side and follow the unique continuation through each quadrilateral and glued old side. Encountering an earlier vertex before the other unglued side would produce a cycle with no possible exit, contradicting connectedness and the remaining unglued side. Thus all vertices are met once and the traversal ends at the other unglued side. In the closed-boundary-strip case all degrees are two, and the same traversal closes into one cycle containing all vertices.

Parametrize every quadrilateral by a rectangle, with its old sides at the two ends in the chain direction and its trace sides at transverse levels zero and one. These parametrizations may be made compatible along successive old-side gluings: choose a PL parameter on the first old side, transport it across each gluing, and choose any increasing PL parameter on the next old side. The resulting four boundary interval maps extend to a PL rectangle map by [F2]. A concrete extension triangulates the boundary breakpoints, adds an interior vertex, and cones the boundary intervals; it is a homeomorphism because its triangular interiors partition the polygonal disk. Each intermediate transverse level then maps to an embedded arc joining the two old sides within that quadrilateral. Gluing the chain gives a PL product rectangle for the entire disk patch. Its two transverse end levels are exactly the two trace arcs, and its other sides are the two original-boundary intervals. The maps therefore give the claimed cellwise trace parallelism without changing an original cell.

In the cycle case cut along one old interval and perform the rectangle construction of step 3.1. Closing that cut identifies its two transverse parameter intervals by a PL interval homeomorphism. If the identification reverses their endpoint order, the two trace sides are joined into one boundary circle, giving the twisted rectangle model of a Mobius band. If it preserves endpoint order, reparametrize one of the end intervals by the inverse identification. The prescribed maps on the two old sides of the adjacent quadrilateral still extend by [F2], so this makes the closing identification the identity without changing the cell containing any point of an intermediate arc. The quotient is then a PL product $S^1\times[0,1]$. For the annulus in the Statement, its two distinct trace boundary circles rule out endpoint reversal. This proves both the product and the stated distinction from a Mobius patch, using only the finite original quadrilateral strip.

Let $F$ be a least-edge-weight essential normal disk in a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. If its normal vector has a nontrivial admissible decomposition, construct the original-triangulation regular diagram and a reduced connected pair $P,H$ using the original-triangulation regular-sum construction and the reduced-connected-pair lemma. Retain their face braids and switch neighborhoods.

After interchanging the two summands if necessary, $P$ is a disk with null-homotopic boundary in $\partial M$, and $H$ is an annulus or a Mobius band. Their intersection consists of $k\ge2$ properly embedded arcs and no circles. Every intersection arc separates $P$ and does not separate $H$. Cutting all the arcs leaves $k+1$ disk patches in $P$ and $k$ disk patches in $H$.

There are at least two patches $E$ of $P$ with exactly one cut-arc side and one original-boundary side. Each has positive edge weight. Choose such a patch of smallest weight. Boundary compression of $H$ along $E$ produces an embedded proper PL disk $D_E$ satisfying

$$w(D_E)=w(H)+2w(E)\le w(H)+w(P)=w(F).$$

If $\partial D_E$ is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then every inequality displayed above is an equality, and normal replacement of $D_E$ can retain an essential disk only at weight $w(F)$. The lemma makes no assertion that this boundary is essential. No irreducibility, orientability or exclusion of projective planes is assumed.

Let $E$ be a leaf disk patch of $P$, with sole cut-arc side $\alpha$. Regularly switch every remaining double arc except $\alpha$, and cut the two parametrizing copies of $\alpha$. There are exactly three disk pieces: $E$, an opposite end disk $E'$, and a middle disk $K$. Their images have pairwise disjoint interiors; their only coincident boundary arcs are the indicated copies of $\alpha$. The irregular switch along $\alpha$ joins $E$ to $E'$ into an embedded proper disk $W$. Its boundary is null-homotopic in $\partial M$.

$$A=K+2E,\qquad A'=K+2E'.$$

Both disks have weight $w(F)$, and their essential normal replacements have exactly $F$'s normal vector and preserve every original edge count. These conclusions do not assert that $E,E'$ are normally isotopic or that their intervening region can be cancelled.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

Let $F$ be a normal surface in a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. Cut $F$ along a finite disjoint trace family satisfying the distinct-normal-side hypothesis of the positive patch-weight lemma, and let $R$ be a connected compact cut patch missing $T^{(1)}$.

If $R$ is a disk with two trace-arc boundary sides and two original-boundary arc sides, then its normal-cell regions form a finite chain of quadrilaterals. The opposite trace arcs are parallel by a PL product parametrization of $R$: every intermediate arc meets each region of this chain in one arc joining its two old sides, and its endpoints stay within the two original boundary sides. These old sides lie in distinct tetrahedral faces.

If $R$ is an annulus whose two boundary components are trace circles and which misses $\partial F$, its normal-cell regions form a finite cycle of quadrilaterals. There is a PL product parametrization by $S^1\times[0,1]$ taking its two trace circles to the two end levels and keeping each intervening arc within its original normal-cell region. A Mobius patch instead has the twisted interval-bundle model and does not have two trace boundary components.

The parallelisms take place on the cut patch, cell by cell in the original triangulation. No ambient three-dimensional product region or cancellation of a separate exchange surface is asserted.

derivations.claim: Put $m=w(E)>0$, using [F1]. Cut $E'$ along all exchange traces in its interior. Every other trace lies wholly inside or wholly outside $E'$: its interior cannot cross the sole trace side in the boundary of $E'$, and all trace endpoints are on the original boundary. Thus this cutting is a proper arc cutting of the disk $E'$. Its pieces are precisely the original cut patches, with the harmless half-switch-band collars of [F3]. They are all disks, and their adjacency graph is a finite tree by [F4]. Exactly one piece can meet the outer trace side of $E'$; mark that vertex of the tree as its root.

Every non-root leaf of this tree is an original leaf disk patch of $P$. Its tree degree equals its full number of trace sides, since the added collars in [F3] preserve that number. If that degree is one, it is a boundary disk patch of one of the original summands. It cannot come from $H$: such a patch would be cut off from $H$ by its sole trace arc and make that arc separating, contrary to [F1]. It is therefore one of the original $P$ leaves and has weight at least $m$. If the tree has only its root vertex, the same argument with its sole exterior trace side shows that $E'$ itself is an original $P$ leaf; this is the asserted case $E'=L$.

Suppose now that there is more than one vertex. The tree has a non-root leaf. By step 2.1 its weight is at least $m$, whereas the weight of the entire $E'$ is exactly $m$ by [F2]. All edge counts of pieces are nonnegative and add: no cut meets an original edge point. Hence there is exactly one non-root leaf $L$, it has weight $m$, and every other piece has weight zero. There cannot be two such leaves, since they would contribute at least $2m>m$. Every finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves. Thus its only leaves are $L$ and the root. It is a path: a vertex of degree at least three would give at least three leaves by extending paths along its three branches. Removing the end piece $L$ leaves a chain of zero-edge disk pieces with a single exterior trace side at either end. Its union is a disk corridor $R$. The remaining sides are two original-boundary arcs, since each interior piece of the chain has two trace sides alternating with its two original-boundary sides.

The patch $R$ is a subsurface of the original normal disk $F$, cut off by its two end traces, and misses every original edge by step 3.1. Those traces satisfy the distinct-side condition [F3]. Apply [F4] to give $R$ its original-cell PL product rectangle. This in particular proves the corridor has no unrecorded twist or fold: its two end traces meet exactly the same chain of original normal cells, with corresponding sides in corresponding faces.

To transport the entire cap, add a small product collar of the inner trace inside $L$. It can be chosen in the same normal cells and disjoint from $T^{(1)}$: in each normal disk the trace is a finite proper polygonal arc away from its vertices, so a sufficiently thin polygonal strip on its $L$ side exists; choose compatible endpoint intervals on the finitely many shared normal sides. The resulting extended rectangle has transverse coordinate in $[-\varepsilon,1]$, with the original inner trace at zero and the outer trace at one. For $0\le s\le1$, compress this transverse interval increasingly onto $[-\varepsilon,s]$, fixing $-\varepsilon$, and fix the rest of $L$. Conjugating by the product maps gives embeddings of the cap, with image $L$ plus the corridor up to level $s$. These maps are continuous in $s$ and PL for each $s$; the interval maps may be chosen affine and the finitely many polygonal product pieces triangulated. The family from $s=1$ to $s=0$ is the asserted cap isotopy. Each moving piece stays within its original normal cell, its boundary endpoints stay on the same old sides, and its support misses every original edge point. At $s=0$ its image is exactly $L$.

The digon whose two sides are paired in the same boundary direction — the
one-polygon word $a\,a$ — realizes the real projective plane
$\mathbb{RP}^2$, taken here as the antipodal quotient $S^2/(x\sim -x)$,
equivalently as the closed upper hemisphere with antipodal boundary points
identified. It is nonorientable and has $V=1$, $E=1$, $F=1$, so
$\chi(\mathbb{RP}^2)=1-1+1=1$
([[def-euler-characteristic-of-a-finite-cw-complex]]). This direct finite
quotient uses no choice axiom.

Here a parametrized PL ball means a finite polyhedron supplied with a piecewise linear homeomorphism, with piecewise linear inverse, to a convex polyhedral ball of the stated dimension. All subpolyhedra and maps in the following assertions are finite.

(a) Let $B_1,B_2$ be parametrized PL three-balls and $D_i\subset\partial B_i$ parametrized PL two-disks. Every PL homeomorphism $f:D_1\to D_2$ extends to a PL homeomorphism $B_1\to B_2$.

(b) The space obtained by gluing two parametrized PL three-balls along parametrized PL two-disks in their boundaries, by a specified PL homeomorphism, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

(c) Let $B$ and $A\subset B$ be parametrized PL three-balls, with $A\ne B$. Suppose $A\cap\partial B=\partial A\cap\partial B=D$ is a parametrized PL two-disk and $A\setminus D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. Impose the following standard boundary-window condition at $C=\partial D$: every point of $C$ has a PL coordinate neighborhood in which
$$B=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0\},\qquad A=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0,\ v\le0\},\qquad D=\{w=0,\ v\le0\}.$$
The equalities are understood after intersection with the coordinate neighborhood, and $C$ corresponds to $v=w=0$. Then $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$, with closure in $B$, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

No assertion about a sphere in an arbitrary PL three-manifold is assumed. In (c) the closure of the set difference is essential: $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb R^3}A$ would retain the interior of the contact disk as an extra sheet. These statements introduce no choice hypothesis.
No closed nonorientable piecewise-linear surface embeds in the standard oriented piecewise-linear three-sphere $S^3$.

derivations.claim: First construct the claimed finite thickening around any compact $C\subset\operatorname{Int}M\setminus T^{(1)}$. Give each tetrahedron its barycentric coordinates $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$. For a sufficiently small common $\epsilon>0$, cut it down to the convex polyhedron $$B_\tau=\{x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i=1,\ x_i+x_j\ge\epsilon\text{ for }i\ne j\}.$$ On an original face its window is the central triangle on which each of the other three coordinates is at least $\epsilon$. Different original face windows are disjoint, because a point in their intersection would have two zero coordinates. The shared windows agree from the two incident tetrahedra. Their union, glued across the interior faces of $T$, contains $C$ in its relative interior for sufficiently small $\epsilon$: the only points where a pair sum vanishes are on original edges, and the finitely many positive pair sums have a positive lower bound on the corresponding compact portions of $C$. Boundary faces do not meet $C$ after a sufficiently small boundary trimming if needed, since $C\subset\operatorname{Int}M$. All pieces and windows are supplied convex parametrized balls and disks.

We record the elementary graph fact needed for the lift. Fix a spanning tree in a finite connected graph and contract its tree edges. Traversing the remaining oriented edges labels each loop by a word in their names and inverses. Cancelling adjacent inverse pairs is exactly path homotopy in the graph: each cancellation retracts a path followed by its reverse, and the space of all reduced paths from a base vertex, joined by the operation of appending one edge and cancelling, is a tree. It has a unique finite edge path between any two vertices, since deleting the last edge repeatedly reaches their longest common initial path. A loop contracting in the graph lifts to a loop in this tree and has empty reduced word, as can also be checked one triangle at a time in a subdivided disk homotopy. If a reduced word $w$ has square equal to the empty word, cyclically cancel its first and last inverse letters until $w=tct^{-1}$ with $c$ cyclically reduced. If $c$ were nonempty, $cc$ would still be reduced and nonempty, so $w^2$ could not reduce to the empty word. Thus $w$ itself is empty. The graph has no nontrivial element of order two.

Separate each glued face window from its two adjacent vertex pieces by thin, disjoint face collars. These have explicit finite PL prism parameters. For completeness, in $B_\tau$ cut the face $x_i=0$ off by $x_i=\eta$, with $\eta>0$ small enough that no other vertex of the polyhedron lies in that slab. Its cross-sections have the same finite face incidence as the central triangle; triangulate corresponding polygonal faces and cone the resulting matching face subdivisions to obtain a PL parameter of the slab as a disk prism. The slabs for different original faces can be chosen disjoint. Cutting them off leaves a convex vertex ball, and the two matching slabs on opposite sides of a glued window form its standard edge prism. The resulting finite space $H$ has disjoint ball vertex pieces and disk-prism edge pieces attached along their marked end windows. It contains $C$ in its interior. Its incidence graph $G$ is the corresponding finite dual graph, allowing loops or repeated edges. Collapse each vertex piece to its vertex and map each prism by its interval parameter. This defines a continuous PL map $p:H\to G$.

Apply the construction with $C=S$, and restrict to its connected component of $H$. The image under $p$ of the core loop in [F1] has square null-homotopic in $G$, because twice that core bounds its face in $S$. By step 1.2 its graph word is empty. Every loop on $S$ is homotopic to a power of that core by [F1], so every loop of $S$ has empty graph word under $p$. There is no appeal here to a choice of a universal cover: the graph paths and their reduced words are explicit finite strings.

Construct the tree of copies of the marked vertex balls and edge prisms by indexing them with reduced paths in the original graph $G$, before contracting its spanning tree in step 1.2. A path has a specified endpoint vertex; deleting successive last edges or appending one edge gives the usual path tree. A window joins the indicated endpoint copies exactly as its original graph edge is appended or cancelled. The projection to $H$ is a local PL homeomorphism, including at the window seams, because it reproduces each finite incident ball/prism chart. The map of $S$ lifts into these copies. One direct finite construction chooses a base point, subdivides the finite surface into pieces lying in ball or prism charts, and assigns the copy at another point by the reduced original-edge path from the base point. Step 3.1 makes this independent of the path: a loop with empty generator word contracts, and its original-edge path cancels to the empty path in the path tree. On each chart this specifies the inverse local projection, and the assignments agree on overlaps. Thus the lift is PL. It is embedded: equal lifted image points would have equal projected image points, and the original map of $S$ is injective.

The lifted finite surface meets only finitely many copies. This can be seen directly in the construction of step 4.1: use a spanning tree of its finite subdivision to choose the chart paths and extend over its finitely many faces; only finitely many finite words occur. Enlarge this finite set of copies by their connecting tree paths and, where the surface meets a window, the adjacent pieces. This gives a finite subtree of parametrized balls and prisms containing the lifted surface; further one-layer enlargement makes its surface points interior. Subdivide each graph edge by a prism node. The resulting finite incidence graph remains a tree, all pieces have their supplied ball parameters, and all attaching windows are the supplied parametrized disks. By the leaf induction [F2] its union is a parametrized PL three-ball. The embedded lift of $S$ contradicts [F1] and [F3]. This excludes the hypothetical zero-edge projective plane and proves the Statement.

Let $P$ be a connected compact surface supplied with a finite PL triangulation. The following conclusions require no choice axiom.

1. If $\partial P\ne\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le1$. Equality holds only for a disk. If instead $\chi(P)=0$, then $P$ is an annulus or a Mobius band; these have respectively two and one boundary circles.
2. If $\partial P=\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P$ is a two-sphere; if $\chi(P)=1$, then $P$ is a projective plane.

Consequently, every positive-Euler connected finite PL surface is a disk, sphere or projective plane. These identifications can be made by PL homeomorphisms between finite polygonal models. In a PL three-manifold without an embedded projective plane, a connected embedded positive-Euler surface is therefore a disk or a sphere.

Let $P$ be a connected compact surface supplied with a finite PL triangulation. The following conclusions require no choice axiom.

1. If $\partial P\ne\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le1$. Equality holds only for a disk. If instead $\chi(P)=0$, then $P$ is an annulus or a Mobius band; these have respectively two and one boundary circles.
2. If $\partial P=\varnothing$, then $\chi(P)\le2$. If $\chi(P)=2$, then $P$ is a two-sphere; if $\chi(P)=1$, then $P$ is a projective plane.

Consequently, every positive-Euler connected finite PL surface is a disk, sphere or projective plane. These identifications can be made by PL homeomorphisms between finite polygonal models. In a PL three-manifold without an embedded projective plane, a connected embedded positive-Euler surface is therefore a disk or a sphere.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$. Every PL embedded projective plane in $\operatorname{Int}M$ meets $T^{(1)}$. The manifold may be nonorientable and may contain projective planes. No irreducibility or choice hypothesis is imposed.

More precisely, every compact subset of $\operatorname{Int}M\setminus T^{(1)}$ lies in the interior of an explicitly parametrized finite thickening of the dual graph, built from convex three-ball vertex pieces and standard disk-prism edge pieces. An embedded projective plane in such a thickening would lift into a parametrized finite tree of these balls, contradicting its nonorientability.

derivations.claim: Suppose $w(K)=0$. The other component of the irregular resolution [F1] is the surface $V$ obtained by joining the two cut-arc sides of the disk $K$. It is connected, embedded and proper; the sole remaining image double arc was resolved. Identifying those two boundary intervals by a joining strip reduces Euler characteristic from one to zero, and its remaining original-boundary intervals are nonempty. Thus $V$ is an annulus or Mobius band by [F2]. It has zero edge weight, since $K$ does and the joining strip misses all edges.

Each component of $\partial V$ is contained in one open original boundary face. Indeed it is a connected polygonal curve in $\partial M\setminus T^{(1)}$, whose components are the open boundary triangles. If $V$ were a Mobius band, [F3] would cap its sole boundary circle by a disk $B$ inside that face. The union $V\cup B$ is an embedded projective plane, still missing $T^{(1)}$. It may be pushed into $\operatorname{Int}M$ while preserving that property. Here a finite local construction suffices: take a compact polygonal subdisk of that same open face containing $B$ in its interior, use the adjacent tetrahedron's affine face prism, and move its bottom subdisk a sufficiently small distance inward, tapering the displacement to zero near the outer prism boundary. Triangulate its finitely many graph-bottom cells and cone matching faces to give an injective PL prism map; on the top and outer sides use the identity. The map moves $B$ and the adjoining collar of $V$ inward. The compact surface misses the old edges, so choose the displacement smaller than its positive distance from them. This gives the embedded interior projective plane excluded by [F4]. Thus $V$ is an annulus.

Label the endpoints of $\alpha$ by $p,q$. Before the join, the two cut sides on $K$ each run from a copy of $p$ to a copy of $q$. In the annular case its two complementary original-boundary arcs connect the two $p$ copies and the two $q$ copies respectively: joining the cut sides without interchanging their ends gives an annulus, whereas interchanging the ends gives the Mobius rectangle model. Consequently one boundary circle of $V$ consists of the $p$-connecting old arc and the short joining arc at $p$; the other is the corresponding $q$ circle. By step 2.1 each such circle lies in the open original face of its endpoint. Its two constituent paths are therefore homotopic with endpoints fixed in that convex face.

The regular disk boundary follows the original boundary arc of $E$, one of the two old arcs of $K$, the boundary arc of $E'$, and the other old arc of $K$, with the directions determined by the annular endpoint matching in step 3.1. The irregular disk $W$ follows the same $E,E'$ arcs with the short joining paths at $p,q$ instead. The endpoint-fixed face homotopies in step 3.1 therefore make $\partial F$ freely homotopic to $\partial W$, up to reversal. But the former is essential and the latter is null-homotopic by [F1], a contradiction. This excludes $w(K)=0$. Finally [F1] gives $w(E)=w(E')$ and $w(F)=w(E)+w(K)+w(E')$, so $w(F)>2w(E)$ as stated.

Choose a least-edge-weight essential normal disk $F$ whose normal vector is lexicographically least among such disks. Suppose a nontrivial vector decomposition has been put into the retained original-triangulation regular diagram and reduced to the pair $P,H$ of the pure boundary-obstruction lemma. Thus $P$ is a disk, $H$ is an annulus or Mobius band, and their remaining intersections are $k\ge2$ proper arcs.

Let $E$ be a leaf disk patch of $P$, with sole cut-arc side $\alpha$. Regularly switch every remaining double arc except $\alpha$, and cut the two parametrizing copies of $\alpha$. There are exactly three disk pieces: $E$, an opposite end disk $E'$, and a middle disk $K$. Their images have pairwise disjoint interiors; their only coincident boundary arcs are the indicated copies of $\alpha$. The irregular switch along $\alpha$ joins $E$ to $E'$ into an embedded proper disk $W$. Its boundary is null-homotopic in $\partial M$.

Replacing either end disk by a second parallel copy of the other produces embedded proper disks

$$A=K+2E,\qquad A'=K+2E'.$$

Both have essential boundary. For every original edge $e$ of $T$,

$$|E\cap e|=|E'\cap e|.$$

Both disks have weight $w(F)$, and their essential normal replacements have exactly $F$'s normal vector and preserve every original edge count. These conclusions do not assert that $E,E'$ are normally isotopic or that their intervening region can be cancelled.

Use the least-weight and lexicographically least disk $F$, reduced boundary pair $P,H$, and leaf/opposite-cap construction of the leaf-cap rigidity lemma. Choose a leaf disk patch $E$ of $P$ with smallest weight among all such leaves, and let $E'$ be its opposite end disk.

View these pieces on the regular full-resolution disk $F$, retaining the two traces of every exchange arc and the exchange rectangle off $F$ between them. Then $E'$ contains exactly one original leaf disk patch $L$ of $P$, with its small half-switch-band collars included. It has $w(L)=w(E)>0$. Either $E'=L$, or the closure of $E'\setminus L$ is a disk corridor with two trace-arc sides, two original-boundary sides, and zero edge weight. In the latter case its original normal-cell product structure gives an isotopy of the cap $E'$ onto $L$ on $F$, fixing its original edge intersections and keeping every point in its original normal cell. This is a finite cap transport on the given normal disk; it asserts no ambient three-dimensional filling or cancellation of a cycle of exchanges.

In the leaf/opposite-cap construction of the leaf-cap rigidity lemma, write the regular disk as $F=E+K+E'$, where $E,E'$ are its two end disks and $K$ is the middle disk. Then $w(K)>0$. In particular

$$w(F)>2w(E)=2w(E').$$

This holds without excluding projective planes from the ambient manifold. The one-skeleton and all switches are those of the original triangulation.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

derivations.claim: There are finitely many original $P$ leaves of minimum positive weight $m$. Map each to the unique minimum leaf contained in its opposite cap, as in [F1]. It cannot map to itself, because the two end caps are disjoint. Iterating this finite function gives a cycle of distinct leaves $E_1,\ldots,E_r$ with $r\ge2$, with indices read modulo $r$. Write $B_i$ for the opposite cap of $E_i$ and $\alpha_i$ for its original exchange arc. Then $B_i$ contains precisely the original minimum leaf $E_{i+1}$ and has weight $m$. The arcs $\alpha_i$ are distinct: one original double arc cuts off only one leaf of $P$ when there are at least two double arcs. Otherwise it would cut $P$ into its two leaves with no room for another cut arc.

The caps $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint. By [F5], non-disjoint caps must be nested or cover $F$ in a pair. Nesting $B_i\subset B_j$ puts the minimum leaf $E_{i+1}$ inside $B_j$, so uniqueness in [F1] forces $E_{i+1}=E_{j+1}$, contrary to distinct cycle indices. A pair covering $F$ gives $w(F)\le w(B_i)+w(B_j)=2m$, contrary to [F2]. Thus neither overlap is possible.

Put $R_i=\overline{B_i\setminus E_{i+1}}$, with closure in $F$. This is the zero-edge corridor of [F1]. It is nonempty. Its outer trace is the opposite-cap trace of $\alpha_i$, while its inner trace is the original leaf trace of the distinct arc $\alpha_{i+1}$. These are disjoint distinct traces by [F3] and [F5], so the two caps cannot be equal. The corridors $R_i$ have pairwise disjoint interiors by step 2.1. Their union carries no original edge point.

Remove the caps $B_i$ from $F$ and retain the closure $F_0$ of their complement. It is a disk with the outer trace of each $B_i$ as a boundary interval: successively removing disjoint end caps from a disk has this effect. All original $E_i$ lie in the removed caps, since $E_i\subset B_{i-1}$. Across the rectangular exchange surface for $\alpha_i$, join $E_i$ to $F_0$ at the outer trace of $B_i$. These attachments are disjoint by [F3]. Attaching each disk along its one interval, with its rectangular collar, gives an embedded disk made of $F_0$, the $E_i$ and the attaching rectangles. Its discarded complementary pieces are precisely the corridors $R_i$, with the other local continuations at these exchange arcs. The next step identifies both continuations in the original diagram.

Fix $i$. Label the original rays in cyclic order $0,1,2,3$ so that $0$ is $E_i$'s $P$ ray and $1$ is $B_i$'s $H$ ray. These are adjacent, as proved by the leaf/opposite-cap supplier in [F1]. The other $P$ ray is $2$, and the other $H$ ray is $3$. The regular full resolution pairs $0$ with $3$ and $1$ with $2$: the other adjacent pairing would join the two end caps and is irregular. The trace between $0,3$ is the boundary of $E_i$, and that between $1,2$ is the boundary of $B_i$. Near the first trace, ray $3$ lies in $R_{i-1}$; near the second, ray $1$ lies in $R_i$ and ray $2$ lies in $F_0$. Thus the attachment of step 4.1 pairs retained rays $0,2$, while the discarded corridors pair rays $1,3$. These are exactly the two original unswitched continuations. There is no irregular switch in this construction.

At every arc outside the cycle retain the original regular resolution. Neither the retained/discarded division nor its frontier crosses either trace of such an arc, because its frontier consists solely of the cycle traces used in step 5.1. Thus each local regular output has both of its incident parts retained or both discarded. At every cycle arc, use the two unswitched continuations of step 5.1. Hence this is precisely the original partial regular resolution that leaves the cycle arcs unswitched and resolves all others regularly. Its normalization splits into a retained union containing the disk in step 4.1 and a discarded union consisting of the nonempty $R_i$ with their indicated continuations. The local pairing check ensures neither union has a frontier in that normalization; intersections of their images along an unswitched arc do not identify their parametrizing sheets.

Every discarded piece and its short continuing strip misses $T^{(1)}$, by step 3.1 and [F3]. Their union is nonempty and is a union of normalization components by step 6.1. Choose one such component. It is a nonempty zero-edge component of an actual partial regular resolution, contradicting [F4]. This contradiction also covers the case where the cycle contains every arc: that partial resolution is just the original unswitched pair, whose tetrahedral disks still have normal vertices. Therefore the hypothetical reduced boundary pair does not occur.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. If $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then it contains a normal disk with that property. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is required. The construction is allowed to replace disk pieces and to change the isotopy class of the original disk; it asserts existence of a normal replacement.

Let $F$ be a least-edge-weight essential normal disk in a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. If its normal vector has a nontrivial admissible decomposition, construct the original-triangulation regular diagram and a reduced connected pair $P,H$ using the original-triangulation regular-sum construction and the reduced-connected-pair lemma. Retain their face braids and switch neighborhoods.

After interchanging the two summands if necessary, $P$ is a disk with null-homotopic boundary in $\partial M$, and $H$ is an annulus or a Mobius band. Their intersection consists of $k\ge2$ properly embedded arcs and no circles. Every intersection arc separates $P$ and does not separate $H$. Cutting all the arcs leaves $k+1$ disk patches in $P$ and $k$ disk patches in $H$.

There are at least two patches $E$ of $P$ with exactly one cut-arc side and one original-boundary side. Each has positive edge weight. Choose such a patch of smallest weight. Boundary compression of $H$ along $E$ produces an embedded proper PL disk $D_E$ satisfying

$$w(D_E)=w(H)+2w(E)\le w(H)+w(P)=w(F).$$

If $\partial D_E$ is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then every inequality displayed above is an equality, and normal replacement of $D_E$ can retain an essential disk only at weight $w(F)$. The lemma makes no assertion that this boundary is essential. No irreducibility, orientability or exclusion of projective planes is assumed.

The reduced boundary pair in the pure boundary-obstruction lemma cannot occur for a least-weight, lexicographically least essential normal disk. The contradiction is in the original triangulation: a finite cycle of minimum leaf patches would give a nonempty zero-edge normalization component of a partial regular resolution, whose tetrahedral pieces are all genuine normal disks.

derivations.claim: Suppose the vector of $F$ were not fundamental. By [[def-normal-surface-coordinate-box]], it would be $x+y$ for two nonzero admissible integer vectors. Their quad supports are compatible, since their nonnegative sum has at most one quad type in any tetrahedron. Thus [F2] supplies its actual original-triangulation reduced boundary pair. The assumed weight and lexicographic minimality are exactly those of [F3], which excludes that pair. This contradiction proves fundamentalness of $F$.

For the consequence, normalize the given essential disk by [F1]. The set of essential normal disks is therefore nonempty. Its edge weights are positive integers, so choose their least value. Among vectors at this value, lexicographic minimization requires only finitely many natural-number minima: minimize the first coordinate, then the second among those retained, and so on through the $7t$ coordinates. Each step leaves a nonempty set, and the resulting vector is realized by an essential normal disk. This finite construction uses no selection from an infinite family. Apply step 1.1 to that disk to obtain the claimed fundamental one in the same triangulation.

derivations.claim: There is an integer $n\ge1$ and two nonzero admissible integer vectors $x,y$, neither proportional to $d$, with $nd=x+y$. Here is the rational linear algebra behind this assertion. The smallest face of the nonnegative matching cone containing $d$ is obtained by setting its zero coordinates to zero. If that face has dimension at least two, its matching nullspace, restricted to the positive coordinates of $d$, has dimension at least two. Adding the equation that coordinate sum is zero leaves a nonzero null vector $h$. The coefficient matrix is integral, so ordinary finite rational row reduction gives such an $h$ rational; clear denominators to make it integral. It is not proportional to $d$, since its coordinate sum is zero while that of $d$ is positive. For a sufficiently large integer $N$, both $Nd+h$ and $Nd-h$ are nonnegative and supported on $d$. They are admissible because that support permits only $d$'s quad type in each tetrahedron, and they sum to $2Nd$. This proves the assertion. Conversely the face could have dimension one only if $d$ were on an extreme ray, contrary to the hypothesis.

Choose $n$ least among these decompositions. It is at least two, since $D$ is fundamental. Also $d$ has coordinate gcd one: otherwise division by that gcd would split it into two nonzero admissible integer vectors. A connected normal component with vector proportional to $d$ must therefore have vector $jd$ for a positive integer $j$. Indeed a Bezout integer combination of the coordinates of $d$ is one, so the same combination of the proportional integral vector gives its proportionality scalar as an integer. By [F1] a realization of $jd$ has the abstract surface of $j$ disjoint copies of $D$; connectedness forces $j=1$. Thus any such component is a copy of $D$.

Among regular diagrams for the least $n$, choose one with the least number of double curves, allowing the diagrams obtained by partial regular absorption as in [F1]. Neither family has a component with vector proportional to $d$. Such a component would have vector $d$ by step 2.1; subtracting it from $nd=x+y$ gives a nonproportional decomposition of $(n-1)d$, contrary to minimality. The remaining vector on its side is nonzero and not proportional, since otherwise the entire side would have been proportional. Every component of either family intersects the other family: a disjoint component survives unchanged into the full resolution, which has the abstract surface of $nD$ by [F1], and would consequently be a copy of $D$, just excluded.

Both families are connected. Suppose, for example, that $Y$ has distinct components, and choose one $Z$. Regularly absorb all the other $Y$ components into $X$, giving a surface $W$. It is embedded and normal: the only remaining old double curves join its sheets to $Z$, so it has no self-intersection, and all tetrahedral pieces remain normal by [F1]. Now $nd=v(W)+v(Z)$. The vector of $Z$ is not proportional by step 3.1, and that of $W$ cannot be proportional either, since then $nd-v(W)=v(Z)$ would be. Thus this is another eligible diagram for the same $n$. Its remaining double curves are exactly the former curves between $X$ and $Z$. There are strictly fewer: every absorbed $Y$ component intersected $X$ by step 3.1. This contradicts the chosen minimum. The same argument interchanging families proves connectedness of $X$.

Their Euler characteristics sum to $n$ by [F3]. They cannot both be closed, since their resolution has nonempty boundary. If exactly one is closed, every double curve is a circle, so the other surface's boundary is unchanged by resolution and consists of $n$ circles. Since $n\ge2$, that connected boundary surface has Euler characteristic at most zero by [F2]. The closed summand has Euler characteristic at most two. Hence $n=2$, the closed summand has characteristic two and is a sphere, and the other has characteristic zero and two boundary circles and is an annulus. If both have boundary, each has Euler characteristic at most one, so again $n=2$ and both are disks. The full-resolution surface has vector $2d$, so [F1] gives its two disk components and their boundary homotopy classes. In the sphere case those are exactly the unchanged annulus boundary curves.

Finally assume the extra weight and essentiality hypotheses and that both disk summands were essential. Their positive weights add to $2w(D)$, while each is at least $w(D)$; hence both equal $w(D)$. Their vectors satisfy $x+y=2d$. If either differs from $d$, at the first differing coordinate the two differences have opposite nonzero signs. One vector would be lexicographically smaller than $d$, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus both equal $d$, contrary to their nonproportionality. At least one disk summand must therefore have null-homotopic boundary, as asserted. No conclusion excluding that case or the sphere-annulus case has been used.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. 1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

Take an actual original-triangulation regular normal diagram, retaining its face braids after any preliminary whole-curve regular switches. Choose a nonempty union $S$ of whole components of its parametrizing normalization. Assume every remaining double curve incident to $S$ has both branches in $S$. Retain its geometric strands, tetrahedral disk pieces and remaining double curves, and write $W_S$ for the total number of its original edge-intersection points, counted on those parametrizing components.

Resolve any selection of these remaining curves regularly or irregularly. If at least one irregular switch is made, and the resulting normalization has a component whose image is an embedded proper disk with essential boundary in $\partial M$, then the original triangulation contains an essential normal disk of weight strictly less than $W_S$.

The chosen $S$ may be a single immersed parametrizing component with self-double curves; no partition of it into two globally embedded normal families is assumed. The closure condition concerns the actual remaining double curves, not merely a selection of tetrahedral disk types.

derivations.claim: Isolate the selected curve as in [F1]. Outside its switching neighborhood all components of $F$ other than $D$ remain unchanged. Inside it both resolved trace germs belonged to $D$, so only the part assembled from $D$ can be affected. If that part's parametrizing normalization has more than one component, it has exactly two, and the remaining double curve joins them. Indeed changing a single crossing pairing changes the number of components by at most one; moreover the full regular resolution joins the affected components into the one connected disk $D$. A component not incident to that crossing would survive as a separate component after full resolution. Each of the two components is embedded: the only remaining double points have one branch on each of them, and each tetrahedral parametrizing disk is embedded by [F1]. They are therefore two nonempty embedded normal surfaces, with vectors summing to $v(D)$ because all the selected tetrahedral pieces and edge points came from $D$. This contradicts [F3]. Consequently the affected normalization must be connected. It has edge weight exactly $w(D)$ and is closed under its sole remaining double curve; its image is disjoint from the unchanged components of $F$.

We specify the local pairing used in the topology below. In a transverse rectangle to the exchange core, regard the exchange interval as horizontal, with its two frontier points at the left and right. Label the upper rays at these points $0,1$, and the lower rays $2,3$. The resolved surface joins the two rays at each frontier point. A cap at the left and a cap at the right are adjacent precisely when their selected rays are both upper or both lower. The unswitched crossing pairs the opposite diagonal rays $0$ with $3$, and $1$ with $2$; the opposite, irregular resolution pairs $0$ with $1$, and $2$ with $3$. This description propagates along the annulus or disk because its given rectangular switching neighborhood is a product. Thus the following component counts can be checked by tracing the cut disk pieces through these two pairs, without using a picture or an ambient sphere theorem.

For a proper exchange disk the two disjoint proper trace arcs cut $D$ into three disks in a path: two outer caps and one middle disk. If the outer caps are nonadjacent, their two rays are a diagonal pair in step 1.2. Undoing the exchange consequently joins those two caps to each other, and joins the two remaining sides of the middle disk to each other. These are separate nonempty parametrizing components. Their possible boundary twisting does not affect their being separate: one contains the two outer caps, the other the middle disk. This contradicts step 1.1. The outer caps must be adjacent.

For an exchange annulus first suppose the two trace circles bound disjoint caps. Cutting them off leaves a disk with two holes. If the caps were nonadjacent, the diagonal pairing of step 1.2 would join the two caps to each other, and separately join the two inner boundary circles of the complementary disk with two holes. Again this gives two nonempty parametrizing components, contradicting step 1.1. Thus disjoint caps are adjacent.

It remains to exclude nested trace circles. Write the three cut pieces of $D$ as the inner disk $E$, the intervening annulus $R$, and the outer annulus $Q$ carrying $\partial D$. At the inner trace the two germs belong to $E,R$; at the outer trace they belong to $R,Q$. There are two cases for the diagonal pairing. If it pairs $E$ to $Q$, its other pair joins the two sides of $R$, giving two components; step 1.1 excludes this. Otherwise it pairs $E$ to one side of $R$ and the other side of $R$ to $Q$, so the affected normalization is one immersed component. In this second case the opposite, irregular pairing joins $E$ directly to $Q$ and the two sides of $R$ to each other. The first of these resolved components is a properly embedded disk: an annulus joins the disk $E$ to the inner boundary of $Q$, and its remaining boundary is exactly $\partial D$. The other is a closed component formed from $R$. These are embedded because the sole remaining double curve has now been resolved and the original construction creates no new intersections.

The connected immersed component in the second case has weight $w(D)$ by step 1.1 and is closed under its remaining self-double curve. Its irregular resolution in step 2.3 has an embedded proper disk with the same essential boundary as $D$. Apply [F2] to that component alone. This does not require the intervening annulus $R$ to have positive edge weight: the retained-subdiagram first-turnback argument also applies when the closed output has weight zero. Both nested cases are therefore excluded. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2 this proves all asserted disjointness and adjacency clauses.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$, and let $F$ be a normal surface. Its normal disks form polygonal cells with three or four sides. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite disjoint family of PL simple closed curves and properly embedded PL arcs on $F$. Suppose $\Lambda$ misses the normal-cell vertices, is transverse to the cell edges, and meets each normal disk in disjoint properly embedded arcs whose endpoints are on distinct sides of that disk.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation. If $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, then it contains a normal disk with that property. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is required. The construction is allowed to replace disk pieces and to change the isotopy class of the original disk; it asserts existence of a normal replacement.

For a finite tetrahedral triangulation, let $B$ record the six local edge-intersection counts in every tetrahedron from its seven normal coordinates. Let $u,v,d$ be nonnegative real normal-coordinate arrays, each using at most one quadrilateral type in each tetrahedron. They need not satisfy matching equations. If $\alpha,\beta>0$ and

$$\alpha Bu+\beta Bv=(\alpha+\beta)Bd,$$

then

$$\alpha u+\beta v=(\alpha+\beta)d.$$

In particular, if $u,v,d$ are actual normal-surface vectors, the hypothesis may be checked on their global triangulation-edge intersection counts. If those counts for $u$ and $v$ average to those for $d$, then their normal-coordinate vectors also average to $d$.

If $d$ is lexicographically least in any set of vectors containing $u,v,d$, this averaging identity forces $u=v=d$. Thus two essential normal disks of the same least edge weight whose edge counts average to those of a lexicographically least such disk must have exactly that disk's normal vector.

derivations.claim: For a proper disk exchange, cut $D$ along its two traces into the outer caps $E,E'$ and middle disk $K$. The irregular resolution of the connected inverse diagram in [F1] joins $E$ to $E'$ along the exchange, producing an embedded proper disk $W$; the remaining sides of $K$ join to form the other component. These pairings are the upper-upper and lower-lower pairs in the transverse four-ray description of [F1]. All other crossings have already been resolved, so these images are embedded. If $\partial W$ were essential, [F2] would contradict the least weight of $D$. Thus $\partial W$ is null-homotopic in $\partial M$.

Form the two cap replacements $A,A'$. For an annular exchange these are $D$ with $E'$ replaced by the disk consisting of the exchange annulus capped by a nearby copy of $E$, and the reverse replacement. They are embedded proper PL disks with boundary exactly $\partial D$. For a proper disk exchange attach two nearby copies of $E$ to the two frontier arcs of $K$, using the exchange strips, to obtain $A$; use two copies of $E'$ to obtain $A'$. These are again embedded disks. In detail take disjoint small product collars of the finitely many PL cap and strip cells; on each transverse exchange rectangle the two cap copies and the middle rays are joined in separate parallel levels. The maps agree along face boundaries by the supplied exchange neighborhood, and outside that neighborhood the disjoint cut pieces are unchanged. A disk joined to another disk along a boundary interval remains a disk, so the two successive attachments give the claimed disk topology. The collars can be chosen small enough to avoid all remaining surface pieces and to move edge points only along their own original edges.

The proper-disk replacements also have essential boundary. To see this precisely, let $u$ and $v$ be the original-boundary arcs of $E,E'$, transporting the endpoints of $v$ to those of $u$ by the two boundary sides of the exchange disk in $\partial M$. The circle $\partial W$ is then $uv^{-1}$ with those connectors. Its null homotopy from step 1.1 says that $u$ and the transported $v$ are homotopic with fixed endpoints. The boundary of $A$ is obtained from $\partial D$ by substituting a transported copy of $u$ for $v$, and the boundary of $A'$ by the reverse substitution. Both are therefore homotopic to $\partial D$ in $\partial M$ and are essential. Together with the unchanged boundary in the annular case, both replacements in step 1.2 are eligible essential PL disks.

Let $K$ now denote the remainder of $D$ after removing the two cap interiors; in the annular case it is a disk with two holes, and in the proper case the middle disk. The exchange strips miss every original edge. The collars and copies of step 1.2 consequently give the exact componentwise identities $N(A)=N(K)+2N(E)$ and $N(A')=N(K)+2N(E')$, whereas $N(D)=N(K)+N(E)+N(E')$. In particular $N(A)+N(A')=2N(D)$. Normalize the two essential disks by [F4] to $U,V$. Their counts satisfy $N(U)+N(V)\le2N(D)$ componentwise. Each has weight at least $w(D)$, while the sum of their weights is at most $2w(D)$. Thus both weights equal $w(D)$ and every componentwise deficit is zero: $N(U)+N(V)=2N(D)$.

Apply the two-output rigidity and lexicographic assertion in [F4]. It gives $v(U)=v(V)=v(D)$ and hence $N(U)=N(V)=N(D)$. Since $N(U)\le N(A)$ and $N(V)\le N(A')$, while their sums are equal by step 3.1, no edge count fell in either normalization. Therefore $N(A)=N(A')=N(D)$. Subtracting their identities in step 3.1 gives $2N(E)=2N(E')$, so $N(E)=N(E')$. Finally [F3] gives their positive total edge weight. All assertions, including the null-homotopic boundary of $W$, now follow. The equality of these edge counts has not been used to infer a relative normal isotopy of the caps.

Its one trace circle bounds the unique disk cap $E_i$ not containing $\partial D_i$. Put $K_i=\overline{D_i\setminus E_i}$. This is an annulus with outer boundary $\partial D_i$. The two end components are disjoint, and the interior of $A$ misses both of them. derivations.claim: First note the proper-disk cutting fact. Transfer a parametrized three-ball $B$ to a convex model, and let $A$ be a properly embedded PL disk in it. Its boundary separates $\partial B$ into two parametrized disk caps $C_0,C_1$ by [F2]. Each $A\cup C_i$ is a parametrized PL sphere: glue two disk parameters along their specified boundary identification and cone compatible boundary subdivisions. By [F3] it bounds a parametrized ball $B_i$. The bounded side is contained in $B$, since the connected exterior of the convex ball $B$ is disjoint from that sphere and is on its unbounded side. Moreover $B_i\cap\partial B=C_i$: points of the other open cap are not on its sphere and have neighbors in the exterior of $B$, so lie on its exterior side. The two balls have disjoint interiors. Indeed the interior of $B_0$ is connected and misses $\partial B_1=A\cup C_1$; near the open cap $C_0$ it lies outside $B_1$, so it lies outside throughout. Finally they fill $B$: local half-ball charts along $C_0,C_1$ and the two opposite sides of $A$ show that their union is a neighborhood of its points relative to $B$; any omitted component would be open and closed in the connected ball. The local charts here are finite PL charts, obtained by coning the polygonal link arcs or circles and their complementary disks, as in [F2]. Thus cutting $B$ along $A$ gives these two supplied balls. Iterating proves that a disjoint finite proper-disk arrangement cuts $B$ into parametrized balls.

Match the two surfaces' points in each edge in their linear order [F1], and extend the match to an increasing PL self-homeomorphism of that edge fixing its endpoints. On each triangular face choose the arc correspondence of [F1]. The disjoint proper arcs cut the face into polygonal disks. Map corresponding arcs by PL interval maps matching their prescribed endpoints; these maps and the edge maps prescribe each complementary disk's boundary homeomorphism. Extend it by [F2] and paste. The result is a PL self-homeomorphism of every face, carrying the arc system to its counterpart and agreeing on shared edges.

Fix a tetrahedron. Its prescribed boundary homeomorphism in step 1.2 matches its normal-disk boundary circles. Choose a PL map of each disk to its counterpart extending that boundary map, by [F2]. Cut each of the two disk arrangements into parametrized balls by step 1.1. Their incidence trees correspond: on the boundary sphere the same matched circles have the same complementary regions, and cutting off one disk splits one region into two. The already prescribed boundary and disk maps therefore give a PL homeomorphism of each cut ball's entire boundary to that of its counterpart. Use their ball parameters and [F3] to extend across each cut ball. These extensions agree along the disk sheets and give a PL homeomorphism of the tetrahedron carrying its disk arrangement to the other and realizing its prescribed face map.

Do this in every tetrahedron. Their face maps were already identical on identified faces, so the resulting maps and their inverses paste to a finite PL homeomorphism of $M$ preserving every simplex and carrying the first normal surface to the second. All constructions used only finite subdivisions and conings of supplied disks and balls. In particular step 2.1 did not presume that arbitrary PL disk replacements were ambient isotopies; their required ambient ball maps were actually constructed using [F3].

For the consequence, take one normal disk $D$ with the common vector. It has a finite normal product collar. To construct it, first choose sufficiently small parallel face-arc families with their matching edge intervals. Extend these prescribed boundaries over the parallel standard disk prisms in each tetrahedron; the preceding relative disk, face and ball extension constructions make the finitely many prism parameters agree with the face parameters. Their transverse interval labels can be chosen consistently on $D$: choose one sign in one chart and propagate through a finite disk triangulation; the only possible inconsistency would reverse the sign around a loop, whereas every loop on the disk contracts through its triangles, on each of which the local product labels agree. This gives the product of that disk with the common labeled interval, including the boundary half-space charts, where its vertical boundary stays in $\partial M$. Its width can be chosen smaller than the positive separation from the finite vertex set. Its fibers stay in the ambient simplex of their central point. Denote its two end disks by $D^-,D^+$. Their union has vector $2v(D)$, as does $D_0\cup D_1$. By step 3.1 an ambient simplex-preserving PL homeomorphism carries one union to the other, matching its connected components up to permutation. Transport the supplied product by that map or its inverse. It is the asserted vertex-free finite PL product between $D_0,D_1$, with the required vertical boundary and fiber incidence.

derivations.claim: First straighten the face strips relative to their end and side data. In a face strip the disjoint arcs of $A$ join its opposite horizontal sides. They match their endpoints in order: two matched pairs in reversed order would alternate on the boundary of the strip and would have to intersect, by [F2]. Keep the lower horizontal arc as the base interval. Choose an increasing PL parametrization of the upper horizontal arc matching these finitely many marked endpoints. Keep the two vertical sides parametrized by their prescribed original edge intervals; their endpoints already agree. Compare this marked arc arrangement with the vertical intervals over the marked lower endpoints in a standard rectangle. Choose its interval maps on the marked arcs and extend over each complementary disk by [F2]. This supplies a product parametrization of the entire face strip making all its $A$ arcs vertical, preserving each of its four boundary sides and agreeing with the selected end and edge parametrizations. When strips share an original edge interval, use that one fixed interval parametrization on both, so the maps agree there.

Fix one tetrahedral prism $B$ and let its lower disk be its base. The frontier arcs of its $A$ rectangles are disjoint proper arcs in that disk. The face-strip maps just constructed match their endpoints to the corresponding endpoints in the upper disk. Each rectangle connects precisely its two lower endpoints to its two upper endpoints; the distinct-face hypothesis identifies the endpoints individually by their original faces. Thus the same boundary-order matching carries each lower arc's endpoint pair to its upper counterpart. These arrangements have the same complementary regions: disjoint proper arcs in a disk have pairings determined by their boundary endpoints, and cutting successively along them produces the same finite disk-region incidence tree. Map the lower disk to itself, map the upper disk to that base by extending its prescribed boundary and arc maps across these regions using [F2], and use the maps of step 1.1 on all side strips. We have a prescribed homeomorphism of the entire prism boundary to the boundary of the standard product of its lower disk with the interval. It maps each actual rectangle boundary to the boundary of the vertical rectangle over its lower frontier arc.

Extend the last boundary map over the prism with its rectangle arrangement, rather than presuming the arrangement is vertical already. The actual rectangles are disjoint proper PL disks in the parametrized ball $B$, so [F1] cuts $B$ into parametrized balls. The comparison vertical rectangles cut the standard product into the balls given by its lower disk regions times the interval. Their boundary incidence trees agree by the endpoint and arc correspondence in step 2.1. Choose maps on each actual rectangle to its vertical counterpart extending the already prescribed boundary map, using [F2]. The outer prism map and these rectangle maps now prescribe the complete boundary map on each cut ball. Extend over each ball by [F1] and paste. This gives a PL product parametrization of $B$ agreeing with every prescribed face-strip and horizontal disk map and making its part of $A$ vertical. Its fibers stay inside this tetrahedron, and on its side strips stay in their original faces.

Perform this construction in every tetrahedral prism. On a common face strip their maps agree with the single map already constructed there, including the horizontal boundary intervals. Their lower disks glue to $D_0$, so the resulting maps paste to a parametrization of all of $P$ by $D_0\times[0,1]$. Each actual exchange rectangle is vertical and their gluings agree through the faces. Consequently $A$ is exactly $\beta\times[0,1]$, where $\beta$ is its frontier circle or proper arc on $D_0$. No original simplex is crossed by a fiber: this holds in the prism interiors and was already imposed on their face and edge strata.

If $\beta$ is a circle, it bounds a disk cap $C$ in the disk $D_0$ by [F2]. The supplied subproduct $C\times[0,1]$ is a product between that cap and the cap on $D_1$, with vertical boundary $A$. If $\beta$ is a proper arc, cutting $D_0$ along it gives two disk caps $C,C'$ by [F2]. Their products give both corresponding cap pairs. The part of each vertical boundary other than $\beta\times[0,1]=A$ is over a subarc of $\partial D_0$, hence lies in the prescribed vertical boundary of $P$ in $\partial M$. Following the fibers supplies compatible normal deformations of all cap pieces with these precise frontier tracks. This is the asserted normal parallelism along $A$, proved from the actual marked prism data.

Let $P$ be a supplied cellwise normal product between disjoint equal-vector connected normal disks $D_0,D_1$ in a finite simplicial three-manifold triangulation. Thus each tetrahedral part of $P$ is a parametrized disk prism between corresponding normal disk pieces, each face part is the corresponding normal-arc strip, and the product fibers stay in their original ambient simplex.

Suppose an embedded exchange annulus or proper exchange disk $A$ lies in $P$, misses the original one-skeleton, and spans $D_0,D_1$. More explicitly, its two frontier components are respectively a circle or proper arc on each end disk; it meets each tetrahedral prism in disjoint proper rectangles, each with one frontier arc on each horizontal end, joining the same two distinct original faces at both ends; its remaining sides are the face arcs of $A$. In the disk case its remaining boundary is in the vertical boundary of $P$ in $\partial M$.

The product parametrization can be chosen to make $A$ vertical, while its fibers still remain in their original ambient simplex. In the annulus case the two disk caps bounded by its frontier cobound a normal product with vertical boundary $A$. In the disk case both pairs of corresponding disk caps cut off by its frontier arcs cobound such products, with the other vertical boundary strips in $\partial M$. In particular these caps are normally parallel along $A$.

derivations.claim: Use the actual small rectangular switching neighborhood of [F1]. Inside each tetrahedron a piece of $A$ is a rectangle with its two frontier sides on the full-resolution sheets and its other two sides in the two distinct faces crossed by that original double arc. Its two frontier sides lie respectively on $D_0$ and $D_1$: these are the two entire frontier components stipulated in the Statement, so following either component cannot change its full-resolution component. The rectangle's interior misses $F$ and all original edges. Different such pieces have disjoint interiors because the selected exchange surface and its switching neighborhood are embedded.

Each such open rectangle lies in one tetrahedral prism of $P$. Indeed the interiors of those prisms are the components between their horizontal normal sheets inside that tetrahedron. Passing from one to another inside the tetrahedron would cross a horizontal $D_0$ or $D_1$ sheet or an original edge; the rectangle's interior crosses neither. Its two frontier sides consequently lie on the two horizontal ends of that one prism. They cannot be different normal pieces on the same horizontal end, since one side belongs to $D_0$ and the other to $D_1$. Thus they lie on the corresponding disk pieces bounding the prism. Their endpoints are on the same two distinct original faces, by step 1.1. Similarly, in a face strip each side of the exchange gives a proper arc joining the two horizontal arcs: it cannot leave the strip across an edge interval, since it misses the original edges. In the proper-disk case the remaining boundary of $A$ lies in $\partial M$ and hence in the prescribed vertical boundary of $P$. Apply [F2] to these finite rectangle and face-strip families.
