derivations.claim: A transverse finite PL closed loop has a well-defined intersection count with $S$ modulo two, and this count is invariant under PL homotopy. Here is the finite representative argument needed for that assertion. Subdivide a homotopy annulus and the ambient finite PL charts until its pieces lie in charts straightening $S$. Put its interior vertices in general position, keeping its transverse boundary loops fixed. Such positions exist by avoiding finitely many affine equalities in each chart; a common finite subdivision makes the constructions agree on chart overlaps. In each chart, transverse intersection is the inverse image of one linear coordinate being zero. On the triangulated annulus these pieces paste to a compact PL one-manifold: interior points have two incident sides and boundary points have one. It consists of finitely many circles and arcs. Each arc has two boundary endpoints, so the total number of intersections on the two boundary loops is even. This proves the asserted invariance, with no orientation signs. The argument also permits an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of a loop or homotopy relative to already transverse boundary data.

Every finite PL closed loop is PL homotopic to an edge loop in $T$. For an explicit finite construction, realize the finite abstract complex in a Euclidean space by its barycentric coordinates. The inverse images of its finitely many open vertex stars cover the parameter circle. Subdivide the circle sufficiently finely that the image of each closed vertex star of that subdivision lies in one of these target stars, and assign that source vertex a witnessing target vertex. The vertices assigned to the ends of a source edge belong to the carrier simplex of every interior image point on that edge; consequently they span an edge or coincide. They define an edge loop. The original map and this edge map are carried by common original simplices, so they are homotopic within those simplices. Explicitly subdivide further where the original PL map changes its carrier, triangulate each homotopy prism, and extend linearly from the two boundary maps; each such extension stays in its convex carrier simplex. This gives the claimed PL homotopy. Since $S$ misses the target vertices and is transverse to the target edges, the resulting edge loop is transverse after harmless parametrization and a small perturbation at its vertices disjoint from $S$.

An edge loop crosses $S$ an even number of times. Indeed each traversal of an original edge contributes its even intersection number, with multiplicity; backtracking and repeated edges do not affect parity. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 every transverse finite PL closed loop has even intersection count with $S$. The argument allows boundary edges: $S$ is disjoint from the boundary of $M$, so any small inward displacement there is disjoint from $S$ and changes no count.

Suppose $M\setminus S$ were connected. Choose one straightening chart at a point of $S$ and a short interval crossing its coordinate plane once. Its endpoints lie in the complement and can be joined there by a finite PL path. To justify the path assertion without a selection principle, the set reachable from one endpoint by finite polygonal paths in PL charts is open and its complement is open; connectedness makes the reachable set the entire complement. Membership supplies just one finite chart chain and finitely many joining points. Concatenate that path with the transverse interval, then perturb away any extraneous tangencies while staying in the complement along the joining path. The resulting finite PL closed loop crosses $S$ exactly once. This contradicts step 2.1. Hence the complement is disconnected. All selections and subdivisions were finite; no orientability or ball bounded by $S$ was used.

In an actual original-triangulation regular normal diagram, suppose two distinct full-resolution components $D_0,D_1$ have vector $d=v(D)$. Let one of its exchange annuli $A$ have one frontier circle on each of these components, with its usual rectangular switching neighborhood and interior disjoint from the full resolution.

Let $E_i\subset D_i$ be the disk cap bounded by that circle. Then $N(E_0)=N(E_1)$ on every original global edge and $w(E_0)=w(E_1)>0$. Replacing either cap by the other cap joined across $A$ gives an embedded proper essential PL disk with the original boundary of that copy. Each replacement has edge-count vector $N(D)$, and every componentwise edge-nonincreasing essential normal replacement of it has vector $d$.

No irreducibility, orientability or fundamentalness assumption is required. Equal edge counts here do not assert that the caps are normally parallel or that the exchange lies in the product between the two copies.

Let two distinct disk components $D_0,D_1$ bound a supplied cellwise normal disk product $P$: its tetrahedral pieces are the disk prisms between corresponding normal pieces, its face pieces are their normal-arc strips, and its fibers stay in their original simplices.

Let $A$ be an exchange annulus or proper exchange disk of that diagram, with one frontier component on each $D_i$, with its usual rectangular switching neighborhood. Suppose $A\subset P$. Then the product can be parametrized to make $A$ vertical while preserving its simplex incidence. In the annular case its two disk caps are normally parallel along $A$. Let $M$ be a connected compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. Let $S\subset\operatorname{int}M$ be a connected closed locally flat PL surface. Suppose $S$ misses the original vertices, is transverse to the original edges, and meets every original global edge in an even number of points. Then $M\setminus S$ is disconnected. Neither $M$ nor $S$ is assumed orientable, and no irreducibility or choice principle is required.

derivations.claim: The union $S=E_0\cup A\cup E_1$ is an embedded PL two-sphere in the interior of the ambient component containing $P$. Its abstract surface is a capped annulus, and its pieces have disjoint interiors. Keep this union as a PL surface without moving its points. It is locally flat: off the attaching circles it inherits the normal disk and exchange-rectangle product charts; along them a transverse switching rectangle contains two incident rays, which straighten by a finite sector map to a line. These are charts for the unchanged subset, so no rounding moves it into the interior of $P$. Its original-edge counts are $N(S)=N(E_0)+N(E_1)=2N(E_0)$ by [F1]. All are even, so [F3] makes $S$ separating.

2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. All double curves are circles, since $X$ is closed. Cut the sphere along them; a leaf region from [F5] is an original disk patch. Thus the finite set of all original disk patches of either family is nonempty. Retain these patches on $D_0\cup D_1$ with their half-switch collars [F1]. Choose one of smallest weight $m$; by [F4], $m>0$. Every trace circle bounds a unique disk cap on its particular full-resolution disk. For the frontier trace of any minimum patch $E$, let $B(E)$ be the disk cap at the other frontier of that same exchange annulus. By [F2] or [F3], $B(E)$ is disjoint from $E$, is adjacent to it, and has edge weight $m$.

Cut $B(E)$ along every trace circle in its interior. A trace cannot cross its outer boundary, so each remaining trace circle is wholly inside or outside it. The resulting planar regions, with their half-switch collars, are precisely original cut patches. Their adjacency graph is a tree, rooted at the region incident to the outer frontier of $B(E)$. Every non-root leaf is an original disk patch with just one trace-circle frontier and therefore has weight at least $m$. If the tree has one vertex, $B(E)$ itself is an original disk patch. Otherwise there is a non-root leaf, and there can be only one: two would already contribute at least $2m$ to the weight $m$ of $B(E)$. Denote that unique leaf by $L(E)$. Its weight is $m$, and every other region has zero edge weight, since these nonnegative counts partition the edge points of $B(E)$. The tree has no branching: a branch of degree at least three would give at least two non-root leaves. It is therefore a path from its root to $L(E)$. Consequently either $B(E)=L(E)$, or the closure of $B(E)\setminus L(E)$ is a nonempty zero-edge annulus between their two distinct frontier circles. This annulus is on the original resolved disk, without any ambient filling or cap isotopy.

The assignment $E\mapsto L(E)$ is a function on a finite nonempty set of minimum original disk patches. It has no fixed point because $E$ and $B(E)$ are disjoint. Iteration gives a cycle of distinct patches $E_1,\ldots,E_r$, $r\ge2$, with $L(E_i)=E_{i+1}$ and indices taken modulo $r$. Write $B_i=B(E_i)$ and $\alpha_i$ for its original double circle. The caps $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint. Caps on different full-resolution disks are disjoint automatically. On one disk they are disjoint or nested by [F5]. If $B_i\subset B_j$, then $E_{i+1}\subset B_j$; the uniqueness in step 2.1 gives $E_{i+1}=E_{j+1}$, impossible for distinct cycle indices. Equality is excluded by the same argument. There is no covering case: each cap is the interior disk bounded by its trace circle, so their union cannot contain the original disk boundary.

First suppose $B_i=E_{i+1}$ for some index. Its frontier is the other trace of the original circle $\alpha_i$, so $\alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_i$ and its opposite cap is $E_i$. The cycle is thus a two-cycle using one original circle, with both caps original disk patches. Label the transverse exchange rectangle with upper rays $0,1$ at its left and right frontiers and lower rays $2,3$. The regular resolved pairs are $(0,2),(1,3)$; the original unswitched pairs are $(0,3),(1,2)$. Adjacency says the two cap rays are both upper, after relabeling, namely $0,1$. They consequently belong to different original families. Each is a disk cut off by $\alpha_i$, and neither contains another double curve. Regularly switching just $\alpha_i$ swaps these two disk patches between the families. A sphere minus its disk patch is a disk, which capped by the other patch remains a sphere. An annulus minus its disk patch is a pair of pants, which capped by the other patch remains an annulus. Both images are embedded: there is no other double curve in either swapped patch, so every other original double curve still joins the unchanged portions of the different families. They are normal by the partial-resolution assertion [F1]. Neither vector is proportional to $d$, since a surface with vector proportional to the primitive vector $d$ is a union of disk copies, not a sphere or annulus. The new sphere-annulus diagram has one fewer double circle, contradicting reducedness.

We may therefore assume $R_i=\overline{B_i\setminus E_{i+1}}$ is a nonempty zero-edge annulus for every $i$. The circles $\alpha_i$ are distinct. Indeed each original circle has just its two frontier traces. If two distinct cycle patches came from it, they would occupy those two opposite caps, making each other's opposite caps and giving precisely the equality case of step 4.1. The annuli $R_i$ have pairwise disjoint interiors by step 3.1. Their outer boundaries are the $B_i$ traces; their inner boundaries are the $E_{i+1}$ traces. Every selected trace appears exactly once in this list, and none is the trace of another selected circle.

Leave exactly the original circles $\alpha_i$ unswitched, retaining the regular resolution at all other circles. Check its normalization directly in each selected transverse rectangle, using the labeling of step 4.1. The cap $E_i$ occupies upper ray $0$ at the left frontier; its complementary germ is lower ray $2$ and belongs to $R_{i-1}$, since $E_i\subset B_{i-1}$. The adjacent cap $B_i$ occupies upper ray $1$ at the right frontier; near that frontier its germ belongs to $R_i$. Its complementary ray $3$ is outside all the $B_j$, by their disjointness. Undoing the regular switch uses the original diagonal continuations $(0,3)$ and $(1,2)$. Thus it joins $E_i$ to the outside remainder and, separately, joins $R_i$ to $R_{i-1}$. This is an original unswitched continuation, never an irregular switch. Its description is consistent along the whole circle because the annular exchange has its given rectangular product neighborhood.

At every other circle keep both regular continuations. The frontier of the union of the $R_i$ consists solely of the selected trace circles listed in step 5.1. Hence an unselected regular trace has either both incident parts in this union or neither: the frontier crosses no such trace. At selected traces the diagonal check of step 6.1 joins every annular frontier to another annular frontier. The annuli, with these short continuations, therefore form a union of entire normalization components of this actual partial regular resolution. This union is nonempty because each $R_i$ is nonempty, and it misses every original edge because all $R_i$ and switching neighborhoods do. Choosing one of its finitely many components yields a nonempty zero-edge normalization component. That contradicts [F1], since every such component contains a genuine normal tetrahedral disk and therefore one of its original normal vertices. The contradiction rules out the hypothetical reduced sphere-annulus diagram. No sphere was filled by a ball, and no normal parallelism of exterior exchange caps was inferred.

Suppose there is an original double circle. An innermost such circle on the original disk $X$ cuts off an interior disk with no other double circle. It contains no proper double arc: the endpoints of such an arc lie on $\partial X$, outside this cap, so entry would require crossing its frontier, contrary to the disjoint double-curve position. It is therefore an original interior disk patch. Choose smallest positive weight $m$ among all such patches on both families, using [F3]. For each chosen minimum patch $E$, its annular exchange has an opposite disk cap $B(E)$ in the full resolution; its disjointness, adjacency and weight $m$ follow from the same-copy or between-copy suppliers in [F1]. No proper trace enters $B(E)$ either: its boundary is a circle in the interior of one resolved disk, all proper trace endpoints lie on that disk's original boundary, and traces are disjoint.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

derivations.claim: Resolve every curve except the chosen proper arc regularly. Only the pieces of $D_0,D_1$ incident to it can be affected by undoing it. Cutting their proper traces gives four disks $E_0,K_0,E_1,K_1$. In the transverse rectangle label the upper left and right rays $0,1$, and the lower left and right rays $2,3$. The full regular pairing is $(0,2),(1,3)$; the original unswitched diagonals are $(0,3),(1,2)$; the irregular pairing is $(0,1),(2,3)$. Thus the inverse diagram has two parametrizing disks $U=E_0\cup K_1$ and $V=K_0\cup E_1$, with their joining strips understood. Each is embedded: the only remaining double arc joins one branch from each component, and neither component has a self-intersection. They are normal by [F1], with $v(U)+v(V)=2d$. The irregular resolution instead gives two embedded PL disks $W=E_0\cup E_1$ and $Z=K_0\cup K_1$. All these joins are along proper boundary intervals, so the disk topology follows by gluing two disk parameters along an interval. All switching neighborhoods miss the original edges; in particular $w(W)+w(Z)=2w(D)$.

The disks $W,Z$ cannot both be essential. Indeed their irregular resolution has a return parametrizing face arc by [F2]. It lies wholly on one of these two disk components, say $W$, and is embedded there because $W$ is embedded. If both were essential, normalize $W$ strictly decreasingly by [F3] and $Z$ nonincreasingly. To spell out the strict alternative, if a preliminary move or discard loses an edge point of $W$, strict decrease is already obtained; otherwise its face curve and the return arc persist, and the edge bigon removes two intersections while retaining an essential disk. The two normal outputs then satisfy $w(W^*)+w(Z^*)<2w(D)$. Both must have weight at least $w(D)$, a contradiction. Consequently at least one irregular output has null-homotopic boundary. This is a joint weight argument, not the old bound of one output by the entire two-disk input weight.

Mark the exchange disk as a rectangle with frontier intervals $\alpha_i:p_i\to q_i$ and boundary connectors $b:p_0\to p_1$, $c:q_0\to q_1$ in $\partial M$. Let $u,u'$ be the original-boundary arcs of $E_0,K_0$, both directed from $p_0$ to $q_0$. Transport the original-boundary arcs of $E_1,K_1$ by $a\mapsto b\,a\,c^{-1}$, obtaining paths $v,v'$ with the same endpoints. The original disk boundaries are $u(u')^{-1}$ and $v(v')^{-1}$, up to basepoint transport, and both are essential. The inverse diagonal boundaries are $u(v')^{-1}$ and $u'v^{-1}$; the irregular boundaries are $uv^{-1}$ and $u'(v')^{-1}$, up to conjugacy or inversion. A null-homotopic path loop $a_1a_2^{-1}$ is precisely a homotopy between $a_1,a_2$ with endpoints fixed. If either diagonal loop and either irregular loop were null, their common path would give either $u\simeq u'$ or $v\simeq v'$ with endpoints fixed. For example $u\simeq v'$ and $u\simeq v$ imply $v\simeq v'$; pairing $u\simeq v'$ with $u'\simeq v'$ instead gives $u\simeq u'$. The other two cases interchange primes. Each contradicts an essential original boundary. Step 2.1 supplies a null irregular loop, so neither diagonal loop is null: both $U,V$ are essential. The connectors are those of the actual rectangle, not arbitrary path identifications.

The two essential normal disks $U,V$ have weights summing to $2w(D)$, so least weight forces each to have weight $w(D)$. Their vectors sum to $2d$ by step 1.1. At the first coordinate differing from $d$, one would be smaller and the other larger. Lexicographic minimality among essential normal disks of this weight excludes that possibility. Hence $v(U)=v(V)=d$.

The original strips are edge-free, and the four cut caps partition the original disk edge points. Thus $N(U)=N(E_0)+N(K_1)=N(D)$, whereas $N(D_1)=N(E_1)+N(K_1)=N(D)$. Subtraction gives $N(E_0)=N(E_1)$. The complementary equalities similarly give $N(K_0)=N(K_1)$. Each of these four caps is cut from one normal disk by the selected proper trace alone, so [F4] makes its total edge weight positive. This proves all assertions without identifying any raw cap replacement with an ambiently parallel normal cap.

boundaries.reason: One actual proper exchange between distinct disk copies is required.

boundaries.evidence: Proof, steps 2.1: The equality weight case still has a return arc on an embedded irregular disk, giving strict improvement.
Proof, steps 1.1: Isolating the one selected proper arc produces four cut disks and two inverse diagonal disks.
Proof, steps 2.1, 3.1: Both irregular disks cannot be essential; explicit boundary words then force both inverse disks essential.
Proof, steps 3.1: Boundary connectors b,c transport all four endpoint paths before null-homotopy cancellation.
Proof, steps 4.1, 5.1: Finite normal replacements plus least-weight/lexicographic minimality give exact equal cap and remainder counts.

Let $M$ be a compact PL three-manifold with a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. Among its essential normal disks choose one of least edge weight, and among those choose $F$ with lexicographically least normal vector. Then $F$ is fundamental in the original seven-coordinate system of $T$.

Consequently, if $M$ contains a properly embedded PL disk whose boundary is not null-homotopic in $\partial M$, it contains such a disk that is a fundamental normal surface. No ambient orientability, irreducibility or exclusion of projective planes is required, and no choice hypothesis is introduced.

Let $D$ be a fundamental normal disk in a finite simplicial triangulation $T$. If its vector $d$ does not lie on an extreme ray of $C(T)$, there are connected embedded normal surfaces $X,Y$, neither with vector proportional to $d$, and an actual original-triangulation regular diagram whose full resolution has vector

$$v(X)+v(Y)=2d.$$

Its full resolution consists of two disks with boundary curves homotopic to $\partial D$. Exactly one of the following occurs:

1. $X$ and $Y$ are disks.
2. One is a sphere and the other is an annulus; both annulus boundary curves are homotopic to $\partial D$.

If $D$ is in addition a least-weight essential normal disk with lexicographically least vector at that weight, the first case has at least one disk with null-homotopic boundary. This is a reduction of the vertex obligation, not a proof that either case is impossible.

Let $D$ be a fundamental essential normal disk in a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Suppose $D$ has least edge weight among all essential normal disks, and lexicographically least normal vector among those of that weight; put $d=v(D)$.

There is no actual original-triangulation regular-sum diagram $X\cup Y$ of the following reduced kind. The surfaces $X,Y$ are respectively a connected normal sphere and a connected normal annulus, their vectors are not proportional to $d$, and $v(X)+v(Y)=2d$. All partial regular resolutions retain normal tetrahedral disk pieces, and the full resolution consists of two copies $D_0,D_1$ of $D$. The number of original double circles is least among diagrams of this kind, including diagrams obtained by regularly switching a subset when the two resulting families remain an embedded sphere and annulus.

No irreducibility, orientability or choice hypothesis is required. The conclusion excludes this sphere-annulus branch only; it does not exclude a sum of two disk summands.

Let $D$ be a least-weight essential fundamental normal disk with lexicographically least vector at that weight, in a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold; put $d=v(D)$. Let $X,Y$ be connected embedded normal disks with neither vector proportional to $d$ and $v(X)+v(Y)=2d$.

Suppose an actual original-triangulation regular-sum diagram for them has full resolution $D_0\cup D_1$, the two disk copies of $D$, and retains genuine normal tetrahedral disk pieces under every partial regular resolution. Choose it with the smallest number of double curves among eligible two-disk diagrams, including those obtained by a partial regular switch when its resulting disk families are embedded and nonproportional to $d$.

Then every original double curve is a proper arc. At least one of $\partial X,\partial Y$ is null-homotopic in $\partial M$. The conclusion does not exclude those remaining proper exchanges, and assumes neither orientability nor irreducibility nor a choice principle.

Let an actual original-triangulation regular normal diagram have full embedded resolution $F$. Suppose a component $D$ of $F$ is an essential normal disk, is fundamental, and has least weight among all essential normal disks in that triangulation.

Choose one original double circle or proper double arc whose two trace curves in the full resolution both lie on $D$. Assume its exchange surface is respectively an annulus or a disk with its usual rectangular switching neighborhood. Then the traces bound disjoint adjacent disk caps on $D$. For a proper exchange disk these are the two outer caps cut off by the two trace arcs. For an exchange annulus the unique two caps bounded by the trace circles are disjoint and adjacent.

Here adjacency means that the two cap germs occupy the same side of the exchange surface in its switching neighborhood. The result concerns these actual original-diagram exchanges, not an arbitrary separately supplied spanning annulus. No irreducibility, orientability or sphere-separation assumption is required.

In an actual original-triangulation regular diagram let a full-resolution component $D$ be a fundamental essential normal disk, of least weight among essential normal disks and with lexicographically least normal vector at that weight. Let an annular or proper disk exchange belonging to this diagram have both trace components on $D$.

Its disjoint adjacent disk caps $E,E'$ have equal counts on every original triangulation edge and positive total edge weight: $N(E)=N(E')$ and $w(E)=w(E')>0$. Replacing either cap by a nearby copy of the other along the exchange gives an embedded proper PL disk with essential boundary. Both replacements have edge-count vector $N(D)$, and their componentwise edge-nonincreasing normal replacements have exactly the original normal vector $v(D)$.

For a proper disk exchange, the alternative disk obtained by joining its two outer caps along the exchange has null-homotopic boundary in $\partial M$. No assertion of normal parallelism of $E,E'$ is made.

Let $D$ be a least-weight essential normal disk in a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold, with lexicographically least normal vector among essential disks at that weight; put $d=v(D)$. In an actual original-triangulation regular diagram whose full resolution consists of two disjoint disks $D_0,D_1$ with vector $d$, choose an original proper double arc whose exchange disk joins a trace on $D_0$ to a trace on $D_1$.

Switch every other original curve regularly and leave this arc unswitched. Its two affected parametrizing components are embedded essential normal disks, each with vector $d$. In the transverse exchange rectangle choose the cap on the upper side at each frontier, denoting these adjacent caps by $E_0,E_1$; write $K_i$ for the complementary disk in $D_i$. Then

$$N(E_0)=N(E_1)>0,\qquad N(K_0)=N(K_1)>0,$$

where equality is componentwise on the original global edges and positivity means positive total weight. The two original diagonal disks are $E_0$ joined to $K_1$ and $K_0$ joined to $E_1$, along their original exchange continuations. The opposite, irregular pairing gives two embedded proper PL disks, at least one with null-homotopic boundary. This holds without fundamentalness, irreducibility, orientability or a choice principle. No normal parallelism of the caps is asserted.

For a finite tetrahedral triangulation, let $B$ record the six local edge-intersection counts in every tetrahedron from its seven normal coordinates. Let $u,v,d$ be nonnegative real normal-coordinate arrays, each using at most one quadrilateral type in each tetrahedron. They need not satisfy matching equations. If $\alpha,\beta>0$ and

$$\alpha Bu+\beta Bv=(\alpha+\beta)Bd,$$

then

$$\alpha u+\beta v=(\alpha+\beta)d.$$

In particular, if $u,v,d$ are actual normal-surface vectors, the hypothesis may be checked on their global triangulation-edge intersection counts. If those counts for $u$ and $v$ average to those for $d$, then their normal-coordinate vectors also average to $d$.

If $d$ is lexicographically least in any set of vectors containing $u,v,d$, this averaging identity forces $u=v=d$. Thus two essential normal disks of the same least edge weight whose edge counts average to those of a lexicographically least such disk must have exactly that disk's normal vector.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold $M$, and let $F$ be a normal surface. Its normal disks form polygonal cells with three or four sides. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite disjoint family of PL simple closed curves and properly embedded PL arcs on $F$. Suppose $\Lambda$ misses the normal-cell vertices, is transverse to the cell edges, and meets each normal disk in disjoint properly embedded arcs whose endpoints are on distinct sides of that disk.

Cut $F$ along $\Lambda$, retaining separate boundary copies of each cut. Let $P$ be the compact completion of one resulting component, and suppose $P\cap\partial F$ has $b$ components, all proper arcs. Define its edge weight by $w(P)=|P\cap T^{(1)}|$. If $w(P)=0$, its polygonal pieces have $k_j\ge2$ trace sides and satisfy

$$\chi(P)=\frac b2+\sum_j\left(1-\frac{k_j}{2}\right)\le\frac b2.$$

Consequently, if $P$ is a disk and $b\le1$, then $w(P)>0$. This applies in particular to disk patches of a proper normal sum: an interior disk patch has one closed trace frontier and $b=0$, and a boundary disk patch has one trace-arc frontier and $b=1$.

The trace hypothesis is satisfied by the usual exchange rectangles: in each tetrahedron a rectangle has two opposite sides on distinct normal disks and the other two sides in distinct tetrahedral faces. No orientability, irreducibility or projective-plane hypothesis is imposed.

Let $T$ be a finite simplicial triangulation of a compact PL three-manifold. Let $x,y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{7t}$ be admissible normal-coordinate vectors such that $x+y$ satisfies the quadrilateral condition. There are embedded proper normal surfaces $X,Y$ with vectors $x,y$, a finite transverse double-curve diagram $X\cup Y$ disjoint from $T^{(1)}$, and pairwise disjoint switching neighborhoods with these properties:

1. In each tetrahedron all double arcs join distinct faces. At every such arc the chosen regular switch preserves the unordered pair of normal disk types.
2. The choices agree through every crossed face and hence along each entire double circle or proper double arc.
3. Any partial selection of whole-curve regular switches gives a finite immersed normal-disk diagram with only the unswitched double curves and no branch points. Its total vector is $x+y$. Switches in disjoint neighborhoods commute.
4. Switching all curves gives an embedded proper normal surface $F$ with $v(F)=x+y$ and $w(F)=w(X)+w(Y)$.

The realization of an admissible vector determines its abstract surface and its boundary curves up to PL homeomorphism of the surface and homotopy of the corresponding boundary curves in $\partial M$. In particular, if $x+y=v(D)$ for a connected essential normal disk $D$, then $F$ is a connected essential normal disk. Thus every nontrivial coordinate decomposition of such a disk has an actual regular normal-sum diagram of this kind in the original triangulation.

No irreducibility, orientability, sphere-separation or choice hypothesis is required. The assertion concerns these explicitly constructed realizations, without claiming an ambient isotopy between arbitrary prior realizations.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation.

derivations.claim: Suppose $d$ were nonvertex and take the reduced diagram [F1]. By [F2], its two summands $X,Y$ are disks and its double curves are proper arcs. There is at least one: with none, each summand would survive as one full-resolution disk and have vector $d$. Each original disk meets the other, so its cut tree has at least two leaves. Every such original leaf patch has positive weight by [F5]. Let $m>0$ be the least weight among all these leaves. There are at least four leaves altogether, and their weights are part of the total $2w(D)$; hence $w(D)\ge2m$. Neither resolved disk is untouched by all traces. An untouched full-resolution component would also be an unchanged connected original summand with vector $d$, contrary to nonproportionality.

For any minimum leaf $E$, let $\alpha$ be its sole original double arc. Its retained trace cuts off that same leaf on its resolved disk. If the other frontier trace lies on this disk, $E$ is an outer cap: it contains no other trace and therefore cannot contain the other frontier. Take the disjoint adjacent outer cap $B(E)$ from [F3]. If the other trace lies on the other resolved disk, take its unique cap adjacent to $E$, again by [F3]. In both cases $B(E)$ is disjoint from $E$ and $N(B(E))=N(E)$, so $w(B(E))=m$. Cut $B(E)$ along all traces in its interior, rooting the dual tree at its exterior trace side. Every non-root leaf is an original leaf disk patch and has weight at least $m$. If the tree has one vertex, $B(E)$ is itself a leaf. Otherwise nonnegativity and total weight $m$ force exactly one non-root leaf $L(E)$, of weight $m$, and all other regions have zero edge count. The tree is a path, since branching would yield two non-root leaves. Thus either $B(E)=L(E)$ or $R(E)=\overline{B(E)\setminus L(E)}$ is a nonempty zero-edge rectangle with two trace sides and two original-boundary sides. In either case $N(L(E))=N(E)$. These are actual cut patches on the original resolved disks; no three-dimensional cap parallelism is asserted.

The equality $B(E)=L(E)$ is impossible for any minimum leaf. In this case both adjacent opposite caps are original leaf disk patches at the same original arc. In a transverse rectangle label upper left and right rays $0,1$, and lower left and right rays $2,3$. Full regular pairs are $(0,2),(1,3)$ and original unswitched pairs are $(0,3),(1,2)$. Adjacency makes the leaf rays $0,1$, so they belong to different original families. Regularly switching just this arc swaps those two leaf disks between $X,Y$. Removing a boundary end disk from a disk leaves a disk; attaching the other end disk along the vacated interval again gives a disk. The swapped patches contain no other double curve, so every remaining curve still joins the unchanged parts of different families. The two new families are therefore embedded normal disks, and all their later partial resolutions are old partial resolutions with this arc already switched. The two swapped leaves have equal edge counts by [F3]. Thus each new disk has exactly its own original family's edge-count vector, and [F4] shows that its normal vector is unchanged. Both new vectors remain nonproportional to $d$. This gives an eligible diagram with one fewer double curve, contradicting reducedness.

First suppose $w(D)>2m$. The finite function $E\mapsto L(E)$ on the minimum leaves has no fixed point because $E$ is disjoint from $B(E)$. Iteration gives a cycle of distinct leaves $E_1,\ldots,E_r$, $r\ge2$, with $E_{i+1}=L(E_i)$; write $B_i=B(E_i)$ and $\alpha_i$ for its exchange arc. The caps $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint. On different resolved disks this is automatic. On one disk nesting would put two distinct minimum leaves in one opposite cap, contrary to uniqueness in step 2.1; covering would give $w(D)\le2m$, contrary to this case. These exhaust overlaps by [F6]. The $\alpha_i$ are distinct. At one original arc, two minimum leaf caps on the same frontier but opposite sides would cover its resolved disk and likewise contradict $w(D)>2m$. Minimum leaf caps on opposite frontiers must be adjacent: the nonadjacent alternative is the complement of the adjacent weight-$m$ cap, of weight $w(D)-m>m$. If two adjacent opposite caps at this arc were leaves, each would be the other's entire opposite cap, excluded by step 3.1. Thus no arc can occur twice in the cycle.

Each $R_i=\overline{B_i\setminus E_{i+1}}$ is a nonempty zero-edge rectangle by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Their interiors are pairwise disjoint by step 4.1. Leave precisely the cycle arcs $\alpha_i$ unswitched and retain the regular resolution elsewhere. Check the original diagonals with the four-ray labeling of step 3.1. At $\alpha_i$, $E_i$ occupies upper left ray $0$; the complementary lower left ray $2$ belongs to $R_{i-1}$. The adjacent cap $B_i$ occupies upper right ray $1$, belonging near that frontier to $R_i$; its complementary ray $3$ is outside all the $B_j$. Hence the original diagonals $(0,3),(1,2)$ join $E_i$ to the outside remainder and join $R_i$ to $R_{i-1}$. No irregular switch is used. At every other trace the regular continuation has either both incident parts among the $R_i$ or neither, since the only frontier traces of their union are the selected ones. Thus these nonempty rectangles with their short continuations form a union of whole normalization components, with any remaining boundary lying in $\partial M$. This union misses all original edges. It contradicts the positive-weight property of actual partial normal resolutions [F5]. The case $w(D)>2m$ is impossible.

It remains that $w(D)=2m$. There are exactly four original leaf patches, each of weight $m$, and every other original patch has zero edge counts: each original disk has at least two leaves and their total weight is already $4m=2w(D)$. Each original disk's dual tree has exactly two leaves and is therefore a path. The resolved disks' cut patches are the same original patches, with the same trace-side counts. Each resolved disk has traces by step 1.1, so each has at least two leaves. Thus each has exactly two of these four leaf patches, all its other patches have zero edge counts, and its dual tree is also a path. A cap at any trace on such a resolved disk consists of its one end leaf and some zero-edge interior patches. Its count vector is precisely that end leaf's count vector.

There must be an exchange between the two resolved disks. Otherwise every original inverse continuation preserves its resolved-disk label. Each connected original component would then use patches from only one $D_i$. There are exactly two original components and both $D_i$ supply nonempty patches, so each original component uses all patches of one $D_i$. Its edge counts are $N(D)$, and [F4] makes its vector $d$, a contradiction. Now any same-copy exchange has disjoint outer caps by [F3]; on that resolved path these contain its two different end leaves. Their equal cap counts make those two leaf count vectors equal. A between-copy exchange equates an adjacent cap pair and its complementary pair by [F3], so propagates this equality to both leaves of the other resolved disk. Then all four leaves have one count vector $a$, and both original disks and both resolved disks have count vector $2a$ by step 6.1. Again [F4] contradicts original nonproportionality. Consequently every exchange in this remaining case joins different resolved disks.

Choose one such exchange. Label the two end leaves of each resolved path $A,B$ so the adjacent caps at this exchange contain the respective $A$ leaves. By [F3] their leaf counts agree, say $a$, and the complementary $B$ leaf counts also agree, say $b$. If $a=b$, all four counts agree and the preceding contradiction applies. Suppose $a\ne b$. At every exchange, the cap on the $A$ side of its trace on $D_0$ must be adjacent to the $A$ cap on $D_1$: adjacency to its $B$ cap would force $a=b$. Orient the two finite resolved dual patch paths from their $A$ leaf to their $B$ leaf. Each interior patch then has one incoming frontier on its $A$ side and one outgoing frontier on its $B$ side. At an exchange, the original diagonal continuations pair an $A$-side patch germ from one resolved disk to a $B$-side germ from the other. These are exactly an outgoing and an incoming frontier; thus the directions paste on the ORIGINAL dual patch paths after all original continuations are restored. Each original path must start at an $A$ leaf and end at a $B$ leaf. This is only a direction on finite graphs, not an orientation assumption on the ambient manifold or its surfaces. Each original disk consequently has edge counts $a+b=N(D)$, since all its other patches have zero edge counts. By [F4] both its vectors equal $d$, the final contradiction.

Both possible values $w(D)>2m$ and $w(D)=2m$ have been excluded, so the assumed nonvertex decomposition cannot exist. Hence $d$ lies on an extreme ray of $C(T)$. Fundamentalness makes its coordinate gcd one: a larger common divisor would split it into two nonzero admissible integer vectors. Thus it is the primitive ray vector. For the consequence, normalize the supplied essential PL disk by [[lem-essential-pl-disks-admit-normal-replacements]]. Choose a least normal disk weight in the resulting nonempty set, and then minimize the $7t$ coordinates successively; these are finitely many natural-number minima and require no choice principle. Apply the proved assertion to this disk. All switches, counts, matching coordinates and partial normal pieces belonged to the original triangulation throughout.

Proof, steps 4.1, 9.1: Finite leaf cycles, fundamentalness and gcd primitivity finish the same-cone argument without choice.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq 1$, and $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$.
For every row $i$ and every column $j$,

$$\det(A)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_{ik}C_{ik}(A) \quad\text{and}\quad \det(A)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_{kj}C_{kj}(A).$$
Every finite matrix over a field is row equivalent to a matrix in row echelon form. The reduction can be obtained by the Gaussian elimination algorithm.

Finite products are taken in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$ of
[[lem-units-of-z]] as in [[def-monoid-finite-product]], and a **list of primes
of length $r$** is a function $p : r \to \mathbb{Z}$ on the von Neumann natural
$r = \{0,\dots,r-1\}$ with every $p_i$ prime ([[def-prime]]).

1. **Existence.** Every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 1$ is $\prod_{i<r} p_i$
   for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and some list $p$ of primes of length $r$
   ([[thm-prime-factorisation-exists]]).
2. **Uniqueness up to order.** Let $p$ and $q$ be lists of primes, of lengths
   $r$ and $s$. If

   $$\prod_{i<r} p_i \;=\; \prod_{j<s} q_j ,$$

   then $r = s$, and there is a permutation $\pi \in \operatorname{Sym}(r)$
   ([[def-symmetric-group]]) with

   $$q_i \;=\; p_{\pi(i)} \qquad \text{for every } i < r .$$

At $r = 0$ clause 2 says that the only list of primes whose product is $1$ is the
empty list, and the permutation condition is vacuous.

Let $m,n$ be positive integers, $a,b\in\mathbb Z$, and
$d:=\gcd(m,n)$. The simultaneous system

$$x\equiv a\pmod m,\qquad x\equiv b\pmod n$$

is solvable if and only if $d\mid(a-b)$. If it is solvable, all its solutions
form one congruence class modulo $mn/d$.

In particular, when $m,n$ are coprime, every pair of classes
$[a]_m,[b]_n$ determines a unique simultaneous class $[x]_{mn}$. This includes
$m=1$ or $n=1$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $b > 0$. Define $\Phi : \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ by

$$\Phi(u,v) \;=\; \begin{cases} (v,\; u - qv) & \text{if } v > 0, \\ (u,v) & \text{if } v \le 0, \end{cases}$$

where in the first clause $q$ is the unique quotient of $u$ by $v$ given by
[[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], so that $u - qv$ is the remainder and
$0 \le u - qv < v$.

Let $R : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ be the unique function
with $R(0) = (a,b)$ and $R(\sigma(k)) = \Phi(R(k))$ supplied by the recursion
theorem ([[thm-recursion]]). Write $R(k) = (a_k, b_k)$; the sequence
$b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots$ is the **remainder descent** from $(a,b)$.

Then:

1. $b_k \ge 0$ for every $k$, and $b_{\sigma(k)} < b_k$ whenever $b_k > 0$;
2. $\gcd(a_k, b_k) = \gcd(a,b)$ for every $k$
   ([[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]]);
3. there is a least $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $b_N = 0$, and $N \ne 0$; writing
   $N = \sigma(M)$, the value $b_M$ is the **last nonzero remainder**, and
   $b_M > 0$;
4. $a_N = b_M = \gcd(a,b)$.

So the descent terminates, and the last nonzero remainder is $\gcd(a,b)$.

derivations.claim: Every $d\times d$ minor, $0\le d\le n$, has absolute determinant at most $d!\le(n+2)^n$ by [F1], interpreting the empty determinant as $1$. Put $B=(n+2)^n$, $M=16(n+2)^4$, $L_M=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,M)$ and $P_M=\prod_{p\le M,\ p\text{ prime}}p$. All these are integers; only $B$ and the small bound $M$, not the complete integers $L_M,P_M$, will be stored.

The bound $L_M\ge2^{M-1}/M$ is elementary. For $N=M-1$ and any $0\le j\le N$, counting multiples of $p,p^2,\ldots$ in factorials gives $$v_p\binom Nj=\sum_{a\ge1}\left(\left\lfloor\frac N{p^a}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac j{p^a}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{N-j}{p^a}\right\rfloor\right).$$ Each summand is zero or one and vanishes for $p^a>N$. Thus this valuation is at most $\lfloor\log_p N\rfloor$, at most the exponent of $p$ in $L_M$. Unique factorization makes every $\binom Nj$ divide $L_M$. The sum of the $M$ binomial coefficients is $2^{M-1}$, so at least one is at least $2^{M-1}/M$, proving the bound.

The exponent of every prime in $L_M$ is at most $\log_2 M$. Consequently $L_M\le P_M^{\log_2 M}$ and $$\log_2P_M\ge\frac{M-1-\log_2 M}{\log_2 M}.$$ For the chosen $M$, $\log_2M=4+4\log_2(n+2)\le4(n+2)$ and $M-1-\log_2M\ge M/2$. The displayed lower bound is therefore at least $2(n+2)^3$, which is greater than $n\log_2(n+2)+3$. Hence $P_M>8B$. Enumerate integers $2,\ldots,M$, testing each for primality by trial division up to its square root. There are polynomially many trials on $O(\log(n+2))$-bit integers. Stop the prime stream as soon as its running product $Q$ exceeds $2B$; the bound just proved guarantees that this happens by $M$. Immediately before the last multiplication $Q\le2B$, so the final product is at most $2BM$. The product accumulator thus has $O(n\log(n+2))$ bits.

For a specified square submatrix $D$, compute its determinant modulo each successive prime by [F2]. Every nonzero residue $h$ modulo a prime $p$ is a unit, with an explicit small-space inverse: apply Euclidean descent to $(p,h)$, maintaining $r_i=s_i p+t_i h$ with initial coefficient pairs $(1,0),(0,1)$ and updates $(s_{i+1},t_{i+1})=(s_{i-1},t_{i-1})-q_i(s_i,t_i)$. The last nonzero remainder is $1$, since a common divisor of $p$ and $0<h<p$ is $1$ by primality. Its coefficient $t_i$ is an inverse modulo $p$. This also constructs Bézout identities for arbitrary integer pairs, and induction gives one for any finite list and its gcd. Thus elimination is over a field; if a pivot cannot be found in a square trailing block, the determinant residue is zero. Row interchanges change its sign, and otherwise the product of the unscaled pivots gives the determinant. This uses one matrix of $O(n^2)$ residues, each with $O(\log(n+2))$ bits, and $O(n^3)$ modular operations per prime. Combine each residue $r$ with the previous representative $a$ modulo $Q$ by $$a_{\rm new}=a+Q\left((r-a)Q^{-1}\bmod p\right),\qquad Q_{\rm new}=Qp.$$ The inverse exists by [F3] and is computed from $Q\bmod p$, so its Euclidean inputs have only $O(\log(n+2))$ bits. After $Q>2B$, the unique representative in $[-B,B]$ is the integer determinant by step 1.1. Only the current residue matrix, the two reconstruction integers and small counters are retained; no list of primes, residues or previous matrices is stored.

For rank, perform prime-field elimination on the original rectangular matrix over the same prime stream, retaining the largest rank found and the original row indices of a basis attaining it. These indices can be selected during elimination without a transformation matrix: after the first $k$ pivots, the unselected rows have only had combinations of the $k$ selected original rows subtracted, so the next pivot row is independent of them exactly when its remainder is nonzero. The rank equals the largest order of a nonzero minor over either field. To see the needed direction directly, elimination selects $r$ original independent rows and $r$ pivot columns; their $r\times r$ submatrix becomes triangular with nonzero pivots after invertible row operations, so it has nonzero determinant. Conversely, $r+1$ rows are dependent and multilinearity makes every minor of that order zero. A nonzero modular minor is a nonzero integer minor, so every modular rank is at most the rational rank $r$. If $r>0$, choose any nonzero $r\times r$ integer minor $d$. If all sampled ranks were less than $r$, every sampled prime would divide $d$. Their product $Q>2B$ would divide $d$, contradicting $0<|d|\le B$. Therefore the maximum modular rank is exactly $r$, and its retained original rows form a rational row basis. For $r=0$ every entry and modular rank is zero.

If the number of columns is $b$ and the rank is $b-1$, let $R$ consist of the $b-1$ independent original rows from step 4.2. For $1\le j\le b$, compute $w_j=(-1)^{j+1}\det R_{\widehat j}$ by step 4.1, retaining the vector $w$. Some cofactor is nonzero because $R$ has full row rank. Expanding the determinant of the matrix obtained by adding any row of $R$ as a duplicate row gives $Rw=0$ by [F1]. Every row of $A$ lies in the rational row span of $R$, hence $Aw=0$. Divide $w$ by the positive gcd of its entries; the result is primitive. If a rational multiple $cu$ of a primitive integer vector $u$ is integral, a Bézout identity $\sum_j a_j u_j=1$ gives $c=\sum_j a_j(cu_j)\in\mathbb Z$, so it generates all integer points on that line. Either overall sign may be selected. For $b=1$, $R$ is empty and its one empty cofactor is $1$, as required.

All counters bounded by $M$ have $O(\log(n+2))$ bits. The residue matrix uses $O(n^2\log(n+2))$ bits, the row-index list $O(n\log(n+2))$ bits, and each reconstructed determinant has $O(n\log(n+2))$ bits. The at most $n$ retained cofactors therefore also use $O(n^2\log(n+2))$ bits; the same residue matrix storage is reused for each one. Trial division, at most $M$ prime eliminations per determinant and at most $n$ cofactor determinants take polynomially many arithmetic operations on polynomial-length integers. Binary multiplication and long division take polynomial time; the Euclidean descent takes $O(\ell)$ divisions on $\ell$-bit inputs because after two nonzero remainder steps the remainder is at most half its previous value. The coefficient-tracking algorithm is needed computationally only for inverses with inputs less than $p\le M$. It has $O(\log p)$ updates and quotients at most $p$, so even the crude coefficient bound obtained by multiplying $2p$ per update has $O((\log p)^2)$ bits. Thus these small inverses need only $O((\log(n+2))^2)$ extra workspace, which fits the asserted bound. Normalizing the cofactor vector needs only ordinary remainder gcds on $O(n\log(n+2))$-bit integers; the existential Bézout identity used to prove primitivity need not be computed or stored. All integer multiplications and divisions can be done by the digit-by-digit algorithms using a constant number of buffers of the operand/output lengths. Thus reconstruction, inversions, gcd normalization, rank and kernel calculations all have polynomial bit time and the asserted workspace. Empty matrices are handled directly by rank zero and empty determinant one. This proves all claims.

boundaries.evidence: Proof, steps 1.1, 6.1: Zero-row/zero-column matrices have rank zero and the 0×0 determinant is one.
Proof, steps 4.2: Rank zero is handled directly because every entry and modular rank is zero.
Proof, steps 5.1: For b=1 and rank zero, the single empty cofactor is one and generates the kernel.
Proof, steps 4.1, 4.2: Singular matrices give zero determinant residues; rank is maximized over primes, not computed modulo a composite.
Proof, steps 3.1, 4.1: Stop at Q>2B; final Q≤2BM and signed reconstruction uniquely recovers the bounded integer.
